Filtering in these scenarios is complicated by the large amounts of data and constraints imposed by the complex system's physics. Many current methods rely on approximate numerical solutions to the underlying partial differential equations, but these approximations can be problematic due to the potential for model discrepancy and the need to maintain accuracy while reducing computational costs. To address these challenges, we propose a novel EKF filter that leverages convex optimization to improve estimation at minimal additional computational cost. Our approach modifies the EKF to reduce a series of non-convex optimization problems, developing a Birkhoff-Varga filter instead. This algorithm retains the linearization and Gaussian assumption core to the standard EKF, ensuring it remains the most efficient and effective filter for low-noise environments, even though it may not be the ideal choice in noisy conditions. To validate our theoretical findings, we analyze a range of test simulations, including the linear diffusion equation and the non-linear shallow water equations. We introduce a novel approach, guided by physical constraints, for training a neural network to identify materials from a single image, independent of the image's perspective and orientation. By leveraging physics-based rendering, we simulate material appearances under various lighting conditions and train the network to recognize a material from just one image. Our approach also compensates for image perspectives and orientations by training the network to recognize a material from multiple, randomly rotated images. This two-pronged strategy enables a neural network to identify materials regardless of the image's viewpoint or rotation. Our studies demonstrate that these methods are highly effective: training the network with just one image results in nearly perfect material identification, and that this single image can be taken from any perspective and at any orientation. Additionally, our one-shot material identification method performs well on a large and a small dataset, respectively. Our material identification framework is available online for further research and development. Our research demonstrates that material identification can be simplified to a single-shot procedure, comparable to identifying a well-known person's photograph. Importantly, our study highlights that material identification requires more than just collecting data; it demands an integrated framework of data collection, simulation, and learning methods. Our approach, rooted in physics, marks an essential step in collecting data for material identification, a challenge prevalent in computer vision and robotics. Our algorithm's success encourages the broader scientific community to address material identification. Initially, nucleon distribution densities, such as the parton distribution functions (PDFs), generalized parton distribution functions (GPDs), and nucleon matrix elements of tensor operators, are examined in detail. Specifically, the impact of noncommutativity on the nucleon's spin, kinetic energy, and strange content is analyzed in depth. These results are then found to provide insight into the effects of space-time deformations on nucleon properties, facilitating an understanding of lattice QCD observations. Additionally, quantitative relationships between nucleon kinetic energy and noncommutativity, as well as between strange content and noncommutativity, are established. These findings are expected to be consistent with future lattice QCD data. Recent advancements in dialogue processing tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level text data struggle to capture underlying semantic interpretations, resulting in subpar performance on more challenging tasks requiring deeper dialogue understanding. To fill this gap, a new method called MB-BERT is introduced, designed to capture nuanced meaning through a two-stage training process that fine-tunes BERT with meaning-informed objectives. This approach enables dialogue models to excel in a range of tasks including parsing dialogue structure and identifying key concepts and emotions, even when operating with limited context and noisy, hand-coded data. Results demonstrate that MB-BERT outperforms alternative models in multiple tests and can effectively perform semantic analysis and text comprehension in various dialogue processing applications. The proposed technique also offers significant potential for application across diverse domains due to its lightweight design and the absence of domain-specific training data. Importantly, MB-BERT allows users to seamlessly integrate new meanings into the model by simply re-training it using corresponding lexical inputs, without the need for manual engineering to adapt the model to different domains. Possible future research directions involving the use of few-shot learning and internal state explanations for MB-BERT are also explored. The proposed technique opens up new avenues for analyzing and interpreting the underlying semantics of dialogue input. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a nonhomogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter's tuning. This regression approach enables efficient exploration of the parameter space and helps to identify the parameters' correlation. Our methodology's efficacy is assessed through thorough simulations and a real-world application, specifically in analyzing extreme wind speeds in Scotland. We compare our approach to other estimation methods, including maximum likelihood and Markov-Chain Monte Carlo Bayesian estimation, finding that our proposed technique yields comparable or better results. Moreover, Bayesian estimation with a broader prior distribution leads to more conservative estimates and wider confidence intervals. Our study's findings emphasize the importance of careful parameter estimation when using threshold-based methods for extreme events. We observe that, as the noise intensity increases, the skip patterns gradually disappear and give way to motion without dispersion, where the particle either ascends the potential hill or remains stationary. We investigated this elevated motion using both analytical and simulation methods. A notable outcome of our research is that, despite the increasing noise, the particle's vertical velocity exhibits periodic behavior with oscillations that grow in amplitude in direct proportion to the noise intensity. This phenomenon is characterized by oscillation frequency equal to half of the skip frequency from the low-noise periodic skipping phase, indicating an abrupt transition from the skipping phase to a motion without dispersion that is essentially steady. This steady motion without dispersion can be considered as a state of dynamic equilibrium, where the force of the descending potential is counterbalanced by the average force generated by the increased noise. We derived the numerical noise intensity value at which this equilibrium occurs and matched it with the results from simulations, thereby validating our theoretical model. In the cloud computing environment, efficient load distribution is crucial for delivering desired quality of service. This paper introduces a new load distribution model called Prepartition that accounts for the reservations of both physical machines and virtual machines during the provisioning process. Prepartition provably finds a satisfactory load distribution at the machine level, even with the presence of heterogeneous virtual machines. Moreover, our evaluation shows that Prepartition outperforms existing load distribution models by reducing welcome wounds and providing better performance overall. Building on Prepartition, we further develop an enhanced algorithm, Prepartition-Pro, which incorporates a key performance indicator into the load distribution process for effective performance improvement. Furthermore, we propose a data-driven method to determine the parameters for Prepartition-Pro based on empirical probability distributions. Experimental results validate the benefits of our proposed algorithms, Load Distributor-Pro and Parameter Estimator-Pro. Notably, Prepartition-Pro offers a 45% better performance compared to other load distribution models. This research aims to provide a comprehensive solution for efficient load distribution in a cloud data center by accounting for virtual machine reservations. The performance of our proposed models has been extensively evaluated using realistic experimental scenarios. However, our work has limitations due to assumptions made about machine loads and the non-availability of detailed cloud data for our model refinement. Nonetheless, our research has substantial practical value given the increasing importance of load distribution in cloud computing for quality of service provision. The main contribution of our study lies in the development of a novel load distribution model, Prepartition, which addresses the reservations of both physical and virtual machines during the provisioning process. This contribution has been recognized by multiple prestigious conferences, with the primary findings published in ICCAC 2019 and FOAS 2020. Nevertheless, our ongoing research aims to further improve Load Distributor-Pro by investigating new models for effective load distribution. The current study represents an essential advancement in this direction with our development of a data-driven method for determining parameters for enhanced performance. The outcome of our research is expected to facilitate quality of service provision in a cloud data center through successful load distribution. Predictive analytics in the field of game theory focuses on forecasting game outcomes and their effect on system stability. This study introduces the concept of FPNet, a family of fixed point networks that can be trained to predict Nash equilibria in both continuous and discrete games. FPNets replace iteratively converging differential equations with trainable layers, making them easier to use and more efficient. FPNets can also predict approximated equilibria, known as approximate pure Nash equilibria, allowing them to account for uncertainty in game parameters. When predicting these equilibria, FPNets show that their performance is comparable to the accuracy of the model used for training, regardless of the game's size or complexity. This study also demonstrates FPNets on various continuous and discrete games, revealing they can be surprisingly simple. For instance, predicting equilibria in rock-paper-scissors games is as simple as training a single neuron to pick the most frequently played action. This study provides the foundation for further research into the use of FPNets for forecasting game outcomes and their potential applications in monitoring system stability. FPNets are implemented using PyTorch, and the associated code is publicly available at: https://github.com/andreoula/fpnet. FPNets were tested using a combination of simulated and real-world data, and the associated data is publicly available at: https://github.com/andreoula/fpnet-data. This research demonstrates that FPNets can efficiently be used to forecast game outcomes and their potential equilibria. Notably, FPNets outperformed traditional methods, such as the von Neumann-Morgenstern normal form approach, by a large margin, especially in continuous games. For instance, in the 3-carrier battle formation game, FPNets's accuracy was around 80% compared to only 20% for the normal form method. This improvement in accuracy likely resulted from FPNets's ability to model mixed strategies more effectively than the normal form method, which can lead to increased stability in predictive analytics systems. Furthermore, FPNets's efficiency, FPNet, was substantially better than existing methods, with the ability to forecast outcomes up to 4 times faster. This study highlights the potential benefits of FPNets in the field of predictive analytics, and we hope that this research will pave the way for the development of FPNets in the context of game theory and beyond. For data analysis, it's often necessary to determine the minimum number of causal links needed to transform one data set into another. This can be achieved using the concept of causal influence, defined as the minimum number of variables required to transform one data set into another. Known as causal coprime variables in the case of discrete data, its continuous counterpart is referred to as the causal frequency separator and is demonstrated to have a lower limit that is a function of mutual information. This work explores a data analysis scenario in which we aim to identify if a linear transformation, applied to a high dimensional data set with many variables, can result in a simplified representation of lower dimension compared to the original. This investigation is linked to the fundamental limits of separating variables by considering the average of mutual information values associated with different subsets of variables. This average is referred to as the mutual investment. The study demonstrates that this quantity serves as a measure of minimum number of causal links needed for the reduction in dimension. This work further demonstrates that mutual investment is lower bounded by the spectral density at zero frequency of a covariance matrix, known as the mutual inventory. Critical infrastructure controllers like power and water distribution require advanced security measures to prevent malicious cyber attacks. However, traditional attack detection methods can be ineffective against stealthy attackers who seamlessly manipulate control inputs to go undetected. To address this, we've devised an innovative effectiveness measure to predict and identify stealthy attacks before they succeed. This metric assesses the bounded discrepancy between estimated and actual system states. Notably, our approach provides attack prediction with no additional hardware requirements, a key advantage. We've also created an online learning algorithm, allowing the predictor to adapt without retraining when the attacker adapts its strategy. This practical method can be implemented in real-world controllers, as demonstrated by our experiments using a power system model. Overall, our work focuses on stealthy attack prediction, a previously underaddressed problem, and offers a feasible solution for operational control systems. This research will be available on arXiv with preprint ID arXiv:2110.1335. An associated project has been launched on GitHub at https://github.com/guoxiaolee/effectiveness-learn. Notably, our approach has been recognized as a top submission at arXiv in 2021. Both the paper and code have garnered significant interest, accumulating over 1M reads on arXiv and receiving over 1700 GitHub stars on GitHub. As a result, our work has been widely influential, as acknowledged by multiple peer reviewers. This informal summary is based on a published paper available at https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9115988.

process, it either identifies the ring of integers mod n for any positive integer 
n or demonstrates that it does not belong to the specified categories. The 
characterization of S-rings of Cohen type reveals that they are essentially 
unified versions of multiple systems of integers mod n, where n is a product 
of distinct prime numbers. On the other hand, S-rings of non-Cohen type possess 
uniqueness of factor properties in their constitution, resulting from the 
intersection of infinite sequences of ideal factors, which may be interpreted 
as a form of relative primality with respect to a fixed ideal. In addition, 
it is proven that every ideal within an S-ring of non-Cohen type is similar 
in nature to a product of prime ideals. Finally, the unification of two

Initially, we investigate the one-dimensional, L-variable Gray code modulation, revealing it to be equivalent to a discrete-time Markov chain. We then formulate the quantization problem and develop a deep learning-based approach to optimize the states of the quantized variables. Notably, our results demonstrate that even with relatively simple models, the Dither Quantization approach can achieve close to optimal performance, on average, using a few iterations. We also extend the Dither Quantization technique to the two-dimensional, M-ary amplitude/phase shift keying modulation. Additionally, our analysis reveals that increasing the number of dither samples or iterations causes the information spectral distance to decrease. This research delves into a novel class of nonlocal games, known as biased QLD games, which involve certain rules and conditions. Players in these games can choose to either perform measurements or utilize maximally entangled states, which are used to generate specific biased states. By investigating a version of these biased QLD games that account for probability leakage, our study shows that winning such games with approximately maximally entangled states is theoretically identifiable. This finding builds upon previous work by Brannan et al., which found that nonlocal games solely utilizing maximally entangled states are completely understandable. Additionally, our study establishes a connection between our biased QLD games and a type of factorization uncertainty principle, which provides an explanation for the fact that approximately maximally entangled states can be accurately determined. This research also utilizes the concept of reverse search to develop an algorithm capable of finding all nearly maximally entangled states that can win a given biased QLD game, which in turn leads to the conclusion that such games with approximately maximally entangled states are completely understandable. This research further demonstrates that winning a different version of these biased QLD games, which accounts for accuracy and probability leakage, is also theoretically identifiable. Consequently, it was found that a particular version of a famous problem in computational complexity, known as Mulmuley-Sazanov conjecture, is less likely to be true. This research further reveals that a version of a different problem, known as strong quantum PCP conjecture, is also less likely to be true. This research further reveals that a version of a different problem, known as compute min-weight edge coloring of a particular graph, is less likely to be true. This research also establishes the theoretical limit for the determineability of a version of these biased LD games, which is known as biased LD games with accuracy. This research further reveals that a version of a different problem, known as compute biased LD games with accuracy for unentangled states, is less likely to be true. This research also establishes the theoretical limit for the accuracy of a version of these biased LD games, which is known as compute biased LD games with approximately maximally entangled states. In a recent study, researchers employed a Guided Genetic Algorithm (GGA) to investigate automated generation of crashes in C programs. This review assesses the efficacy of the GGA in producing crashes on a dataset comprising 100 failed tests from the Defects4J platform. Contrary to the original study's outcomes, our replication found that the GGA did not successfully reproduce crashes for 80% of the failed tests (versus 19% in the original study), with only 40% of the failed tests yielding crashes (compared to 60% in the original study). Moreover, our analysis revealed a substantial, inconsistent discrepancy between the expected and actual number of genes involved in producing crashes,  which could impede the GGA's generalizability to other domains. Based on these observations, we offer several potential explanations for the perceived divergence between our results and the original study, while also proposing a few speculative avenues of future research that could address these challenges. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that the GGA demonstrates promise in producing crashes, albeit in a relatively limited context. The relevant code and execution logs for this replication study are publicly accessible at https://github.com/harsha507/Replication-GGA. In line with current best practices, our replication includes an detailed description of the GGA's implementation, which replicates the findings presented in the original study, as well as comprehensive logs of our configuration files and execution outputs. Due to technical constraints, our replication does not replicate the original study's visualization components (e.g., Figure 2 and Figure 5). Future research could seek to enhance the GGA's generalizability by addressing the gene participation imbalance issue through the incorporation of attributes-based sampling methods. In addition to our analysis, other potential limitations of the GGA have been identified by other researchers, who explored enhanced evolutionary search strategies in a more controlled setting. Following a thorough evaluation of these potential extensions, our team intends to replicate a second strategy in the near future. In the meantime, our comprehensive review serves as an important contribution, as it raises crucial concerns about the GGA's performance in producing crashes in a wide range of contexts. Ultimately, our concerns may limit the GGA's practical applicability in fields such as software testing. In response to these potential limitations, our team recommends several important future research directions that could address these challenges, ultimately advancing the state-of-the-art in automated software testing. Quantum matter exhibiting higher-order topological properties within disordered states forms an increasingly significant area of study.  We have demonstrated the establishment of a consistent relationship between bulk and boundary properties in these disordered states.  Specifically, for a specific type of topological state known as an order parameter-free Haldane topological insulator, the boundary phases are classified into fragile and robust categories.  Importantly, the consistency of bulk and boundary properties in this case is attributed to the emergence of extra protection mechanisms which originate from inherent surface characteristics, specifically from time-reversal and chiral symmetry on one-dimensional edges and fermionic systems at points of high multiplicity on multi-dimensional edges.  We have further shown the potential for bulk-boundary correspondence to be violated in systems lacking these extra protections, as well as in systems exhibiting bulk-boundary correspondence but failing to meet certain energy constraints.  We have developed a mathematical framework in the form of a bulk-boundary conformal disorder matrix that can be used to systematically investigate the relationship between bulk and boundary properties in these topological states.  We have further provided multiple examples to support the validity of the proposed framework.  We predict that the bulk-boundary correspondence holds universally for a very broad range of topological states but is restricted in cases involving time-reversal breaking or bulk topological orders.  We propose that the bulk-boundary correspondence serves as a general principle applicable to various types of disordered topological states and that the extra protections playing a crucial role in this principle may be essential for understanding other topological phenomena.  We have further used the bulk-boundary correspondence as a starting point to explore the phase transitions between topological orders and develop a theoretical model to describe these transitions.  Our work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of topological phases and associated phase transitions.  It also opens up a new area of study, the study of extra protections, with the extra protections proposed here providing a new way to understand topological phenomena.  It further provides a potential tool to investigate the bulk-boundary correspondence and related extra protections.  We have further used the bulk-boundary correspondence as a tool, tool to investigate the bulk and boundary properties of disordered Haldane topological insulators from both classical and quantum perspectives.  We first demonstrate that the bulk-boundary correspondence holds for a specific type of topological state known as an Abelian Haldane topological insulator but fails for a different type known as a non-Abelian Haldane topological insulator.

Reinforcement learning mechanisms drive decision-making and behavior in various aspects of biology and mathematics. Belief-based reinforcement learning is particularly significant in fully or partially observable environments. We focus on the latter in this paper, using recurrent neural networks to represent the underlying state of nature and an agent's confidence in its representation through a probability distribution. We demonstrate that, in a partially observable environment, a reinforcement learning agent can achieve optimal performance by incorporating an auxiliary task minimizing a belief-maintenance metric. This auxiliary task allows the agent to learn a state representation that not only enhances its observation skills but also improves its overall decision-making capabilities. We apply this approach to a scenario in which an individual evaluates the trustworthiness of other members in a random sample for social decision-making and find that the learned state representation is distinct from a standard representation used in this context. Moreover, we observe that the learned state representation is capable of capturing temporal patterns in the underlying state of nature. We also note that our method has potential implications for various areas, such as computational biology and computational evolutionary theory. We compute the optimal policy and believe-maintenance metric for a simple example with two actions and an underlying state transition structure resembling a Markov chain. Additionally, we compute the optimal probability distribution for which the agent's action choice does not provide any new information when used as an additional observation in a Bayesian conditional. We also outline a general approach to obtaining such a distribution in a partially observable environment. Our method has also been successfully tested on a more complex economic model of computational evolutionary theory. However, our code is not publicly available at this time. We plan to integrate our approach with a publicly available code from another study and make it accessible to the broader community in the future. This study aims to improve weakly-supervised action detection by incorporating the context by establishing instance-level connections between scenes and key frames through graph convolutional networks. This framework can effectively extract information from videos, even when the action occurs for a short period or the setting is complex, as it merely requires bounding boxes around the action target to operate. The results of experiments conducted on ActivityNet and VIRAT Ground truth demonstrate that our method yields very competitive performance and requires only weak supervision. Furthermore, the study reveals the significance of context in video action detection and highlights the need for novel approaches that can effectively extract information from settings in which the action occurs. This paper addresses the communication efficiency challenge in distributed federated learning environments where high-latency networks prevail. To overcome this issue, we developed DP-REC, a novel technique combining differential privacy and robust encryption methods. DP-REC enables secure and efficient modeling of complex, multi-dimensional data without requiring data aggregation at a central server. Instead, model updates are created locally and transmitted in encrypted, compressed segments. We optimized these segments for minimal size and enhanced security using encryption methods, reducing communication overhead. Comprehensive tests conducted across diverse data sets, network conditions, and model types proved successful implementation of DP-REC, achieving substantial results. In specific, DP-REC achieved substantial reductions in both model update size by a factor of 190, including security enhancements, and delayed transmissions due to low-latency network connectivity. These outcomes illustrate DP-REC's ability to balance security and efficient resource allocation in distributed federated learning environments. Furthermore, DP-REC's effectiveness in such settings has also been demonstrated in resource-constrained edge environments. We have made the DP-REC framework available as open-source software. The experiment outcomes are presented in a clustered format, enabling easier comprehension. We have also addressed potential countermeasures, emphasizing the importance of implementing a synchronized model updating mechanism to prevent malicious agents from exploiting the literature's proposed methods, including gradient masking and adversarial training, to circumvent differential privacy implementations. We have also initiated an active discussion on developing a framework that integrates various Federated Learning frameworks, including FedAVG and FedAVG-SGD, as part of a broader effort to develop a generalized framework for federated learning that incorporates multiple techniques as needed. Such a framework would promote a more detailed understanding of federated learning's intricate inner workings, as well as its inherent challenges. We hope to contribute to this emerging area of study and advance the associated infrastructure. The open-source framework DP-REC is proudly based on the frameworks FedAVG and FedAVG-SGD, as well as the research-oriented framework FLGA, developed by the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), respectively). We plan to engage in a more detailed analysis and testing of additional techniques as part of this research project. However, tables often contain irrelevant information within the structural elements and semantic details, making standard document retrieval approaches ineffective for access. Population growth is a key factor influencing these plans, increasing the need for more accurate and up-to-date population estimates. The initial phase of the Population-Based Estimate Model, established by the National Institute of Statistics, involved gathering data from 24 provinces through a 5-year high-profile census. Building on this model, we aim to enhance the estimation of population dynamics by incorporating new variables that can compensate for the limitations of the initial dataset. Although the standard CAP model excels at short-term estimates, it falls short in providing long-term population dynamics forecasts, a critical aspect of the census's mission. Therefore, we will also investigate the feasibility of incorporating spatial and temporal filtering techniques to optimize population estimation in provinces with incomplete data. Current approximate membership query filters utilizing advanced technologies such as Bloom filters and Count-min sketches still produce positive false results even when a collection is completely empty. This leads to a significant security risk if the contents of the collection are supposed to remain private. In this paper, a new technique called FP-free is proposed, aiming to eliminate false positives from existing filters without requiring substantial modifications to the data structure. Introducing the concept of 'use-once' filters resolves the issue, combined with a novel approach for combining multiple such filters to achieve a false-free configuration. This technique also allows the construction of large-scale FP-free collections through a distributed method, utilizing a distributed framework called DistFP. Extensive experiments were conducted to test the performance, scalability, and overhead of the proposed technique. This techniques is also evaluated in terms of storage efficiency, query time, setup time, and the impact of repeated queries. Moreover, a calculator to determine the optimal number of 'use-once' filters required to achieve a desired false-free configuration is provided for various collection sizes and desired accuracy levels. This research proposes a pioneering method to achieve a false-free collection using existing data structures, eliminating the need for further advancements in research. The technique is already applied in certain scenarios as seen in existing applications such as Google's vector similarity search service and certain electronic cash systems. This research is attributed to providing a security solution to a critical issue which has been overlooked in research until now. The proposed technique allows for a noise-tolerant membership query filtering functionality which opens up possibilities for diverse applications in research. This research aims to eliminate false positives in approximation-based data structures without requiring innovations in research, applying the principles of FP-free and vector similarity search along the way. The main contribution of this research is eliminating false positives in research and developing a mechanism to achieve a false-free collection using existing data structures. This research also introduces DistFP, a novel framework for distributed construction of large-scale FP-free collections, allowing distribution of the construction process using the framework. The research concludes by showcasing and measuring various aspects of the technique using performance metrics and experiments. This research confirms its contribution and confirms the feasibility of achieving a false-free collection using the technique. A recently introduced TTS model called FastPitch allows for separate control of pitch and tone, however the current version of the system is unable to produce tones with high frequencies as a result of its restricted pitch range. In order to expand the pitch range of FastPitch (FP) while maintaining the quality of the speech, a method of generating augmented pitches was developed which does not impact the timbre. This method preserves the ensemble learning benefits of FP's spectrogram synthesis, just by adding a new pitch permutation. Following this augmented step, FP is able to synthesize these new pitches. In order to further improve the voice, a teacher-student training framework was applied using two pre-trained voices. The results of the experiments show a significant 60% increase in the naturalness of the augmented pitches as scored by mean opinion score (MOS). In addition, a method of retraining FP was developed which allows for the synthesis of higher range tones even when only listening to a male role model. This retraining method was found to yield an MOS increase of 0.307 in a male voice as well as 0.356 in a female voice. What is more, this retraining was found to be beneficial across the entire range of pitches and not just the higher range. Finally, implementing FP with a newly introduced augmentation method resulted in the production of many more nuanced expressions when speaking, increasing the overall impressionability of the voice as a whole. This was particularly true in scenarios where the speaker was supposed to be either emotionally constricted or extremely passionate in the story. In summary, FP was improved in several key areas. While increasing the range of a voice allows for a more natural, higher quality of playback, it was found that a certain threshold of augmenting the pitch range was not met with a notable increase in the overall quality of the voice as a whole. However, this was rectified through the implementation of an augmented method. Moreover, the concept behind the teacher-student training, particularly 'voice copying,' may yield an increase in the impressionability of a voice as a whole, provided the conditions under which the training takes place are properly fine-tuned. Ultimately, FP, in conjunction with this newly implemented augmentation method, was found to produce a more natural, higher quality of playback, extending the range of a voice as a whole. Following the proper implementation of this method, FP was able to produce an increase in the overall quality of the voice as a whole, outperforming state-of-the-art voices in the process. This work introduces Hopper, a multi-hop spatiotemporal deep learning model that
accurately predicts future points on a map for autonomous vehicles. Hopper's
unpredictable nature is mimicked by incorporating random jumps in its map
predictions, which can be guided by its understanding of the environment. The
model consists of an encoder that uses a standardized map representation and a
decoder that generates probabilistic distribution of future map locations. The
model learns to accurately replicate map features and account for uncertainties
through a locally approximate map prediction. Hopper's predictive capabilities
are maintained using an online prediction mechanism that trains on the model's
predictive distributions. Hopper demonstrates superior performance on a map
prediction dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art models, as demonstrated on the
Dataset0 dataset. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/hopper.

Understanding how the mass of the W boson is constructed from the characteristics of quarks at high-energy collisions is essential in testing the fundamental structure of the Standard Model and identifying potential signs of new physics under certain conditions. In this research paper, we examine two specific methods used to measure the mass of the W boson in such collisions, and we analyze how accurately they can determine the mass by accounting for various factors and uncertainties. We found that errors stemming from the way we model the behavior of gluons have a significant impact on their precision, and we developed a more efficient approach to calculating one of these models that incorporates both experimental data and important physical principles. Additionally, we compared the effectiveness of the two methods used to make these measurements and provided a clearer picture of the sources of uncertainty involved. This research is also relevant to planned experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. Although the accuracy of these measurements is currently limited by their available data, we can expect significant improvements in their precision to the order of a few thousandths for certain measurements when more data becomes available in the future. In summary, this research is focused on refining our theoretical understanding of how the mass of the W boson is measured in high-energy collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. We investigated two specific measurements, analyzed their accuracy, and compared their effectiveness while also enhancing our theoretical models and principles. We discovered that the accuracy of these measurements is currently limited by various factors but can potentially reach significant precision in the future. This research was partially based on previously published results and is a summary of a number of papers by the authors and other researchers, including ATLAS collaborations, that studied W boson mass measurements using various types of data and observed no clear evidence of deviations from expected models. These measurements, including both individual and combined results, have demonstrated that their mass remains consistent at 80.434 ± 0.024 GeV with the current data. This research has a specific relevance to a type of measurement that uses $b\bar{b}$ pairs and presents a new theoretical model that provides a more efficient calculation while also understanding how the mass of these quarks at high-energy collisions is constructed from the characteristics of gluons. Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. A crucial factor for these robots' acceptance is ensuring users feel as if they are actually present, which relies on the overall Quality of Experience (QoE). To evaluate the QoE for remote-controlled robots, a unique method was designed to incorporate real-time subjective assessments, rather than relying on more conventional experimental approaches. This study involved a controlled experiment where participants remotely controlled a robot to complete a task and evaluated the QoE via a web-based survey immediately after, while also observing their behaviors when interacting with the robot. The results indicated that the proposed method yielded comprehensive data without introducing biases that can occur in post-experiment reflections. Specifically, this approach revealed that users' expectations regarding the robot's movement capabilities and the quality of their remote viewing experiences positively affected their QoE. Additionally, the findings showed that the presence of distractions and whether the user was active or passive had a significant impact on their perceived experiences. We discovered that inactive remote users experienced more problems than active ones and, contrary to expectations, passive viewers did not report better experiences, which may be due to the fact that they spent more time in the virtual environment and encountered more issues with the streaming. Finally, the study demonstrated that the proposed method enabled a more precise evaluation by highlighting the importance of remote participants' activities, which poses a significant challenge for providing high-quality Telepresence robot experiences. Based on these results, suggestions were provided to improve the Quality of Experience for remote-controlled Telepresence robots. This paper introduces a novel hierarchical Bayesian model called BAYHLAM by adapting the Bayesian Item Response Surface model. BAYHLAM is defined through (1) a student ability distribution, (2) a item ability distribution, (3) a knowledge function that relates students' and items' abilities to observed scores, and (4) two nuisance parameters. Importantly, BAYHLAM provides precise, semi-parametric estimation of student abilities and enables semi-parametric estimation of the item ability distribution. In addition, BAYHLAM offers refined estimates of the global and local effects of external variables on observed scores. To compute parameters, a Markov-Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm is employed. Initially, BAYHLAM will utilize observed scores as a proxy for latent variables to relate external variables, but future developments will incorporate the most accurate score transformations. The capability of BAYHLAM to produce accurate estimates without any score transformations makes it a valuable option. The parameterization of BAYHLAM ensures that item ability distributions weighted by student ability are smooth and consistent, but this smoothness can be controlled if desired. BAYHLAM provides a comprehensive framework for exploratory and confirmatory analysis of the effects of various factors using pseudo-F tests, and it is particularly suited for exploratory analysis as a "workhorse" to identify factors that have a significant influence on observed scores, even without any prior knowledge. BAYHLAM can then be expanded to a focused model through the principle of local polynomials, allowing for a more precise, targeted analysis to confirm the effects of specific variables. The proposed Bayesian hierarchical method is'soft', meaning it does not impose the normality assumption on student abilities as is traditional. Instead, the proposed model offers a broadest-fitness function and the estimated parameters reflect the best fit. In this study, the proposed BAYHLAM method is compared with traditional Bayesian local polynomial models by simulating data with time-varying external variables and then applying both models to the data to demonstrate their capabilities and accuracy. The results show that BAYHLAM produces more accurate estimates and provides a reliable solution for interactive effects. In real-world scenarios, the proposed method is applied to examine the influence of urban density on student scores in Singapore and the findings reveal complex, significant relationships between the two variables. The use of BAYHLAM in this example highlights the importance of accounting for the non-linear, interactive effects of density when assessing its impact on student performance. This research centers on a peculiar phenomenon where twin giant planets develop in close proximity to each other, and we investigate how their formation is impacted when they simultaneously accumulate gas from their surroundings. Building upon existing studies, we used a detailed code to simulate planet growth and the surrounding disk under various conditions, including scenarios with or without hydrodynamic interactions between the planets. As a result, we discovered that when the planets are far from affecting the disk and each other, their mass growth differences largely stem from their initial mass disparities. Conversely, when they do affect the disk and potentially each other, their mass accumulation varies in tandem with their angular separation, and this can result in significantly distinct final masses. More surprisingly, even when they do not interact with one another, we found that hydrodynamic effects play a crucial role in determining their unique mass distribution and the resulting implications for their angular separations. Consequently, we suggest that concurrent planet formation remains an unresolved factor in understanding planet mass distributions and the structures of gas-rich disks. The electrical conductivity of a single purified single-wall carbon nanotube film exhibits a temperature-dependent behavior due to an unusually low, nonlinear resistance. Notably, the temperature at which the conductivity starts to increase, approximately 15-20 Kelvin, closely matches the energy difference between the vibrational modes of the carbon nanotubes' phonons. This finding aligns with theoretical predictions suggesting that phonons play a pivotal role in electrical conductivity across isolated carbon nanotubes. Moreover, the observed temperature at which the conductivity begins to increase is significantly lower than that of metallic films made from doped single-layer graphene or conductive gate materials. Overall, the findings indicate that carbon nanotubes remain superior conductors even when compared to the newly developed graphene technologies. Nonetheless, the use of high-purity carbon nanotubes is shown to be essential in observing the distinct phonon-assisted electrical conductivity. This research demonstrates that pure carbon nanotubes offer a unique platform to study the intricate relationships between electronic and phononic systems. It also highlights their considerable potential as building blocks for developing innovative and efficient phonon-engineered devices that have so far remained unachievable with other materials. Further experiments investigating the magnetic response, optical properties, and quantitative magnetic resonance measurements are needed to verify the impurity levels present in the carbon nanotubes. It is anticipated that the techniques employed in this study can be directly applied to evaluate the purity of other two-dimensional materials. This research expands our understanding of the thermal instability present in ultra-pure materials and it is likely that the vast majority of existing films contain contaminants similar to those described here. Importantly, the findings suggest that the phonon-assisted conductivity discovered in this research could also occur in other materials where the energy gap at 15-20 Kelvin is closer to the thermal vibration temperature. Future investigations of carbon nanotubes at even lower temperatures should then be able to reveal the distinct phonon-assisted electrical conductivity. It is also proposed that the techniques developed in this study can be used to evaluate the purity of graphene films and monitor their electrical conductivity as a function of temperature. This research demonstrates that the phonon-assisted conductivity across individual carbon nanotubes within a conductive matrix can be directly observed. It is also shown that the techniques employed in this study can fail to detect the distinct phonon-assisted electrical conductivity in impure single-wall carbon nanotube films. Notably, the findings indicate that the use of highly purified single-wall carbon nanotubes is essential in observing the distinct phonon-assisted electrical conductivity

Mixtures of experts, a type of neural network composed of several expert networks and a gate network, have been found in various applications such as through Bayesian deep learning. However, training such mixtures has been a challenging task, particularly because their loss functions exhibit non-convex regions. Consequently, very few algorithms are able to recover the optimal parameters of the mixture and its component networks. This paper explores the limitations of existing algorithms for training mixtures of experts by examining the behavior of two widely used methods: hard expectation maximization and variational inference with local reparameterizations. By developing a new framework based on these algorithms, we are able to explain the inconsistencies in existing methods and provide a basis for a new algorithm, called EM-EVI, which accurately matches hard expectation maximization's performance while significantly increasing the convergence speed of the algorithm. Our investigations also reveal the impact of the mixture component distribution on the model performance, thereby enabling us to recommend a Gaussian mixture distribution with expert capacities evenly spread across the unit interval for optimal performance. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our new algorithm in multiple contexts by training mixtures of experts on data sets such as damped spring mass systems and tidal flow patterns in the Hooghly river. Our results show that the new algorithm is able to produce highly accurate output by recovering the optimal parameters of the mixture and its component networks, which is in contrast to the variational inference with local reparameterizations that is able to recover the optimal parameters but fails to match the performance of the hard expectation maximization algorithm. This research has broader implications in the modeling of mixture distributions and their potential application in various areas of application. Furthermore, we also identify an area of future research by demonstrating that the new algorithm is in its current form not scalable to very large data sets, which necessitates the development of a more efficient algorithm in the future. This set of notes offers a concise overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, specifically focusing on the spin versions of these theories. It is intended that these notes serve as an introductory outline for the more in-depth treatment presented in arXiv:2108.13908v2. While the current work builds upon previous research, the underlying concepts are introduced within the accompanying paper arXiv:2108.13908v2. Please note that the current work employs the orientation of edges in the definition of chip-firing games, whereas the accompanying paper uses the alternative approach based on duality relationships. Both theories ultimately yield the same outcome, and a detailed comparison of these approaches is presented in the conclusion of these notes. Further, the current work focuses on the combinatorial aspect of chip-firing games on metric graphs, but it does not delve into the broader category of chip-firing games on undirected graphs, which is explored in the accompanying paper. Finally, the current work is primarily based on the foundational work in arXiv:0704.0442, but it must be noted that the theory of spin Jacobians and Pryms is rooted in the research of Otter, Caporaso, and Verrill, presented respectively in arXiv:1208.4836, arXiv:1104.3692, and arXiv:0809.4582. Early detection and prediction of Alzheimer's disease are critical for effective treatment and its progression should be forecasted as early as possible. Currently, a widely used method for monitoring Alzheimer's disease is cognitive testing, but it doesn't work well for early detection and isn't suitable for large-scale studies. A new, advanced deep learning method called Deep InfoMax has been used to predict conversion to Alzheimer's based on structural MRI data from the prodromal stage, with long-term prediction in mind. This approach combines multiple features to predict brain region volume changes over time. Our results show that Deep InfoMax achieved an accuracy of 87% for 1-year predictions, 79% for 3-year predictions, and 69% for 6-year predictions, with a high Conordance Index of 87% for 1-year predictions, 82% for 3-year predictions, and 80% for 6-year predictions. These findings are the first to use predictive modeling for a large-scale, longitudinal dataset like ADNI, and they demonstrate the effectiveness of Deep InfoMax in predicting conversion to Alzheimer's based on structural MRI data in the prodromal stage. Furthermore, our long-term predictions are particularly notable due to the lack of literature on this topic in the field of medical image analysis. Our code is available on GitHub to facilitate replication and new applications. Overall, our study highlights the importance of early detection and prediction of Alzheimer's disease, and it opens up new avenues for using predictive modeling in the clinical setting. A new theoretical approach explores how a strong magnetic field impacts the electronic structure of a correlated metal, resulting in an effective spin-orbit coupling (SO) that far exceeds its inherent SO. This anomalous SO, resulting from inter-electron interactions, surpasses the metal's regular SO and as large as in typical SO-coupled materials, and is responsible for large anomalous Hall angles and weights, and new insights into quantum state transitions of electrons. These findings demonstrate the importance of interactions between electrons under strong magnetic conditions and offer fresh avenues for discovering novel materials through magnetic field applications. An experimental technique to measure this interaction-driven SO has also been developed. It was discovered that the interaction-driven SO is reduced once long-range ordering of magnetism happens as it re-establishes the regular SO of the metal. Furthermore, in high magnetic fields, the interaction-driven SO can be inverted by changing the orientation of the magnetic field. An additional discovery was that in interaction-driven SO, the interaction-driven anomalous Hall effect does not diminish in magnetic orders, but rather, it preserves its large effect even in the presence of long-range ordering of magnetism. A theoretical model for an exotic form of matter, called conformal shadow matter, has been proposed, where its interaction with light is described through a novel and unconventional process. This phenomenon can be observed in the vicinity of a black hole that is nearly, but not exactly, spherical in shape. Our analysis reveals that this unusual matter leaves distinct imprints on the patterns of light emitted from regions near its equator. These unique features might hold clues to the existence of this exotic form of matter. Additionally, we specifically examine how a particular type of spherical deformation affects the emission patterns of two distinct types of light, namely Thomson scattering and Breit-Rosenfeld scattering. It is found that the shape of these patterns can be transformed into each other under specified conditions, and we identify the time frames in which this conversion occurs. Moreover, we identify specific times or intervals when these patterns remain unchanged or change abruptly. Finally, we provide examples of black hole shapes where these transformations are particularly simple and predictable. This theoretical study may have implications for the observation of exotic phenomena, such as shadows, in real-world contexts, including astrophysical and cosmological investigations. It is intended that this research inspire experimental observations to verify the existence of this exotic form of matter. To ensure AI-powered medical devices provide safe and accurate diagnoses, accurate evaluation of their performance is necessary, particularly in clinical settings where predictions must be reliable and stable. Current methods for assessing AI models, such as cross-validation, may fail to detect underlying issues, like predicting a cat as a dog, which could lead to severe consequences. We develop a distribution shift divergence estimator, enabling the assessment of AI models' performance in clinical settings and the detection of potential issues, such as the dog-cat mistake. Our method performs well in comparison to traditional evaluation techniques and detects performance problems in medical image AI models, further improving the trustworthiness of AI-powered medical devices. Our work and associated code are available online.

Measuring the complexity of neural networks is crucial for assessing their optimisation difficulties and predictive capacities.  Although several information-theoretic measures exist, their equivalency is not well understood.  This research investigates multiple measures of complexity in Boltzmann machines, a fundamental neural network architecture, and examines how they change in response to various adjustments.  By doing so, the study gains insights into the similarities and differences between these information-theoretic measures, providing guidelines for their use.  Interestingly, the results show that some measures of complexity exhibit contrasting behaviour under different types of modifications, highlighting the importance of considering the context when applying these measures to Boltzmann machines. We derive the Faber-Krahn inequality for the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, demonstrating that the optimal constant factor depends solely on the underlying weight function's geometric mean radius. Additionally, we establish the equality condition and provide relevant examples where equality occurs. Furthermore, we also investigate the asymptotic behavior of the optimal constant factor as it pertains to weighted Hermite operators. The main outcome of our approach involves the generalized isoperimetric inequality, and the key instrument employed in this inequality is a suitable version of the Alexandrov's lemma, adapted for pairs of functions. Another crucial method employed in this inequality is a suitable version of the hyperbolic inequality for the exterior normal to the surface, as defined by a given geometric mean radius. Our inequality also naturally lends itself to applications in the study of isoperimetric problems associated with the underlying weight function. The equality conditions that arise from our methods are further elaborated upon in a series of complementary results, which ultimately reveal that equality occurs when the associated measure is concentrated on a single point. Our study primarily focuses on the unbounded case in which the underlying weight function has at most logarithmic growth. However, the main results of our work can also be extended to the broader scenario in which the weight function has suboptimal growth characteristics. Our investigation of the general case is based on a suitable modification of the provided evidence. Our aim in this paper is to provide a comprehensive exploration of the spectral properties associated with the generalized Hermite operator, which has significant applications in various contexts, particularly under specified Robin boundary conditions, as demonstrated by the works of Agostinacci, Branciaroli, and Patacchini. In our study, we consider the spectral set to be composed of nonnegative values, which yields a generalization of the well-known Dirichlet-Faber-Krahn inequality. To expand the capabilities of kernel methods, researchers have developed
various polynomial-based kernels. Nevertheless, these kernels have limitations
in incorporating the benefits of infinite-series expansion, namely, they lack
recognition of non-exchangeable properties found in data sets, such as those
in NLP, and they fail to learn an adaptive significance order for constructing
the kernel matrix. To address these drawbacks, we introduce a novel, data-driven
approach for kernel discovery, named NFT-K, which is derived from a generalized
lattice polynomial technique, but unlike existing methods, it has the capacity
to recognize non-exchangeable characteristics and automatically determines the
best significance order for constructing the kernel matrix. As a result, NFT-K
offers improved scalability with its ability to dynamically reduce the dimension
of the kernel matrix. When applied to a range of popular and advanced
dataset-benchmarking tasks, NFT-K consistently outperforms the topst-performers
in multi-task learning, including MMLP and GP-NN. Our implementation of NFT-K
is publicly available at https://github.com/cclayson/nft_k. The results of our
experiments are accessible via https://nft-k.cclayson.com. Furthermore, the
nft_k library, which provides the NFT-K algorithm, is part of the PyMLP library,
a powerful machine learning framework for designing multi-task linguistic programs. 

For more information on the PyMLP library, please visit its online repository at https://github.com/cclayson/pymlp. The PyMLP library is designed around an
modular architecture for independent development and easy integration of its
various components, including nft_k, mlp_lattice, linguistic programs, and
multi-task inference. The library aims to provide a flexible foundation for
the rapid prototyping, performance-driven development of machine learning programs
tailored to specific linguistic tasks and use cases. As a result, PyMLP can be
easily extended to support a wide range of natural language processing (NLP)
tasks and other related tasks beyond its current scope, which includes the
implementation of both neural and symbolic machine learning programs for
performing a variety of NLP tasks. 
The PyMLP library is part of a larger vision for unifying machine learning
programs under a single, systematic approach, which is designed for promoting
programmatic research and expediting the design, development, and testing of
machine learning programs.

This theoretical work has significant implications for the design of correlated topological non-Hermitian materials. A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed, where neutrino masses are produced through one-loop interactions, resulting in a bosonic dark matter candidate within the range of approximately 0.01-50 GeV. Stabilization of dark matter occurs due to a combination of nonzero modular weight and residual Z2 symmetry derived from the U(1)_(B-L) symmetry. Indirect naturalness of dark matter mass arises from radiative mass generation in neutral fermions that interact with dark matter. Therefore, dark matter in this model remains undetectable by direct observation but may be identified by missing energy signatures at colliders or an enhanced neutrinoless double beta decay rate. Notably, this model also helps explain the experimentally observed mass differences between neutrinos, mainly by accounting for approximately 50% of their total masses. Models of modular A4 and U(1)_(B-L) symmetry, including both cases when these symmetries are strictly flavour non-conserving and conserving, are evaluated to determine their implications on neutrino oscillation parameters. Calculations yield a lower mass limit of approximately 0.3 GeV on dark matter in the non-fermionic sector. Additionally, dark matter in the fermionic sector, consistent with present experimental data, requires a mass range of approximately 4-45 GeV and needs to be more heavily in the range of 30-45 GeV to accommodate future experimental findings on neutrino masses. Lastly, this model is shown to be compatible with constraints from leptonic processes. For instance, this model can account for the global constraint of gamma ray flux at Earth's centre, imposed by the Fermi-LAT collaboration, if dark matter consists of non-fermionic particles with masses in the range of approximately 0.1-50 GeV. Moreover, this model also helps to resolve issues with the muon anomalous magnetic moment and the long-standing pentaquark np anomaly. Notably, the U(1)_(B-L) symmetry provides a new solution to the matter-antimatter paradox by proposing a model where baryon (B) and lepton (L) asymmetries heavily intersect, resulting in highly equivalent amounts of baryon and lepton asymmetries. In fast rotating nuclei, the degree of freedom related to the minimum length influences the dynamics of the angular harmonic oscillator. Taking this into account, the Hamiltonian for a triaxial oscillator is modified as $H = \hbar\omega(\hat{a}^\dagger^2 + \hat{a}^2) + \hbar\Omega\hat{J}_3$. Based on the Dirac oscillator approach, the minimum length effect distorts the symmetries and properties of this Hamiltonian, leading to changes in the energy spectrum. Our investigation focuses on how the modified single-particle movement and collective dynamics of the triaxial oscillator behave under the influence of the minimum length effect, observing that this effect causes energy splitting in the single-particle states and alters the collective movement. When $\omega = \Omega$, a flat energy density of states appears for certain single-particle states. Additionally, the K-fold symmetry in the quasiparticle energy spectrum of the triaxial oscillator is explored and discussed. This research employs the formalism of the modified Dirac Hamiltonian with a specific harmonic potential. Its results indicate that the number of degeneracies in the quasiparticle energy spectrum depends on the K-value of the symmetry. Considering that this effect provides a microscopic understanding of the $\gamma$-deformation parameter in nuclei, the minimum length is found to weaken the deformation in triaxial nuclei. When $\omega = \Omega$, the deformation parameter is reduced to 20%. In contrast, if $\omega \neq \Omega$, the degradation is more pronounced. This study demonstrates that the number of degeneracies in the quasiparticle energy spectrum of the triaxial oscillator is related to the K-value of the symmetry. Therefore, the degeneracies can serve as an indicator of this symmetry. Calculations for the minimum length effect on quasiparticle energies were conducted for specific values of $\gamma$ and $\epsilon$. These results reveal that the minimum length has opposite influences on prolate and oblate nuclei. While the former experiences weakening of the deformation parameter, the latter experiences strengthening, which could result in a significant deformation parameter. The possibility of emerging new phenomena may depend on the sign of the minimum length parameter. If used appropriately, the degeneracies in the energy spectrum can serve as an indicator of novel physical phenomena related to the minimum length effect. This use may circumvent the limitation that the number of degeneracies serves as a measure of the $\gamma$-deformation parameter

One of the key applications of classification algorithms is change detection, a process that entails identifying changes in imagery over time, a direct result of natural events or human intervention. By utilizing time-series data, researchers can monitor events like land cover transformations, environmental disasters, or economic fluctuations in real-time. The main challenge in change detection lies in devising an efficient algorithm that balances speed and accuracy to process large datasets. The current leading approaches employ spectral-statistical or deep learning-based methods to achieve enhanced performance. Notwithstanding their achievements, these techniques struggle to handle the complexities of high-resolution change detection due to their high computational demands. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a pioneering deep neural network, known as DiffCONN, which can adaptively learn the optimal number of features to support effective change detection while reducing processing time. The approach combines the strengths of convolutional neuromodulator (CONN) and diffusion models and is capable of producing sharp feature representations from both fine and coarse image granularities. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through comparisons with state-of-the-art algorithms on the LAI PRO sale 8 dataset. The results show that DiffCONN delivers an exceptional balance of speed, accuracy, and interpretability, a trait not typically found in current change detection solutions. The source code for this research has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/Prof-Emerson/DiffCONN. The LAI PRO dataset can be obtained at https://ai4r.gforge.inria.fr/. The model checkpoints are hosted on GRAIL at https://grail.inria.net/diffconn. The research uses computing resources provided by GRAIL and the Brazilian National Grid Infrastructure (SGI). The researchers would like to express their gratitude to the LAI PRO dataset providers, the INRAe and University of Avignon's teams, and the DiffCONN's users for their valuable feedback. The researchers also wish to express their gratitude to the INRIA's InLab for supporting the diffusion model's development. The research does not involve human participants. The diffusion model does not collect or process any user-private data. The researchers also do not use any pre-trained models that were developed for data augmentation purposes

A comprehensive study examines how a measure of disorder, residual entropy, relates to the movement of molecules in fluids that are composed of simple units, both in reality and through computer-simulated models. By using a key idea introduced by Rosenfeld in 1977, a universal relationship between disorder and the size of molecules in fluids that obey a certain condition is predicted to exist. Although Rosenfeld's original concept was initially limited to ideal gases, researchers have extended its application to various types of molecular interactions. In this research, the idea is extended even further to include the effects of polar interactions, for both real-world molecules and through computer-simulated models, with impressive results. In addition to verifying theoretical concepts, the study also demonstrates its applications in developing more accurate computer models of molecular interactions. Moreover, the study identifies potential avenues for further refinement of the model, leading to the hope that it will contribute to a deeper understanding of molecular behavior and potentially inform the design of molecular structures. Ultimately, the study highlights how analyzing molecular behavior can reveal underlying principles and potentially yield novel insights. It addresses renowned challenges, notably the nature of time and the necessity of reducing the tension between quantum theory and relativity. This paper delves into a more comprehensive examination of the theory's hidden-variable aspect, focusing on its underlying assumptions and mathematical frameworks. Our analysis reveals both strengths and limitations, suggesting potential avenues for further exploration. Ultimately, we evaluate the theory's potential resolution of the quantum-era problem, assessing its likelihood of overcoming the associated obstacles. Although our analysis is not exhaustive, our objective is to provide a thorough and respectful examination of the theory as a proposed solution to one of physics' enduring mysteries. Natural Language Processing tasks are typically performed on high-capacity devices, requiring significant storage and processing capabilities. With the rising importance of edge AI in applications like virtual assistants and information retrieval, researchers are now focusing on enabling these capabilities on devices such as smart speakers, smartphones, and IoT devices with limited resources. This study addresses this challenge by developing a lightweight neural network model for identifying key phrases from given texts on devices with restricted resources, like those utilizing Android phones or IoT devices. We tested various types of neural network models integrated with a word-embedding scheme called ALBERT, and compared their performance with a baseline model built using recurrent neural networks. The experimental results show that the most efficient model achieved an accuracy of 84.8% on an internal dataset, while requiring only 10.8% of the original model's parameters and both processors with limited resources. Furthermore, we investigated ways to apply the word embedding model alone to the keyphrase identification task and evaluated multiple models using an English dataset and one produced by Baidu. We also demonstrated the effectiveness of the developed model on devices, including an Android phone (Google Pixel 3a) and an IoT device (Raspberry Pi 4). This research makes the developed model's source code available for public use. The model's performance was evaluated using the F1-score as well as traditional accuracy measures. The developed model's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/dsphillip/albert-kp-ssd. The ALBERT model's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/sthubiszwewald/albert-ssl. Working with categorical data for statistical regression analysis is
complicated by the high dimensionality of features, which is expanded in
each category, making it difficult to apply statistical models. This paper
uses group andating methods with Lasso penalties to improve model selection
and perform variable selection for continuous and categorical variables.
However, when categories are unknown, using the group Lasso alone can make
interpretation difficult, so we propose a refined approach that combines
Lasso and group Lasso for both selection and to prevent the "anti-correlation" issue that can occur when highly correlated features are penalized negatively. This extended method is evaluated on simulated data with various dimensions and orders of magnitude, compared to existing approaches, and finally applied to data from the US Census to predict voting behavior. Available as a package called sgd.group in the R language. 

Keywords: Categorical features, Group Lasso, Lasso, Anti-correlation, SGD method, Voting prediction.

In embedded real-time systems, the presence of non-real-time applications like web browsers and media players, which require high processing resources, commonly interferes with the targeted real-time applications' performance. Integration of these services into regular real-time systems poses significant challenges as they often surpass the allocated time limits, exceeding the allowed response time. Our research proposes T-Visor, a hypervisor designed to enhance the real-time capabilities of current embedded platforms. By leveraging support from the latest hardware virtualization support, T-Visor efficiently manages guest services and achieves near-native performance while maintaining robust real-time capabilities. Its ability to allocate precise time slices and prioritize real-time applications ensures timely resource allocation and superior overall system responsiveness. Our experimental results confirm T-Visor's effectiveness in improving real-time applications' response times. The notion of higher-dimensional slice algebras emerges from the simplex diagram structure of multi-layer diagrams. We establish that this concept is a specific manifestation of the generic algebraic structure associated with multi-dimensional diagrams. Furthermore, with simplicity in mind, we explore the potential relationship between slice algebras and associative algebras over a field. Finally, as a direct consequence of this framework, the classical concept of Jordan algebras is rediscovered. To demonstrate the utility of this new perspective, the framework is applied to the study of hypercomplex structures within vector spaces. This approach leads to the definition of a new category containing traditional complex, quaternionic, and octonionic algebras as fundamental members. The new perspective yields an easy and consistent generalization of well-known theorems, such as Albert's theorem on octonions. The framework is also seen to provide a natural method for categorizing multi-layer diagrams. For those with a mathematical background, the concept of Jordan algebras may seem an appropriate tool for exploring hypercomplex structures, but for those with a physical background, the simple definition of a complex number within the diagrammatic framework holds the potential to shed new light on this concept. Similarly, the framework may hold the potential to reveal new insights into other concepts, such as triplons in octonions. To take a broad perspective, the relationship between algebraic structures and physical concepts such as triplons and monoplons may warrant further investigation. As an initial step, we inform the reader that a monopole in physics is essentially equivalent to an element within a monoidal algebra in mathematics, leading to the potential for further discussion on the cross-fertilization of concepts between these two fields. As an example, if we consider triplons within the framework of octonions, then using the simple definition of a complex number within the diagrammatic framework, the relationship between physics and mathematics becomes clear, but whether this leads to new insights remains to be seen. To broaden the scope even further, the potential for further research on the representation of particles within the diagrammatic framework is investigated in a concluding section. This section demonstrates that in certain cases, the relationship between particles and diagrams is deep and rich, but whether this leads to new insights on fundamental problems, such as the particle composition, is for the reader and the author (who is also the speaker) to decide. To narrow the gap between the two fields, the conclusion is written in a manner reminiscent of a pedagogical lecture, blending mathematical precision with conceptual clarity
