Living systems rely on information that is passed down from one generation to the next. Although the concept of heritable information is widely understood, it remains unclear how it arises in complex systems, especially where randomness is present. This textbook explores the emergence of endurable patterns in stochastic systems, with a focus on biosocial and social phenomena that are influenced by both biology and technology. By integrating concepts from physics, biology, and economics, this book provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the origin of heritable information and its connection to phenomena such as cultural transmission, disease spread, and financial market fluctuations. Ultimately, this book provides a foundation for studying these systems and their relevance to human society. Examples and exercises are included throughout to enhance comprehension and apply the theoretical insights presented. While this book delves into advanced topics, it is written in a way that is accessible to readers from various backgrounds. Despite its focus on advanced topics, the mathematical level is generally equivalent to an upper-divisions undergraduate introduction to probability and statistics, with some concepts from information theory and nonlinear stochastic dynamics that are relevant but not extensively explored. This book does not aim to provide a detailed mathematical derivation for its conclusions but rather offers an endurable conceptual framework for understanding the origin and impact of heritable information. Its primary goal is to demonstrate that, even in complex systems driven by randomness, endurable patterns can arise and shape human society. Additionally, this book seeks to correct a critical oversight by pointing out that the field of social science has historically failed to utilize the power of endurable information, often treating it as a fixed property, with little consideration for its dynamic aspects. Conversely, this book takes a more holistic approach, recognizing that the origin, flow, and preservation of heritable information are interconnected and form a unified concept. Please note that the final chapter is currently under development. Its contents and focus will be different from what is typically expected in this subject. While this book does not cover topics related to human values, politics, or ethics, it does explore the technical link between stochastic systems and the heritable information they contain, as well as their various applications. These discussions are an extension of what is typically covered in this subject and will culminate in the chapter on coevolutionary endurable information, which will examine the dynamics between technology and heritable information. Please note that the initial chapter will also touch on these broader topics in its conclusion. Please refer to the list of recommended readings for further insights on these subjects. We examine the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non model, which is a twin pendulum system with H\'{e}non's twist, in terms of its basins of attraction. The H\'{e}non model's behavior becomes even more intricate when it is expanded into a third dimension. To understand the nature of its attractors, we plot the escape rates of periodic orbits, a measure developed by P. Teixeira and T. Tel. These results are then visualized using the Mandelbrot plot, which confirms the existence of organizing centers for this 3D version of the H\'{e}nomal model. These centers correspond to compact, attracting attractors, which are in turn surrounded by regions of chaotic behavior. Ultimately, our findings highlight the significance of a recent study claiming that H\'{e}non's model does not exhibit chaotic behavior despite initial claims to the contrary. Our work demonstrates that this study's conclusions are valid only under highly constrained conditions, and that this 3D version of the H\'{e}nomal model, which is similar to H\'{e}non's original model, must necessarily exhibit chaotic behavior in its vast majority of parameter spaces. 

The code for our research can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/igorfilipovic/Henon3dBasins.

We analyze the statistical properties of hook lengths in Young diagrams that fit within the boundary of randomly selected semistandard Young diagrams within the shape parameterized by (n, n/k), where k is a positive integer greater than or equal to 2. We calculate the average and the variance of the sum of the hook lengths divisible by either k or both k and a second integer, represented as $\ell$, as well as the square of the sum of the hook lengths divisible by the product of two integers, k and $\ell$. The analysis relies on a formula representing the generating function of the hook lengths in Young diagrams, which requires a difficult-to-access concept of the space of partition operators. We develop a novel approach to overcome this difficulty by modifying the concept and calculating the relevant generating function directly, making the analysis feasible. Additionally, this approach yields an alternative proof of a known result concerning the probability distributions of the heights of Young diagrams in the grand canonical ensemble for rectangular shapes. We also explore the special cases where the shape has a width (n,1), the largest possible value for $\ell$, and find that in these instances, the average and variance of the relevant hook lengths tend towards infinity as they become highly divisible. For the special case where k equals 2, the analysis also explores the more complex problem of the co-occurrence of pair and length hook lengths, and in the case of the rectangular shape, it reveals that their joint probability distribution tends towards a normal distribution as the size of the Young diagram tends towards infinity. We derive a sequence of equations describing the relevant probabilities and use it to derive the limit distribution by iterating the equations until a limiting value is reached. We also address the limitation of our main result by noting that it does not apply to the case where the sum of the relevant hook lengths is squared, likely due to a failure in our code, and instead provide a simplified proof for the case of the rectangular shape. Finally, this approach yields an alternative proof of a known result concerning the probability distributions of the heights of Young diagrams in the grand canonical ensemble for rectangular shapes. One of the most compelling aspects of quantum mechanics is the phenomenon of Bose-Einstein condensation occurring in highly excited states of a collective of particles. Historically, mathematicians have developed a nonlinear extension of the Schrödinger equation, known as the Nirenberg-Serrin equation, to describe this process. The well-established equation is known to have solutions that are highly sensitive to their initial conditions, and a considerable amount of research has been conducted to demonstrate the existence of global solutions, however the question of minimizing the number of excitations remains unresolved. The newer discovery, on the other hand, is predicted to produce solutions that are significantly more robust to variations in initial conditions and may even exhibit infinite decay. By exploring these differences, this study aims to gain a deeper understanding of the two formulations and their potential to offer fresh insights into the theoretical framework of quantum mechanics. The infrared region in high-energy scattering processes of gravity and gravitational waves is heavily influenced by the behavior of the gravitational field. In recent years, new tools have emerged allowing for a precise examination of this region: advances in gauge-invariant techniques for analyzing field theories, novel mathematical frameworks like AdS/CFT, and unique characteristics of soft gravitational waves. Our talk will explore how the different methods mentioned above fit together to form a cohesive whole, with a particular focus on the role of the BMS symmetry group, which is a key feature of the infrared regime in asymptotically flat space. We'll also discuss how the BMS symmetry operates across various field theories, including massless and massive gravity, with a special emphasis on the relationship between the BMS symmetry and the discovery of new finite-dimensional symmetry groups in the case of subleading soft gravitational waves. Furthermore, we'll outline how the BMS symmetry operates in the context of the post-Newtonian and AdS/CFT frameworks and illustrate the results with several examples, including the investigation of the emission of gravitational waves from localized sources and the analysis of the gravitational signature of cosmic strings. We'll also delve into several open questions that remain to be addressed and the potential future developments in this area. Importantly, we'll demonstrate how the BMS symmetry operates in the case of the polymeric version of the M2D theory, which is an example of a massless gravity theory that is reparameterized-invariant rather than gauge-invariant. In addition, we'll address whether the BMS symmetry can be used to explain the discovery of double soft theorems, which is a key feature of the infrared regime in the case of massless gravity. Finally, we'll outline a possible connection between the BMS symmetry and the emergence of a new, 'dynamic' form of symmetry in the case of the 2D gravitational wave scattering processes. Though this idea is still in its early stages, it has the potential to form a key component of a more comprehensive theory of symmetry dynamics in the infrared regime in gravity and be a vital part of a theory of quantum gravity that is reparameterization-invariant rather than gauge-invariant. We'll also explore whether the BMS symmetry operates in the case of higher-dimensional gravity and whether the symmetry is preserved under quantization. In generalized geometry, the study of almost products manifolds plays a significant role, with its various applications linked to the theory of Courant algebroids. This paper explores generalized metrics and their connection to Ricci flat four-forms on almost products manifolds. Specifically, the metrics are defined as a combination of an ordinary metric and a twisted metric, with the latter depending on the four-form. It's shown that a generalized metric exists if and only if the four-form is Ricci flat when restricted to the Dolbeault subspace. In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination techniques, we establish novel categories of sparse permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders, with various degrees of diffusion. Further, we confirm several of these proposed permutation polynomials and provide several examples of their corresponding designing matrices by solving systems of linear equations. Ultimately, we present several instances of sparse permutation polynomials with optimal resistance to linear and weakly-regular attacks. Additionally, we highlight several instances of sparse permutation polynomials with low weight that can serve as components in the construction of total permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders. Moreover, we present several instances of sparse total permutation polynomials with low weight for use in the construction of spread and nearspread difference sets. Lastly, through an initial evaluation of their corresponding directing vectors, we obtain several instances of sparse total permutation polynomials with low weight that can serve as a foundation for the construction of generalized polinomial sequences with optimal resistance to linear and weakly-regular attacks. Several of these proposed sparse total permutation polynomials have not been seen before and, with the aid of the accompanying software package, have been validated for various orders. In particular, some of these proposed sparse total permutation polynomials for orders $q=2^{3},\ 3^{3},\ 7^{3},\ 9^{3},\ 17^{3}$ are presented for the first time in recent literature. Additionally, some of these proposed sparse total permutation polynomials for orders $q=5^{3},\ 13^{3},\ 25^{3},\ 73^{3},\ 257^{3},\ 729^{3}$ were previously known but not included in recent publications. A technical note on software-related aspects is provided in the accompanying document. The constructed permutation polynomials with low weight and high diffusion have the potential to enhance the security of multivariate schemes. Moreover, some of these proposed sparse permutation polynomials for orders $q=2^{3},\ 3^{3},\ 7^{3},\ 9^{3},\ 17^{3}$ are the first of their kind in the literature, as well as some proposed sparse total permutation polynomials for various orders. A related presentation was made at the International Conference on Information Theoretical Applications to Biomedical Data in May 2020.

Human intestinal parasitic infections pose a significant threat to global health, as they cause severe discomfort, chronic illness, and even death, and are particularly hazardous in areas with underdeveloped sanitation systems. In many of these underserved regions, traditional parasitic diagnosis methods involve tedious egg collection and manual examination, a labor-intensive and expensive process. Recent advancements in digital microscopy have led to the adoption of computer-aided image analysis for accurate and efficient parasitic egg identification. Nevertheless, this technique's effectiveness is limited by the requirement for extensive, disease-specific image datasets for its operation. To address this challenge, our research proposes a novel Deep Belief Network-based approach for categorizing intestinal parasitic eggs. Our approach was tested using a dataset of eggs from three parasitic species: hookworm, Trichuris, and Ascaris. Our results show that this method represents a reliable and efficient image-based paradigm for parasitic egg identification, thereby facilitating the development of accurate diagnostic tools for underdeveloped communities. For the sake of replication, our dataset, experimental code, and model specifications have been publicly released at https://github.com/josemaruszqz/DBN-intestinal-parasites-categorization. Our findings indicate that DBN can serve as a valuable tool in the creation of efficient, image-based diagnostic tools for underdeveloped communities. Our research was fully explained in a paper published in Sensors, as part of a distinguished issue on underdeveloped regions' Judicial Frameworks. This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance the control strategy's performance and achieve a stable flight. The development of the derivative filter is critical due to many commercial flight control systems being compromised by noise and oscillations. The proposed PIDA control strategy combines a derivative filter based on the Dual Simplex Algorithm and Genetic Filter, achieving optimal performance and tracking capabilities. The system's effectiveness was tested using nonlinear math model samples derived from the ねこ plane model, and results demonstrate that the integrated derivative filter has a significant impact on noise and oscillation reduction. The genetic filter introduced in this research further improves the control strategy's performance, as demonstrated by the root mean square (RMS) input and error values. The system's performance has also been evaluated using performance metrics such as rise time, peak time, system rise time, overall system peak, and error cost. The application of the Dual Simplex Algorithm with Genetic Filter leads to a reduced error of 72.9 percent, achieving a stable and smooth flight with a rise time and peak time of 3 s and 4 s, and a controlled output with a rise time and peak time of 3 s and 4 s, and a controlled output with a controlled rise and peak. The use of a derivative filter with a Low Pass characteristic leads to a reduced noise at 1 s, but slightly increases the system's rise and peak times. The application of the genetic filter, on the other hand, improves the control strategy's performance by accelerating the system's rise and peak times but slightly increases the output noise. The system's performance under noisy conditions reveals that the Dual Simplex Algorithm with Genetic Filter offers the most effective solution, followed by the Dual Simplex Algorithm, Genetic Filter, and conventional PID control. The conventional PID control, while simple, is outperformed by the other algorithms due to its lack of robustness against noise and oscillations. The systems' performance under noisy conditions is further explored through a comparison, with the Dual Simplex Algorithm with Genetic Filter emerging as the top performer, followed by the Dual Simplex Algorithm, Genetic Filter, and conventional PID control. The application of the Dual Simplex Algorithm with Genetic Filter successfully achieves a stable and smooth flight with a controlled rise and peak time, and a controlled output with a controlled rise and peak. The system's performance under realistic flight conditions highlights the importance of incorporating a derivative filter, further emphasizing the need for a performance optimization algorithm

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per transverse area known as the saturation momentum.  In certain large-energy situations within saturated conditions, an extensive characteristic gluing effect among gluons emerges, resulting in significant variations in physical processes at a fundamental level, an phenomenon known as geometrical scaling.  Historically, geometrical scaling was theoretically proposed for dedicated large Bjorken-x regions in high-energy eA scattering; however, it can also occur across a broader range of values of Bjorken-x, as low as approximately 0.3, as observed within numerous large-system ion collisions.  Notably, the phenomenon of geometrical scaling was recently experimentally confirmed for the first time within peripheral proton-proton and A-A collisions at sqrt(sNN) = 5.44 TeV using data obtained from the LHCb collaboration.  Furthermore, the phenomenon of geometrical scaling is anticipated to simultaneously occur across various range of values of Bjorken-x, as observed within high-energy eA scattering, and at ultra-high energy corresponding to LHC energies.  An thorough understanding of the relationship between the free parameters of the non-linear QCD equations and the value of saturation momentum, as well as the degree of gluon saturation, is achieved via a well-known procedure known as the scale transformation, resulting in the determination of the value of saturation momentum.  An example of scale transformation procedure is demonstrated for the non-linear QCD equations of both the DREs and BFKL equations, resulting in the determination of the value of saturation momentum as a function of the square of the square of the momentum transfer.  An extensive investigation has been conducted on the non-linear evolution equations of gluon distribution, as a result of which an alternative evolution equation of gluon distribution has been derived, as well as the determination of the value of saturation momentum via scale transformation procedure for the alternative evolution equation.  An extensive analysis has been conducted to establish a connection between the alternative evolution equation and the differential equations of motion for recombining gluons, as a result of which an experimental signature of the recombination of gluons has been identified.  An investigation has been conducted to establish a connection between the evolution equations of gluon distribution, as a result of which a relationship between the degree of gluon saturation and the value of saturation momentum as a function of the transverse area has been achieved via scale transformation

A comprehensive analysis of metallicity and photometric data for 83,142 low-metallicity stars in the open cluster NGC 6791 reveals a clear link between metal content and width of the luminosity distribution. For stars with the lowest metal levels, the distribution is Gaussian, but as metallicity increases, the distribution widens, taking on a Lorentzian shape. Our findings are consistent with previous studies of similar low-metallicity stars in the Galactic Bulge and low-metallicity blue horizontal branch stars. By comparing our data with synthetic spectra, we rule out varying surface gravity as the primary cause of amplitude dispersion. Furthermore, the Lorentzian shape of the luminosity distribution suggests that the cause of amplitude dispersion is due to a metallicity-dependent suppression of helium oscillations. Utilizing synthetic spectra to determine the expected helium oscillation amplitudes as a function of gravity and temperature, we create mock luminosity distributions that are then fitted with a Gaussian process using the GPZELDA package. Our mock distributions demonstrate that the GP model can replicate the observed Lorentzian shape, implying that a metallicity-dependent helium oscillation suppression is the most likely explanation for amplitude dispersion. We note that a physical mechanism behind the suppression, thought to be present in the operation of driver elements or the occurrence of convective overshoot, is required. Our data does not provide sufficient information to determine the primary driver of amplitude dispersion. However, the relationship between amplitude dispersion and surface gravity may indicate that the suppression is more prevalent in regions of higher surface gravity. Regardless of the underlying physics, the amplitude dispersion serves as a valuable indicator of the stellar mass distribution within open and globular clusters, particularly visible in the mass function as a 'valley of the giants'. Ultimately, the peculiar Lorentzian shape of the luminosity distribution of low-metallicity stars poses a new challenge to researchers, underscoring the need to further investigate the effects of helium oscillations in low-metallicity stellar populations. As an initial step, we recommend that mission concepts for future space missions include spectroscopy with high spectral resolutions as essential components, allowing researchers to directly observe and analyze individual helium oscillations in low-metallicity stars. When accomplished, this will provide a profound understanding of the complex dynamics at play in low-metallicity stellar populations, ultimately revealing more about the nature of the stellar mass distribution in the Milky Way. A distinguishing feature of machine learning models is their ability to handle complex datasets with high dimensionality, often producing predictive analyses superior to those of deductive methods. However, these models can be vulnerable to manipulations in datasets, such as gradients obfuscation attacks that can alter a model's classification outcomes without changing its parameters. To address this concern, we have created a suite of tools to investigate and analyze the stability of machine learning models. This includes a framework to test for local perturbation in model parameters and a method to measure the optimal parameters that would result in a specific model performance. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel, our application involves analyzing the financial literacy of individuals in Germany and demonstrating how the new tools can be utilized to find the most optimal parameters for measuring financial literacy. Additionally, we have discovered a notable connection between the optimal parameters generated by our methods and those of the well-established method of Item Response Theory. Furthermore, our results suggest that the optimal parameters generated by machine learning models are capable of providing valuable information that can be used to simulate realistic economic events and their effects on economic productivity in the actual economy. Consequently, our paper demonstrates that the evaluation of machine learning model predictions offers a new and valuable contribution to the field of econometrics. The code for our analysis and the tools that we have developed is publicly available through our repository on the Code Ocean platform. This will enable other researchers to easily employ these tools in their own studies and contribute to the development of the code to make it even more user-friendly. Such collaborative development on the Code Ocean platform has led to numerous successful contributions from other researchers in the past. An instance of this is the development of the peformer code which is part of the 2021 NAS Dataset Challenge and was significantly improved by contributions from other researchers. By taking advantage of this collaborative approach, we are confident that the code and the new tools that we have introduced can be further optimized and generate more accurate results in empirical studies. The novel tools that we have introduced in our study have the potential to expand the existing toolbox of machine learning model assessors and analysts, however their application is restricted to specific scenarios in which the classification outcomes in model output correspond to the actual class labels in the dataset that were used to train the model. Therefore, our study is more relevant in the context of supervised learning scenarios rather than semi or unsupervised learning scenarios. We've developed SQUID, a quantum clustering algorithm, which leverages parameter-free nature and adaptable metrics to produce high-quality output. Unlike traditional clustering methods, SQUID utilizes a quantum annealing process, facilitated by Adaptive Recurrent Quantum Annealing, ensuring its workings and output are fully traceable under probabilistic uncertainty. We validated SQUID's effectiveness by applying it to two datasets, obtaining results equivalent to those achieved by established clustering methods. With its well-documented, open-source nature, SQUID provides a reliable foundation for both quantum and classical machine learning approaches. We also explore its potential applications in unsupervised learning tasks, particularly for problem-solving in industry settings. Furthermore, we discuss training a classifier after extracting crucial features from a dataset using SQUID, contributing significantly to the field of Quantum Machine Intelligence. Finally, we speculate on SQUID's capabilities in dealing with multi-modal datasets and real-world unlabelled data, representing pivotal steps toward full implementation of Quantum Machine Intelligence. Moreover, we outline a series of experiments designed to determine the optimal arrangement of qubits within SQUID. We anticipate these findings to represent crucial milestones in the advancement of Quantum Machine Intelligence, ultimately leading to the widespread adoption of this concept. We also discuss a promising future research direction, where QMA is utilized not only as a solver but also as a generator, producing diverse solutions to a given problem. We examine multiple approaches to the application of QMA, starting with the simplest model that employs isolated clusters to generate solutions. Following this, we delve into a variation that is represented as a graph, allowing for its embedding onto a group of qubits. We then describe a method for transforming the produced solutions into points in classical parameter space. As an example of this concept's potential, we outline an experiment where an input string is transformed into multiple outputs, effectively serving as distinct answers to a given question. We speculate that this investment in research may eventually lead to significant breakthroughs in the field of Quantum Machine Intelligence. A forthcoming dissertation will elaborate on the described concepts and experiments.

Based on theory, these defects should produce distinguishable changes in the inhomogeneous broadening of their excited states in response to both nuclear and electron recoils. Given that nuclear recoils result in minimal distortion, this differentiation becomes particularly significant. Quantum information systems rely heavily on quantum channels, which are channel states mapping to free systems. A crucial aspect is performing quantum channel tomography, which involves reconstructing an unknown channel based on collected data. Current tomography methods struggle with low visibility due to the inherent characteristics of channel states. We show that by introducing shadow spaces in the Birkhoff inequality, visibilities of channel states can be significantly improved. Furthermore, this advancement enables more accurate state reconstruction in quantum channel tomography. Our research applies this improvement to two key scenarios: (1) verifying the completeness of a set of convergent quantum channels and (2) reconstructing an arbitrary quantum channel using only few probes. We achieve this by implementing a novel algorithm that effectively constructs a positive operator-valued measure from few probe data. Our findings indicate that the utility of the shadow space leads to enhanced visibility and, thus, more reliable channel state estimation. Additionally, this improvement enables the construction of accurate PVMs from limited probes, which was previously thought impossible by classical principles. Our implemented algorithms achieve nearly optimal results in both scenarios. The growing accessibility of low-cost, high-performance Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones is expanding their utilization in various real-world applications, particularly in multimedia transmission, surveillance, and mapping services. This research focuses on the strategy planning for UAVs to accomplish multiple objectives, which can include reducing communication delay and maintaining line-of-sight with ground stations. To tackle the computational complexity of this optimization problem, we introduce an efficient model predictive control (MPC) method that builds upon a linearization of the UAV's route, making it easier to simulate and predict its flight path. This approach also incorporates diverse weather conditions and allows the evaluation of various flight routes to determine the most suitable one. Furthermore, it accommodates various UAV types by estimating their flight time based on their specified capabilities, which is incorporated into the control function as an integral component. The outcomes indicate that our strategy is suitable for various UAV configurations and can provide substantial performance enhancements, even when the basic assumptions are slightly breached. The developed code is now publicly accessible on GitHub to facilitate future development and integration with other tools. The computational complexity of the control algorithm is approximately 0.2 milliseconds per time-step, making it possible for real-time strategy planning and adaptation. This approach is particularly suitable for application-layer control as it is capable of instantly adjusting the strategy in response to changes in UAV or ground station positions. This real-time responsiveness also enables the evaluation and selection of various ground stations or UAVs to optimize the strategy. This real-time control is made feasible due to the incorporation of instantaneous linearization of the non-linear flight dynamics of the UAV into the simulation model. The main drawback of this approach is the requirement for continuous data exchange between the UAV and the strategy planner, which is necessary for up-to-date strategy planning and adaptation. The development of fully autonomous UAVs is now possible due to the availability of various swarm optimization algorithms that are extremely efficient and effective in finding suitable parameter values to achieve specified objectives. The incorporation of the GPS location of the UAV and accurate mapping of the environment can facilitate up-to-date strategy planning and adaptation. Nonetheless, this approach may be prone to some limitations in the presence of obstacles as the simulation model assumes the presence of line-of-sight with ground stations. The development of novel swarm optimization algorithms is now highly recommended as the future of autonomous UAVs depends on their ability to seamlessly adapt to their changing environment. A key issue in quantum physics measurements involves conducting a sequence of 
operations with a machine that may fail, such as the Ramsey sequence used to 
measure field strengths. Since the experiment is prone to failures, the standard 
statistical analysis methods aren't effective, as they were designed for successful 
trials. This study presents a novel solution to overcome this challenge by 
adapting the Bayesian method originally applied to characterizing quantum gates 
in order to arrange experiments in a way that maximizes the information gained 
given the restricted number of successful measurements achievable within a set of 
attempts. By using this approach, the resulting measurements can be used to extract 
the Ramsey sequence mean estimate more effectively than traditional methods. 
Furthermore, the proposed approach can be easily extended to more complex 
measurements, such as those requiring low temperatures or high magnetic field 
precision, without significant increases in computational complexity. Initial results 
using simulated data demonstrate the proposed approach outperforms standard methods 
in estimating Ramsey sequence means. Finally, the theoretical foundations of this 
approach are carefully outlined, and potential extensions are explored including 
the addition of multiple measurement types and the use of optimality criteria outside 
of minimum variance. This extension is particularly desirable when considering 
temperature distribution measurements, for instance. Verification of this extended 
methodology using simulated data from a quantum magnetism experiment is soon to 
follow. Moreover, the source code for the experiment arrangement protocol remains 
available online for further evaluation and to facilitate its application in a 
variety of measurement schemes. 

Keywords: Ramsey method, Bayesian experiments, adaptive measurements, Ramsey
sequence, characterizing quantum gates, magnetic field strength measurements.

author's name M. P. Almeida.

Network centrality metrics measure node importance using various characteristics,
such as connectivity, node importance, and distance to other nodes. Unlike other
metrics that focus on local properties or computationally intensive community
definitions, Gromov centrality focuses on the entire network and is defined
mathematically through a triangle inequality excess (IE) framework. By scaling
the IE to network size, the centrality scales linearly with network size, and
due to its multi-scale nature, the method offers clear definitions of local,
group, and global centrality. Additionally, the method incorporates a factor
to account for node degree when calculating the IE, resulting in a metric that
more accurately reflects the behavior of individuals within the network,
illustrated by examples in human movement and social media messaging systems. 
The method demonstrates the potential to inform multi-scale surveillance and
analysis by providing detailed information about individuals, groups, and the
overall network.  The Gromov centrality metric outperforms existing metrics in
predicting important properties such as group formation and traffic patterns,
and it offers significant computational advantages, operating in real-time with
no additional data collection.  The code for the analysis is available on
github at https://github.com/uscinfo/nbc/gromov centrality. The empirical

This research examines bundles of matrix operators defined by a field or a local field, considering them under strict equivalence. A key finding shows that two bundles of matrix operators are strictly equivalent if and only if the local constancy of their central values can be represented as the sum of squares of integers. Additionally, we establish a strict equivalence criterion for bundles of matrix operators, and we provide an example of a bundle that fails this equivalence criterion. Moreover, this research investigates the properties of strongly central bundles of matrix operators and determines the conditions under which they can be decomposed into irreducible components. A key finding here is that every strongly central bundle of matrix operators has a finite number of irreducible components. Finally, this research defines and implements a novel invariant of bundles of matrix operators, which we call the 'order' invariant, and we demonstrate its utility in various contexts. Our analysis of this order invariant reveals that its value is always even for finite bundles of matrix operators but can take odd values for infinite bundles. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to homogeneous periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric periodic solution trajectories exhibits prevalence among initial conditions. These probabilistic analyses also establish the prevalence of stationary solution convergence, a prevalence which is exemplified by the quadratic family's behavior at its interval endpoint, x=2. Moreover, the Prousky-Steinman Theorem's archetypal prevalence results are found to be limited by a prominent exception, where a linearly stable cycle is shown to be prevalent yet not asymptotically stable, thus highlighting a prominent challenge to probabilistic analysis in discrete-time systems. A new approach to learning a generative model involves training an encoder that minimizes the differences between a sample's log likelihood and its approximate value based on lower-dimensional features. Unlike traditional techniques that rely on Monte Carlo methods, this model uses deterministic approaches to estimate these differences. However, these approaches often yield suboptimal representations due to their potential for bias. To overcome this limitation, this study develops a method to calculate a systematic bias, and then introduces the deep generative encoder, which incorporates this bias into its training. As a result, the DGE can learn accurate representations when maximum likelihood estimation is impossible, making it suitable for training deep generative models. Furthermore, this study explores the connection between the DGE and autoencoders that minimize reconstruction errors, and demonstrates its potential in training deep generative models. Examples illustrate that the DGE can be extended to deep models, and can also be used as a variational autoencoder that samples realistic data given a target distribution. The study also discusses its implications for variational and generative models. Importantly, the DGE provides a framework for estimating the parameters of these models without relying on Monte Carlo methods. Furthermore, the study demonstrates its capabilities in generating causal or underlying representations using a framework for identifying causal structures in graphical models. Representations from these examples are available online. The source code for these experiments can be found at https://github.com/jasg/mmlj/tree/deep-encoder. Lastly, this study considers the potential applications of the DGE in variational and generative models, and suggests future research directions. One potential direction involves extending the DGE to variational Bayesian inference on generative models. Similar to the DGE, this approach can explore the space of possible priors while minimizing approximately calculated samples using a maximum likelihood estimator, and can select the prior that yields the most accurate estimates. Importantly, the DGE allows for the calculation of a systematic bias, which can be used to determine the extent of bias in each prior. Consequently, this approach can avoid sampling biases, and as a result, it can learn accurate representations by incorporating the calculated bias into its training. We anticipate that these ideas will serve as a foundation for future research. The study is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.13155. The related GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/jasg/mmlj/tree/deep-encoder. The generated DGE results can be found at https://jasg.github.io/pmlj/data/dge.

Our study presents the first in-depth ethane and cyclopentadiene observations of a main-belt comet, alongside a comprehensive survey of carbon monosulfide and water, obtained from Comet C/2015 ER$_{61}$ (PanSTARRS) during its 2017 perihelion passage. Ethane and cyclopentadiene were detected at concentrations of 350$\pm$70 ppm and 320$\pm$60 ppm respectively, serving as the strongest evidence for the presence of frozen ethane in a main-belt comet. Conversely, CS was previously the sole derived carbon-bearing molecule in this type of comet, but our observations reveal a significantly reduced abundance, at 340$\pm$60$\times$10$^{10}$ cm$^{-3}$, exhibiting a high excitation temperature of 173$\pm$7 K and a primarily even rotational excitation temperature of 44$\pm$4 K. This discovery suggests the presence of a dispersed CS molecular layer, further supporting the hypothesis of an origin from the outer solar nebula. Our findings may have significant implications for the synthesis of heavy molecules in the snowline region of protoplanetary disks and provide an opportunity to study ethane's role in the formation of organic particles on Comet C/2015 ER$_{61}$ (PanSTARRS). Finally, the presence of a dispersed gas layer on this comet indicates that it may be necessary to revise the assumed gas surface density used in future missions designed to investigate the nebulae of main-belt and Jupiter trojans. In light of these discoveries, we recommend conducting comprehensive ethane and cyclopentadiene analysis in upcoming missions, and we further propose that C/2015 ER$_{61}$ (PanSTARRS) serves as an ideal test case to study the formation processes of these molecules. Our findings will have a critical impact on the exploration of the organic-rich environments found in some outer solar system bodies, and ultimately contribute to the understanding of their origins. Future investigations into the organic-rich targets, encompassing main-belt asteroids and Trojan planets, are poised to advance our comprehension of their constituent materials, driven by the success of the here-presented derivation of ethane and CS abundances in C/2015 ER$_{61}$ (PanSTARRS). We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis system that learns to generate speech from pre-recorded interviews. Unlike previous systems, our model is straightforward, using only two components and relies on an existing neural vocoder for synthesis. Our system directly predicts the spectrogram from the audio signal, bypassing the need for a separate feature extraction step. Additionally, it utilizes a simple and versatile normalization method. Our results indicate that this system can achieve high quality at a low computational cost, outperforming a more complex unservised model in both quality and efficiency. Furthermore, we observed that the effectiveness of the system depends on the quality of the input audio, with optimal results from high-quality, well-balanced audio contents such as interviews. Our model code will be publicly available in the future.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, incorporating a complex form of the essence model as a boundary to define the Hubble horizon's size within a mini superspace cosmological setup. We formulate two distinct cases, corresponding to real and imaginary coefficient values for the Tsallis energy density, denoted as $q_1$ and $q_2$. We solve the equations of motion for both scenarios, yielding static or dynamic universe models (similar to Lambda-CDM for $q_1$ and a model similar to de Sitter for $q_2$), and we then analyze the correspondence with observational data for both cases. Furthermore, we also examine the differences in behavior caused by the complex nature of the essence model as a boundary to the Hubble horizon's size. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, encompassing both real and complex form evaluations, thereby contributing to the understanding of holographic dark energy theories. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Although sentiment polarity can be considered as an emotional state, it is not an emotional expression of any kind. We hypothesize that capturing implicit emotions in texts is crucial for effectively understanding sentiment polarity. Unfortunately, labeled data for supervising models on emotional knowledge is scarce. We devised a novel, self-supervised pre-training approach to obtain a model that can represent explicit emotions and sentiment polarities. Subsequently, we applied this model to improve the accuracy of aspect-based sentiment analysis. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing countermeasures that rely on cross-attention for adapting to changing contexts. Moreover, the proposed model excels even when trained without the context of the aspect, thereby approximating the effect of incorporating emotional knowledge. All the code used in this research is openly available on our GitHub page. We believe that incorporating emotional knowledge holds the potential for enhancing the accuracy of sentiment analysis. Although supervised pre-training is often effective in mimicking the process of learning implicit emotions during natural language processing, we show that a more tailored, more sophisticated self-supervised pre-training approach can yield even greater benefits. Interestingly, a more refined self-supervised pre-training approach can lead to improved emotion recognition. Furthermore, combining a more refined self-supervised pre-training strategy with downstream training can substantially boost the accuracy of the machine learning model in the specific context of the product review. Ultimately, a more optimized self-supervised pre-training strategy leads to more robust sentiment analysis.

The concept of Executive Function is often described as "using the right brain cell" for decision-making and problem-solving, a process that creates new connections between brain cells, or as a critical function for controlling behaviors and regulating emotions. In the context of AI agents, a model with Executive Function would be one that can intentionally stray from its original goal, or not, when faced with a choice. Utilizing the idea of a "virtual brain," researchers defined a mathematical model of Executive Function and demonstrated its ability to enhance the performance of reinforcement learning agents by giving them the ability to follow rules and exhibit a range of behaviors. In addition to its ability to enhance agent performance, the model can also be used to analyze the characteristics of behaviors exhibited by human agents, or "level 0" Executive Function, and how they can be influenced by factors such as emotions, perception, attention, and memory. By examining cases of human behavior using the model, researchers were able to identify a new mechanism of human decision-making that involves a conflict between a agent's goal-oriented, or goal-affecting, behavior and its goal-transgressive, or goal-disregarding, behavior. This conflict, which is influenced by a agent's intention to follow rules and their ability to do so, leads to a variety of behaviors including, but not limited to, hesitation, regret, and a form of behavior known as "eating one's own tail." Furthermore, researchers were able to demonstrate that this conflict is influenced by a agent's intention to follow rules and their ability to do so, as well as their goal-oriented behavior and its relationship with their perception of the world, or "reality." Using the idea of a virtual brain and a range of computational methods, researchers were able to develop a novel form of machine learning known as Contrastive Value Strategy, or CVS, which is designed to help agents to develop and use a two-layered model of their environment, or "reality," and the benefits of different behaviors, or "value." This model, which is known as the CVS model, is based on the idea that there are two layers to most environments, or "reality," and that they can be influenced by factors including, but not limited to, the availability of food. This is known as the "two-layered food hypothesis," or TLFH, and it serves as the basis for a range of computational methods known as the two-layered summary of food, or TLFH. We studied the solar wind energy flow into the inner solar system using data from the Solar Wind Electrons, Aerosols and Dust experiment on board the Parker Solar Probe. These observations included data from the periods just before and after the solar equator passage in 2018 and 2019, focusing on three different solar distances ranging from 28 to 35.9 times the Earth's radius. Close approaches to the Sun enabled us to measure the solar wind energy output near the Sun, resulting in energy increases of 45% to 70%. The ratio of thermal to kinetic energy decreased from 0.1 to 0.05, while the temperature of the solar wind decreased significantly, dropping to a third of its former value. The solar wind energy measurements were accompanied by enhanced electron density and aerosol particle counts, along with increased electron flux, but the size of these aerosol particles did not change as the Sun was approached. The data indicated that the solar wind energy behavior could be better explained by the changes in the solar atmosphere pressure rather than the intensity of the magnetic field. A crucial discovery showed that the solar atmosphere pressure is not completely lost during the transition from the outer to the inner heliosphere, suggesting that about 30% of the pressure can still be preserved at a distance of 28 solar radii. This finding is consistent with theoretical simulations predicting that the solar atmosphere pressure is reduced, but not completely lost, near the Sun. Moreover, the data demonstrated that the ratio of the parallel to perpendicular magnetic field components, a measure of the magnetic field's anisotropy, did not follow the expected outcomes of the reconnection and turbulence scenarios, thereby favoring the reconnection theory. These observations, obtained in a historic first, provide the groundwork for a more thorough understanding of the solar wind behavior and help in maintaining stability in the solar system by explaining the solar wind's behavior close to the Sun. These stability efforts are facilitated through solar and auroral modeling, a comprehensive solar wind energy model, and Earth's magnetic field protection mechanisms, all facilitated by the invaluable data from PSP along with other laboratory and field experiments. A critical element of these modeling efforts involves the hydrodynamics modeling that has been successful in explaining various solar wind stability aspects for six solar cycles, a achievement facilitated through the collaborative solar community efforts. In this research, we examine an optomechanical system with fast and slow light, featuring a single cavity embedded in a microwave environment where the cavity's resonance frequency is modulated by a mechanical oscillator. To account for the microwave behavior, we incorporate the $q$-deformation of the electromagnetic field. Our findings reveal that this system exhibits enhanced transmission patterns with both fast and slow light phenomena occurring within a defined frequency range of the mechanical oscillator. Notably, the number of peaks in these patterns depends on the parameter $c$, indicating a system based on $q$-deformation can produce clear and distinct light transmission patterns with a wider range of mechanical oscillator frequencies. Furthermore, our analysis shows that by adjusting parameters such as the optical resonance frequency and Rabi frequency, the system's transparency can be optimized. Our results also demonstrate that fast and slow light can occur simultaneously in the system when the mechanical oscillator's frequency falls within a specific range. Additionally, we have identified a range of parameters allowing for nearly 100% light transmission in the system when the mechanical oscillator's frequency is within a certain range. Our research shows that adjusting the mechanical oscillator's frequency can significantly impact the system's light transmission patterns. Finally, our analysis confirms that the system's optical properties can be effectively modified by adjusting the mechanical oscillator's frequency. The results presented demonstrate the potential for robust and precise optical phenomena in optomechanical systems with a $q$-deformed microwave environment. These findings have the potential to contribute to the development of innovative optical experiments and studies in various mechanical effects. Moreover, our research demonstrates the feasibility of adjusting optical phenomena in optomechanical systems through careful selection of mechanical oscillator frequencies. The presented model is grounded in classical mechanics and electromagnetic principles, allowing for the development of novel mechanical and optical effects that could potentially find application in emerging research areas. Notably, our research reveals the significance of adjusting optical and mechanical coupling in $q$-deformed optomechanical systems, leading to the prediction of increased transparency and light transmission. Our findings show that these effects can become pronounced at specific times in the mechanical oscillator's cycle. The presented results validate the potential of robust and precise light transmission in optomechanical systems with a $q$-deformed microwave environment. The study of these effects using photonic and electrical approaches may lead to the development of efficient optical phenomena in optomechanical systems with a wide range of mechanical oscillator frequencies. In a theoretical context, we analyze the implications of mirror symmetry breaking on a specific type of quasiparticle state, identified as the adverse R-parity state. This particular state corresponds to a collective excitation, characterized by the same collective behavior as the R-parity state, but with a reversed rotational pattern. In order to study this phenomenon, we utilized the Two-Rotors Model as a practical example to demonstrate the existence of such quasiparticle states and to identify their distinctive characteristics. Furthermore, we observed that these adverse R-parity states can potentially serve as indicators of mirror symmetry breaking. Notably, their dynamic and static properties will undergo significant changes following a break in the mirror symmetry. In general, the adverse R-parity states exhibit dynamic behavior that differs from their R-parity counterparts, characterized by a change in signature and the presence of mirror symmetry-allowed transitions. This can be seen in both the general case and the Two-Rotors Model, where various theoretical indicators such as energy systematics, degeneracies in the one-quantum state, and the presence of chiral dipole modes can confirm the adverse R-parity collective excitation. In the case of the Two-Rotors Model, our findings reveal that the adverse R-parity states exhibit a two-fold degeneracy in the one-quantum state and possess a specific chiral dipole mode. This chiral behavior is a distinctive feature of mirror symmetry-allowed transitions, distinct from the chirality observed in R-parity states, which exhibits a single-fold degeneracy. In conclusion, our analysis of the adverse R-parity states provides significant insights into the collective excitation phenomenon and serves as crucial indicators of mirror symmetry breaking. Additionally, their dynamic behavior is distinctly different from their R-parity counterparts, indicating that they are essential for understanding the adverse R-parity collective excitation in a specific type of system. In particular, their presence can potentially shed light on the role of mirror symmetry in the physics of such systems. This research explores theoretical indicators of adverse R-parity states as collective excitations, demonstrating their distinct characteristics based on their difference from R-parity states. These adverse R-parity states are specific examples of mirror-symmetry-allowed transitions and exhibit a unique set of properties, differing from their R-parity counterparts, which can potentially be observed in experiments involving Two-Rotors Mirrors and other systems bounded by deformed mirrors in three dimensions. A novel neural network approach, distinct from the conventional neuron-arc-length formulation, directly integrates mean values of spatial nodes, whereas those values are typically calculated by integrating over discrete grid points using neural networks. This results in a more streamlined framework with fewer parameters. Furthermore, we prove the convergence of the discrete equation to its continuous counterpart under certain conditions. Extensive numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the efficiency of the new method, and results indicate that it can achieve high accuracy with fewer degrees of freedom compared to traditional neural network methods. Examples involving the heat and Poisson equations are also used to demonstrate the method's capability to yield accurate solutions without requiring additional parameters. Moreover, we successfully extend this approach to solve the Navier-Stokes equations with large time steps, and our results are in line with theoretical findings. Notably, we also obtain an upper limit for the error in time, and our numerical method outperforms a high-order finite difference method in this aspect. The method is also capable of handling non-linear equations by incorporating a rescaling technique, and this is illustrated by solving the Burgers equation. Where relevant, we compare our approach with existing neural network methods and provide a detailed analysis of its performance. The method presented in this work possesses a straightforward implementation, and we believe it has the potential to be an useful tool for solving various types of partial differential equations. The associated source code can be found at https://github.com/huanghao123/CmeanNEU. 

KeyWords: neural networks, parabolic PDEs, hyperbolic PDEs, Navier-Stokes equations, high-order finite difference method, large time steps, robust transport, non-linear equations, heat and Poisson equations. In this scenario, the static observer remains unperturbed; consequently, the manifestation of the Unruh effect can only be detected through the evolution of an initially entangled state between the static and accelerating observers. The entanglement of this initial state over time signals the emergence of the Unruh effect via a process known as the Berry phase, where its rate of change defines the temperature of the Unruh effect. The evolution of the entangled state can be described using a Hamiltonian root of the Berry phase, where solving this Hamiltonian allows for the calculation of the Unruh effect temperature via the geometric potential it contains. Applying this approach to a specific case, we find that the static observer must remain in a state separated from its past and future to directly observe the Unruh effect via its geometric potential. Furthermore, we determine a suitable laboratory setup for the timelike Unruh scenario, where a state separated from its past and future can be achieved with a particle separated from its emitted photons. The approach enables the Unruh effect to be detected via measurements of the geometric potential or the Hamiltonian it contains. Consequently, measurements of the geometric potential can serve as a scalable method for detecting the Unruh effect in laboratory conditions and potentially even via quantum simulations. Lastly, we reflect on the broader implications of the approach for fundamental theories. The approach enables the detection of the Unruh effect in a laboratory setting, where it can serve as a testing ground for quantum field theories in flat spacetime. This paper seeks to address the current shortage of data and methods for processing incident extraction across multiple languages. A new multilingual dataset, MEE, containing violent incident descriptions from online news sources in three languages, has been created. The dataset comprises French, Arabic, and English, and each text related to a specific country where the incident occurred has been labeled. The dataset's utility is illustrated through experimental results, including the first attempt at incident extraction for Arabic and French, and further analysis on an English subset to identify key characteristics of the dataset. The full MEE dataset is publicly available.

This proof relies on an earlier implication that when pulled forward to a more refined bundle, forms of degree d are at least O(|E/F| to the power of d) in magnitude. For any refinement of E/F and any vector bundle of rank r over E, we establish that the Chern forms of degree two or more in a bundle of rank r over E, are at least O(|E/F| to the power of 2) in magnitude. Moreover, we demonstrate that push-forward formulae for Chern classes in a bundle of rank r over E, are at least O(|E/F| to the power of 2) in magnitude when pulled forward to a more refined bundle. Interestingly, we derive an appropriate push-forward formula for refined Hirzebruch genera when pulling forward a vector bundle of Chern forms of degree d that are at least O(|E/F| to the power of d) in magnitude. This generates an extensive list of genera push-forward formulae for various, modified forms of Chern classes, Chern-Weil forms, and Hirzebruch genera, which hold under the condition that the push-forward is performed to a bundle of rank less than or equal to the dimension of E, a condition which far more readily provides useful, applicable results than the earlier, more restrictive condition of being pulled forward to a more refined bundle, which was shown to produce push-forward formulae of magnitude O(|E/F| to the power of 2). Furthermore, we leverage these more general, useful, applicable push-forward formulae to prove that Chern classes, Chern-Weil forms, and Hirzebruch genera of manifold bundles are zero, and that the Chern classes and Chern-Weil forms of projective varieties are zero. A low-mass X-ray binary system's inner disk can make a significant contribution to the variability observed in the outer disk when the outer disk is fully established. To quantify this impact, we studied Cyg X-1 in the hard state using multiple observations with XMM-Newton and INTEGRAL, focusing on the inner disk's variability. We observed that the inner disk's long-term evolution caused a natural variability pattern, which was similar across different energies. This inner disk's variability accounted for approximately 40-70% of the outer disk's variability in the 3-80 keV energy range. We further analyzed this by examining the inner disk's free-fall time and the outer disk's natural variability time. The inner disk's free-fall time ranged from 11-29 minutes, which was consistent with the outer disk's natural variability time. Using this, we calculated that the inner disk's free-fall time could be as short as multiple minutes or as long as several hours. This would have significant implications if the inner disk's variability was typically driven by inner disk evaporation rather than stellar activity. However, considering our specific results and adding them to previous observations, we found that the inner disk's variability did not significantly contribute to the outer disk's variability in any of the specific observations examined. This was likely due to the outer disk's variability being primarily driven by a corona located significant distances beyond the innermost observed variability component. Therefore, the outer disk's variability was typically not greatly affected by the inner disk's variability. Nevertheless, the inner disk's variability did contribute to the outer disk's variability on occasion when the outer disk's variability was primarily driven by boundary layer variability. This was seen in the 2008 observation when the inner disk's variability contributed to nearly all of the outer disk's variability. Furthermore, in some instances, the inner disk's variability could contribute significantly to the outer disk's variability in future observations, which would occur when the outer disk's variability is driven by a corona located closer to the neutron star than the innermost observed variability component. This could potentially be seen in future observations through further analysis of various low-mass X-ray binary states. Our specific results from the 2008 observation placed an upper bound on how much inner disk variability could contribute to the outer disk's variability, which was 100%. Although the physical ether has been disproven, a mathematical representation of an ether-like term within non-relativistic quantum mechanics remains feasible. In our study, we derive a mathematical model for an ether-like term based on the non-abelian U(3) symmetry. The resulting expression relates to a U(3)-invariant tensor that can be applied to any U(3)-invariant Hamiltonian. This is followed by the demonstration of its significance in a simple harmonic oscillator and a hard-cube potential at both zero and finite temperatures. The inclusion of this term in the fermonic ethertensor Hilbert space results in the thermodynamic properties of odd-particle systems being modified in terms of temperature dependence. The distinct behavior of ethertensor modified fermonic systems is observed in the thermal occupation numbers, energy per particle, and specific heat capacity. The ether-like term is also shown to influence the thermal fluctuations in the x-component of the fermonic ethertensor modified hard-cube system. The total thermal fluctuation in the ethertensor modified fermonic hard-cube particles can be reduced by raising the temperature, and the reduced fluctuations at zero temperature correspond to a U(3)-invariant degenerate ground state. The ethertensor modified Harrel-Slater Hard-Cube Particle System displays a distinct and non-degenerate zero-temperature QCD-like phase at low enough particle densities, in addition to the degenerate ground state. Researchers have long sought to unify syntax and semantics parsing but the enhanced performance of rule-based syntax analysis across languages suggests further exploring this combination of parsing methods. Drawing from the foundations of Montague grammar, we introduce a novel semantic parser that seamlessly integrates syntax analysis by the state-of-the-art Universal Declarative Parsing (UDP) system. This parsed syntax is then translated into Montague grammar-like tree structures through a procedure called "universal meaning parsing". The resulting system is called Joint Universal Parsing (JUP). Experimental findings for simple logical statements indicate that JUP operates with similar or superior efficiency when compared to UDPA, used alone for syntax-only analysis, while opening up opportunities for its further development and application on more complex languages. Moreover, JUP offers a new approach to implementing "syntax is semantics" idea. The source code of JUP is publicly available at https://github.com/aczieberer/jup-udpa. 

Video presentation of JUP is available at: 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KqspoKsR8Og (IIIS Lunch-Time Seminar Series) 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QoYkxkx6Y6E (CILS Seminar Series). 
Both seminars offer additional explanations and demonstrations of JUP's inner workings. 

Researchers whose work is closely related to JUP include Dr. Zhang's team, University of California, who implemented Montague grammar for Russian parsing as part of their broader linguistic inquiry into semantic parsing, though the traditional syntax analysis was not integrated into their system. 

The current JUP is a prototype that still requires further enhancements such as its existing conceptual simplicity, limited semantic language capabilities, slow processing speed, particularly when dealing with more intricate logical statements, and the absence of implemented syntax analysis, though it could be potentially replaced with the state-of-the-art transformer models. Moreover, additional features are needed including its compatibility with other UDPA-compatible syntax analysis systems, such as the state-of-the-art byte-level neural syntax analyzer, and the broadening of its language to include more than just English. 

The resulting improved parsing system could then be applied in various fields including natural language understanding, machine learning, computational linguistics, information extraction, Montague grammar-based computational semantics, and the like. 

The idea for JUP originated in the lecture series on the state-of-the-art transformer models' semantics analysis by Prof. Dr. Guangping Le, Fudan University, as well as the seminars on the various applications of the UDPA system

The formation of magnetically arrested disks around magnetically driven disks in binary neutron star mergers offers an ideal setting for efficiently producing jets and neutrino-induced outflows that can last for months. This is particularly beneficial for generating less intense jets that persist for a longer period than typically expected from previously predicted values. By analyzing a range of disk configurations with varying parameters, we have conducted a comprehensive study on the mechanical effects of these outflows using one-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. Our findings indicate that the gas dynamics in these persistent outflows is characterized by significant cooling effects from neutrino emission, particularly in low-temperature regions, which reduces gas temperature by approximately 30%. Although this cooling effect reduces the initial mass of the outflow, its impact on the rate of spindown of the neutron star and the overall gas dynamics in the disk is relatively minor. However, the main consequence of cooling on the flow results in a faster rate of acceleration for higher-mass disks, resulting in weaker magnetic field strength at maximum elevation. This is notably contrasted by the presence of a persistent magnetic field boundary layer that contributes to increased magnetic field strength at maximum elevation. Nonetheless, the main attribute of these persistent outflows remains their dependence on a strong magnetic field, which significantly affects the resulting outflow morphology and the supernova explosion mechanism. Our predicted rates of energy release, ranging from 5% to 25% of the total energy release from neutrinos within the initial 540 seconds, are substantial enough to cause significant effects on the surrounding disk material, resulting in the ejection of less massive gas compared to the expected mass for standard magnetic disk outflows. Conversely, the persistent nature of these outflows allows for the ejection of more protons than electrons at earlier times, resulting in a shift towards a more oblate magnetic field configuration. This is opposed to the expected magnetic field structure in magnetic disk outflows, which shows a net electron dominance due to photoionization. Our predicted difference in magnetic field structure leads to variations in the resulting supernova nucleus mass and the rate of SN explosion based on the interaction between the neutron star and the persistent outflow. Ultimately, the resulting mass of the SN nucleus is influenced by the persistent nature of these outflows and depends on several factors, including the mass of the persistent outflow and the rate of SN explosion. Early-type galaxies with exceptionally large mass have a limited number of nearby satellite galaxies that they can absorb through mergers, yet they continue to exhibit stellar structures that suggest they have undergone multiple mergers. We investigated this paradox by analyzing data from a sample of 44 massive galaxies, finding that they have an average of four to six neighboring galaxies that are close enough to be absorbed through mergers. By utilizing tidal-dwarf candidate catalogs, we calculated a merger rate of 0.26 per unit galaxy mass, which is significantly higher than previous estimates. We also discovered that the ratio of tidal features to total galaxy light is 5-8%, which indicates that these galaxies have sufficient material to fuel a rate of 0.26 per unit galaxy mass for 0.84 Gyr or more. We propose that mass loss due to tidal stripping, rather than mergers, is the primary source of these galaxies' mass distribution, which is reflected in their outer diffuse mass components. These findings support the long-standing theory that these massive galaxies formed through mass loss due to tidal stripping, rather than mergers. However, they appear to be at odds with available simulation data, which preferentially produce mergers over tidal stripping in the formation of these galaxies. We also observed a potential issue with how galaxy mergers are detected in these simulations, which might contribute to the discrepancy with our findings. Alternatively, our results could imply that simulated galaxy mergers occur later in the galaxies' lifetimes than their observed rates of mass distribution. We suggest that these discrepancies could potentially be resolved by examining simulated galaxies' properties on a per-galaxy basis, rather than treating mergers as a universal phenomenon. Before pursuing this investigation further, we noticed that our findings may also imply that simulated galaxy mergers are contaminated by the inclusion of accretion, which could result in the formation of in-situ stars, whereas our observations likely capture the effects of tidal stripping, which does not lead to in-situ star formation in these galaxies. Recent studies have shown that language models possess inherent capabilities similar to text-to-speech systems, allowing them to visually perceive their environment even if they aren't actually able to see. To further investigate this notion, our study aims to develop a method enabling large language models to incorporate visual information to enhance text generation. Building on existing research, we propose a new framework called the Observer Framework, allowing large language models to access a visual context to support text generation more effectively. To put our proposed framework to the test, we created the Observing NLP lead20k dataset, a substantial dataset combining natural images with corresponding prompts and generated text, used to evaluate the framework's performance. Additionally, we introduced a new evaluation metric called the observation loss, measuring how well visual information aligns with the generated text. To evaluate the framework's effectiveness, we employed BART as our base model, integrating it with multiple techniques, including a masked language model pre-training approach, a dual decoder design, and separate image and text encoders. Our experiments demonstrate that by leveraging the Observer Framework, language models can utilize visual information to generate more coherent text, as supported by both automatic and human evaluations of the generated text. Furthermore, our study reveals that a significant proportion of the observed environment consists of irrelevant information; thus, developing effective methods to filter out irrelevant content is necessary for boosting text generation performance. To achieve this goal, we introduced an image filtering approach based on few-shot learning, significantly reducing the impact of irrelevant image components and thereby enhancing the overall performance of the Observer Framework. Overall, our study provides new insights into the visual capabilities of large language models and offers a novel framework for integrating visual information to improve text generation effectiveness. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD that addresses the task of training neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network training into a continuous optimization problem that can be solved. Our algorithm relies on three key components - the initialization of models with suitable parameters, a unique updating rule for parameters, and a specific approach to delay rounding, which enables convergence. We provide a theoretical validation of AskewSGD's convergence by proving its subgradient property and convexity under certain conditions. When applied to LeNet-5, ResNet, MobileNet, and VGG models, AskewSGD demonstrates superior performance by achieving lower accuracy losses compared to other state-of-the-art methods on various quantized neural network benchmarks. Its efficiency allows it to complete training in less than 10 minutes on a GPU, with significantly reduced resources and a simplified codebase. Furthermore, AskewSGD's results on both synthetic and real datasets outperform other optimization techniques such as SGD, SignSGD, Uniquad, and L2Ridge, also surpassing recently improved versions of these methods. AskewSGD's performance on CIFAR10-RMSProp benchmark indicates that it recovers up to 90% of the performance loss introduced by quantization, which is a 2 to 5 times greater recovery compared to other techniques. Our results show that AskewSGD's unique design allows for a substantial improvement in performance for neural networks with quantized weights. The source code for AskewSGD is available at https://github.com/alexeyufimtsev/askewsdc/askewsdc.py. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05900) for details.
