The ALICE experiment has measured the production of prompt and non-prompt D mesons in proton-proton collisions at 5.02 TeV, as reported in the study. D meson production was found at three different rapidity intervals: in the mid-rapidity range with transverse momentum greater than 4 GeV/c for both prompt and non-prompt mesons, and greater than 8 GeV/c for prompt mesons and greater than 20 GeV/c for non-prompt mesons in the forward-rapidity range. These results were compared with theoretical models that predict different transverse momentum spectra for prompt and non-prompt mesons, showing that the data follows the trend of the PYTHIA 8 model with the monash2013 tuning. Moreover, the study evaluated the transverse momentum dependence of non-prompt to prompt D meson ratio, examining various factors that influence it, such as charm quark strangeness suppression, dependent on the state's kinematics, and observed that for mid-rapidity range, the ratio remains nearly constant at around 0.24, independent of the meson's transverse momentum, and also at around 0.25, independent of the event multiplicity, at both the forward and mid-rapidities. These results agree with the calculations of two theoretical models, pYTHIA 8 with the monash2013 tuning and COLOR-PROMPT + SILICHE, but not with the calculation from eprompt, which shows a dependence of the ratio on the transverse momentum of the meson. These ratios do not exhibit significant changes when examined over different centralities and rapidity ranges. The ratio remains consistent with predictions from models that describe the formation of heavy-flavour jets as a combination of prompt and non-prompt components. The study also derived model-independent estimates of the average transverse momentum dependence of the non-prompt to prompt D meson production ratio, as well as estimates for minimum bias and forward rapidity ranges. These estimates will be helpful for future studies that aim to understand the relationship between the non-prompt to prompt D meson production ratio and the transverse momentum of the meson. These measurements will also be useful in establishing constraints for the value of the strangeness suppression factor for charm quarks in the unquenching K factor of the PYTHIA 8 model. developed at Fermilab to serve both scientific research and applications in quantum computing. 
Feasibility studies have been conducted, and the magnetron design has been developed, paving the 
way for a demonstration experiment. This experiment will utilize superconducting radio-frequency

and the utilization of existing cleanrooms. A 2.0 K cryogenic system, encompassing cryogenic components, 
has been assembled and tested, and a 1.0 K cryogenic system is currently under development. A 0.5 m x 0.5

quantum computing. This paper presents an overview of the magnetron concept, associated cryogenic 
components, experimental setup, and potential applications in quantum computing.

Previous studies into the most common errors made when using cryptographic libraries were conducted within the community, focusing on client-side development: researchers analyzed source code from open-source repositories, conducted surveys, or gathered information through expert judgment, ultimately identifying a limited set of error types. In contrast, we have conducted the first comprehensive analysis of actual errors found in deployed crypto code by scraping issues from GitHub, an extensive source of information on how crypto algorithms are employed. Our results show that errors found on GitHub differ significantly from those previously reported; the substantial number of unique error reports indicates that many more issues remain unreported, and we provide new insights into client-side crypto issues based on our findings. Furthermore, we have developed the first open-source tool capable of automatically detecting incorrect cryptographic primitives usage, which we have successfully applied to analyze the issues of several prominent cryptographic libraries. Through this analysis, we have demonstrated the significant cryptographic exposure posed by incorrect usage of the SHA-224 and AES-GCM algorithms. Like CryPy, which checks Python crypto errors, we propose a new tool called PyCryptCheck that can scan locally deployed Python applications to detect and report incorrect usage of cryptographic primitives, potentially mitigating related security vulnerabilities. By shedding light on the existing crypto issues, we hope to encourage developers to correct their code and make deployment more secure. The source code, data, and results are available for further research. The study was conducted on GitHub's Core Issue dataset with 246 million total issues (as of March 2022), which we annotated with 206 unique error types after applying the filtering process. Historically, cryptographic errors have been difficult to classify; to overcome this, we employed a novel taxonomy by mapping issues into six broad error types and 13 common error categories. Our analysis clearly shows that errors found on GitHub notably differ from those previously reported. The prominent error types identified through the study (sorted by frequency) include low-level issues such as MD5 hash computations, AES implementations, SHA-256 hashing, RSA signing/verifying, HMAC usage, ECDSA operations, ECDH computations, DSA operations, as well as correct but less secure alternatives like SHA-1 hashing or AES in the CBC mode without MAC. Conversely, error types that were previously considered common, such as RSA encryption or AES in the CTR mode, were surprisingly absent from the deployed code. Furthermore, issues that affect performance, such as slow and obsolete algorithms like DSA or SHA-1, were still found in the deployed code, indicating that developers tend to underestimate the exposure to security vulnerabilities.

We propose a novel framework, 'variable design matrix inversion', where data matrices can be modified freely. However, developing an efficient algorithm for this type of inversion is highly challenging, particularly under strict sparsity constraints. To address this issue, we introduce a 'non-uniform sparse prediction network' based on the proximal average theory, which effectively approximates the optimal solution by minimizing the proximal average objective function. We further develop a practical'seismic reflectivity inversion using non-uniform sparse prediction network' based on the wavelet convolutional norm and proximal average theory. Our numerical experiments confirm the superiority of the proposed method in terms of computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, especially when dealing with complex seismic data characterized by non-uniform sparse patterns. We believe that our variable design matrix inversion framework holds the potential to become a standard technique in seismic inversion and hydrocarbon production optimization. We intend to further improve the precision of the proposed method by incorporating additional constraints such as non-differentiable functions, and exploring the potential of developing a semi-unsupervised model that can simultaneously estimate seismic wavelet convolutions and sparse patterns. Results indicate that a set-valued approach yields more accurate outcomes and is more suitable for analysis. To resolve this issue, an innovative system has been developed, consisting of a formal specification generator and a conversion assistant. The former module translates city requirements into a formal model, while the latter module offers guidance and support, enabling city planners to refine their requirements and ensure their correctness before they are translated. To achieve this goal, the system was designed to utilize knowledge representation methods, specifically describing City Requirements as Ontology (CRO). In addition, the system incorporates a formal model checker like Alloy, which generates CRO instances to facilitate the understanding of city requirements. Furthermore, the system's agility allows city planners to make modifications at any stage of the translation process, with the assistance of the conversion assistant. A recent discovery has highlighted the potential for leveraging user-defined error patterns in the construction of quantum error correction codes, rather than solely relying on universal quantum gates. This study examines the application of a hidden inverses protocol to correct errors in superconducting quantum circuits, utilizing a single auxiliary qubit and a variational phase shift gate. Through simulations and experimental verification, we demonstrate that this protocol can effectively correct a single-phase-flip error in any qubit within a quantum register. Furthermore, we evaluate the scalability and flexibility of the protocol, showing it to be both highly efficient and adaptable. An added benefit of this protocol is that it facilitates the simultaneous execution of multiple quantum operations, a characteristic we term'synergistic computing'. This'synergistic computing' phenomenon is explored in detail and is shown to be a natural consequence of the hidden inverses protocol. The time-saving potential of this protocol is also quantified, illustrating a significant 50% reduction in the time required to perform two quantum operations compared to conventional methods. Lastly, we outline the limitations of the protocol and suggest potential research paths for its further development. Overall, our research demonstrates that the hidden inverses protocol is a valuable tool for quantum error correction in superconducting quantum devices. Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the Cope-Palm theorem, we examine the patterns of extreme sea level events that occur in tandem with wind speed. This multivariate approach accounts for the underlying spatial relationships in the data through the specification of a stable, multivariate spatial process, enabling us to estimate the extremes' natural covariance and provide a theoretical framework for the probability of joint events. By applying this model to sea level and wind data from Australian locations, we demonstrate the significance of considering joint extremes, identify correlations consistent with local transportation mechanisms, and highlight the effectiveness of using filter-based estimation to handle the computational challenges associated with multivariate extreme analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate how the model's extensions can accommodate a variety of extreme events, such as storms and cyclones, providing a potential method for predicting extreme marine environments. 

The findings from this research appear in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C, under the title 'Multivariate spatial conditional extremes for extreme marine environments'. 

The associated R code can be found in the'rextext' package on CRAN and on GitHub at https://github.com/oliverbridge/rextext.

A new, systematic method referred to as the Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian equations. This method involves a three-step process analogous to the canonicalization process for Lie algebras, leveraging bi, tri, and quadric relations to eliminate Lie-Poisson brackets and their derivatives, ultimately retaining a Poisson tensor. Notably, the key bi, tri, and quadric relations remain unchanged throughout the process, while the Poisson tensor's structure becomes the primary indicator of the system's integrability. Although the additional steps are required to obtain the Hamiltonian form, the resulting Hamiltonians are unique and represent a specific cohomological class. The method has been successfully demonstrated through the canonicalization of the heavy top, Helmholtz Hamiltonian, and Euler-Poisson systems. Furthermore, the study highlighted the need for a quadric condition to emerge during the final step of the canonicalization process, similar to the Virasoro-Chasles reciprocity relation. The proposed method provides a standardized approach for Lie-Poisson systems, including applications where Lie algebras are not applicable. Additionally, the study offers a framework for representing Lie-Poisson systems through the Clebsch variables, which can be utilized for various purposes, including numerical integration and geometry studies. The proposed technique has been implemented using a Julia package available at https://github.com/ivaniliev/clebsch_canonization.jl. The package's performance is illustrated through four practical examples. Due to the low visibility of COVID-19 lesions on chest CT scans, experts rely heavily on serological tests, which, however, have significant drawbacks of their own. Recently, there has been a significant interest in using artificial intelligence to help identify COVID-19 patients by analyzing lung scans. Although contact tracing has accelerated this process, using standard CT scans remains challenging because of the small size of COVID-19 lesions and the lack of mammography experts. To overcome these challenges, we developed an innovative machine learning framework that incorporates a capsule network to detect COVID-19 patients from low-dose CT scans, which outperformed all other models by incorporating multiple features, such as respiratory segmentation and infection detection. In particular, we incorporated a filtering system based on a U-Net architecture, which efficiently isolated the lungs while removing noise, followed by a refined capsule network that effectively detected COVID-19 lesions. To further enhance the accuracy of our model, we employed a curriculum learning strategy, which simulates the process of increasing the intensity of features in real-world situations. Additionally, we utilized a dataset consisting of 1088 patients with COVID-19 and 1168 non-infected patients, which we preprocessed by applying respiratory segmentation to isolate the lungs and remove extraneous information. Upon pre-processing the scans, we found that our framework achieved an impressive accuracy of 98.5% and a loss of 0.2% in fairness, which significantly surpasses all existing literature. We also conducted an additional 1000-fold cross-validation test to assure the reliability of our model, which we made publicly available on https://github.com/ongarofal/r2dcnn_covid19. In summary, we developed a state-of-the-art framework that efficiently detects COVID-19 patients from low-dose CT scans by incorporating a capsule network, respiratory segmentation, and a curriculum learning strategy. To further enhance the visibility of COVID-19 lesions, we incorporated a filtering system based on a U-Net architecture. To ensure the efficacy of our model, we conducted an extensive evaluation by performing a 1000-fold cross-validation test. We also made the dataset and source code publicly available on https://github.com/ongarofal/r2dcnn_covid19. What's more, our framework has the potential to be applied not only to COVID-19 but also to the detection of other diseases such as pneumonia and cancer from low-dose CT scans. A preliminary study on optimizing the layout of satellites within a Low-Earth Orbit constellation is conducted to determine the most efficient spatial arrangement, defining efficiency as the minimal distance between satellite footprints on the Earth's surface. Three variables are considered in the analysis: the number of active satellites in the constellation, the orbit width, and the replenishment rate, to identify the best configurations for different space-based applications. We find that, for systems with continuous data transmission, the optimal layout involves satellites on the orbit's equatorial plane with interstitial gaps between orbit circles. However, as the replenishment rate of inert satellites increases, the optimal configuration shifts to a two-layered structure, with active satellites on the equatorial plane and inert satellites at angular distances from the former, positioned in a circular pattern. The study further shows that moving inactive satellites to this intermediate layer can reduce space usage and delay the need for re-orbiting inert satellites, while increasing the replenishment rate in a growing constellation optimizes space usage under certain conditions. Moreover, the study demonstrates that arranging inactive satellites at angular distances from the active satellite layer minimizes space usage and lifetime extension via re-orbiting. Conversely, this configuration also increases collision risks, prompting the need for measures to mitigate this conflict between space efficiency and safety considerations. The study highlights potential applications and challenges of this optimal efficiency configuration, including trade-offs between space efficiency and collision risks. Ultimately, the research lays out a framework for future optimization and presents a method for promoting space efficiency and reducing waste in Low-Earth Orbit constellations. These theories encompass various models such as the double field theory and the novel three-field theory proposed in our previous work. By adopting a specific background solution with multiple space-like directions with opposite signs, we demonstrate the feasibility of applying the $S$-matrix method, which yields well-defined results in this specific context. Moreover, we automate the computation of the $S$-matrix using a map of the dual field and expand our calculation to the higher-derivative terms of the three-field theory for the first time. Furthermore, we suggest a specific interpretation of the two-particle $S$-matrix and provide empirical evidence that it behaves as a weakly singular function. Utilizing the optical theorem, we calculate the cross-sections of the elastic scattering processes involved and observe that they exhibit finite limits when one of the momenta approaches zero. However, the cross-sections do not display momentum dependence invariants in the three-field theory. Conversely, we demonstrate that a specific effective field theory derived from the three-field theory does exhibit momentum dependence invariants, which are also present in its dual description. Ultimately, we outline further research directions inspired by these findings. This model takes into account an external force that introduces instability and is constrained by no-slip boundary conditions. The goal of our work is to stabilize such systems through finite dimensional feedback controls, even when initially near unstable equilibrium states. To achieve this, we employ a sophisticated mathematical approach that utilizes H\"older continuous control and the Barles-Brin solution technique to navigate nonlinear problem resolutions. This research yields results in critical Lebesgue and Besov spaces, thus covering a wide range of unstable initial data configurations. Moreover, our outcomes extend to the study of finite dimensional global attractor components and the stabilization of multiple Karhunen-Loeve amplitudes in spatial turbulence models. Ultimately, this work is facilitated by a distillation of the theories previously established in Bilansky, Choe-Jarnyk, and Milman (2015), Lin (1995), and Caillat (1994) into a unified framework. These theoretical contributions are then applied to derive the corresponding feedback controls in this work. This research represents a comprehensive solution to the uniform stabilization problem in a wide range of unstable fluid models, thus covering the most critical spaces within this field. The theoretical outcomes presented here have also been implemented in a series of numerical studies, thus enhancing their practical utility. Language primarily functions through communication, and words carry
meaningical weight that shapes human understanding. Vocabulary plays an
essential role in embracing diversity and promoting cultural and linguistic
exchange. Although languages are continually evolving, existing dictionaries
often fail to reflect this change due to outdated information. To bridge this
gap, an online dictionary named LitMind Lexicon has been created to provide
users with a dynamic and informative resource for exploring words. This
dictionary serves several purposes: first, it clarifies ambiguous words with
clear definitions; second, it explores word meanings in various contexts;
third, it showcases sentence examples based on user-submitted contributions;
fourth, it offers a platform for discussing words and their significance;
fifth, it allows users to customize their learning through customizable word
lists and scheduled review sessions. Furthermore, this dictionary incorporates
multi-media content, such as images, audio files, videos, and color-coded
tags, to enhance user experience. Users can access a wide range of 23,664
words, with 4491 definitions, 523 example sentences, and various other
customized features. All processes, including word selection, definition, and
example writing, are automated to keep operations efficient. LitMind Lexicon
has also introduced a unique tokenized system, where users can submit a single
token and access multiple words, examples, and definitions. This innovative
feature allows users to gain a deeper understanding of complex words by
submitting non-English tokens. Examples of this include the word "chocolate"
in Japanese and the term "posh" in English, where users can learn about words
related to these concepts, such as the Japanese word for'melanoidine', the
chemical compound created when cocoa reacts with proteins in the body. Users
can explore various topic clusters, like Christmas, using a word cloud
customized by LitMind Lexicon. This resource enables users to discover
meaningical connections between seemingly unrelated words, much like the
connection between 'ghost' and'spectral'. This paper introduces an innovative
resource for word learning: an online dictionary called LitMind Lexicon, where
users can discover new words, develop customized learning features, and
contribute to word-related discussions. Furthermore, this study provides an
overview of system design, emphasizing user experience and the importance
of a user-friendly interface. Ultimately, this dictionary serves as a unique
resource for promoting cultural and linguistic exchange through language.

The growing interest in transparent AI has led to an increase in research on explainable recommendation systems. Among these, post-hoc methods have been identified as the most practical solutions for complex models that operate as "black-boxes." Recent studies have demonstrated that an enhanced LIME method can provide more accurate explanations for black-box recommenders by addressing the fluency and coherence of the generated explanations through the adherence and consistency principles. However, a thorough examination of the explanatory power of this advanced post-hoc technique, especially in terms of the clarity and relevance of the explanations, remains a gap in the research. In an effort to investigate this further, an expert evaluation was conducted to determine the explanatory effectiveness of the advanced LIME method in real-world settings, focusing on the impact of the method's key factors, including the localness, number of generated explanations, adherence, and consistency. The results revealed that an enhanced LIME method, especially when optimized for explanation generation rather than accuracy, can provide more engaging and expert-friendly explanations, but may not necessarily improve the overall explanatory quality. Additionally, key factors were identified as significantly influencing the quality of the generated explanations, with a notable preference for explanations that were both fluent and consistent. In response to these findings, the authors propose a new framework aimed at enhancing the explanatory capabilities of post-hoc techniques, including the advanced LIME method, ultimately leading to more transparent and understandable transparent recommendation systems. This phenomenon, known as radiation reaction, occurs when the particle's motion generates radiation, causing the magnetic field lines to fluctuate at the particle's pace and in the direction of its movement.  A particular scenario involves a charged particle moving steadily within a magnetic field, which enables the establishment of an equilibrium state where the particle's force of acceleration is counterbalanced by the force of electric field along the particle's trajectory, and only the force of radiation reaction remains effective.  This results in the particle experiencing a dragging effect characteristic of inertial frames, which is known as radiation reaction drag.  This study demonstrates that the effect of drag is comparable to that on a particle moving through a dynamic magnetic field, and it is proportional to the square of the particle's acceleration while moving in a direction that is inversely proportional to the magnetic field's intensity. In the context of unevenly distributed classes, the majority vote method for nearest neighbor classification is not reliable, as it often overpredicts the minority class and underpredicts the majority class. As a result, the perceived error rate is artificially decreased or increased based on the number of observations in each class. To mitigate this issue, we propose a bias-corrected version of the majority vote method, referred to as BCFV. This adaptation involves adjusting the weights of votes from each predictor variable to reflect the imbalance of the data. By assigning a greater weight to the predictor variables with stronger associations to the minority class and reduced weights for those with weaker associations, the BCFV method improves the classification accuracy. When no associations with the predictor variables can be established, a random classifier is employed as a baseline within neighborhoods. Following model selection, the bias-corrected majority vote method exhibits performance comparable to other unfolding-based classifiers, such as the biased nearest neighbor, weighted nearest neighbor, and local boundary weighted nearest neighbor. Furthermore, the proposed approach outperforms deep learning in classification accuracy on imbalanced datasets. Additionally, the bias-corrected majority vote method demonstrates the least amount of bias among the evaluated classifiers. We explore novel view generation -- the challenge of generating distant, unseen scenes from a single perspective -- through the lens of unconditional and conditional diffusion models. Our core contribution involves modifying these models to accept input view pairs, thereby enhancing their generative capabilities in novel view generation. Specifically, we showcase the superiority of conditional diffusion models over traditional generative models for this task. To further advance this area, we develop and release "DiffDreamer" -- a conditional diffusion model-based approach for novel view generation -- alongside a comprehensive dataset of unlimited training data, known as "iPERO". iPERO serves as a vital resource for novel view generation research. Our results demonstrate that DiffDreamer achieves superior viewing angles and image quality when compared to prior generative models. To ensure generalizability, we conduct an in-depth analysis of model performance across numerous views and observation positions, highlighting the effectiveness of DiffDreamer in generating realistic scenes. Our approach also allows Dreamer to synthesize plausible 3D scene representations, revealing the advantages of utilizing generative models in novel view generation. Ultimately, these findings highlight the potential of DiffDreamer in applying novel view generation to real-world scenarios effectively. We investigate the temporal Lipschitz stability for solutions of the Hunter-Saxton equation, as well as its extended model incorporating an additional constant. We devise a theoretical framework establishing the maximal Lipschitz stability with a specific fixed constant for certain classes of initial conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the H-S equation exhibits optimal Lipschitz stability when considering all possible initial conditions within a specific function space. Our research also reveals that adding a certain type of non-linearity to the HS equation is necessary to achieve enhanced stability for a wider class of initial conditions. These findings are supported by corresponding examples and counter-examples. Moreover, we demonstrate that the results derived are applicable to solutions of the THS equation over extended periods of time. Finally, we prove that adding a certain type of dissipation to the HS equation results in exponential stability. To achieve these outcomes, we employ and develop various challenging methods. Specifically, we modify the Calderon-Zygmund theory and establish a new version of the PDE-based Calderon-Zygmund theory, which can be applied to PDEs with singular potentials. Moreover, we also develop a novel version of the chain rule for distributional derivatives in Banach spaces. The results obtained are also generalizable to a broader class of singular conservation laws. The last section of this thesis is dedicated to the exploration of the relationship between the Hunter-Saxton equation and the point vortex system. This paper introduces an innovative method for generating synthetic speech durations 
by utilizing a non-parametric model. Specifically, we use a median-based approach 
to create realistic speech duration times. Our approach distinguishes itself from 
other methods by building a density model of the target variable without making 
any assumptions about its underlying distribution. This technique is then applied 
to several languages, including English, German, French, and Italian. Experimental 
results indicate that the proposed median-based approach is more effective than 
existing methods in producing synthetic data durations that closely resemble the 
original. Furthermore, the synthesized data is usable in text-to-speech systems, 
enabling the creation of high-quality synthetic speech with accurate duration. 
This technique is particularly beneficial when working with limited amounts of 
recorded data, as the proposed method can easily adapt to new datasets. Ultimately, 
the proposed median-based approach is a versatile and efficient technique that is 
well-suited for speech synthesis applications. Implementation details and the 
underlying code are available on GitHub at https://github.com/ashish9147/Median-Based_Synthetic_Speech_Duration_Generation.

Multi-input multi-output neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of tasks. However, many MIMO architectures struggle to effectively share features, which hinders their overall capacity and leads to inefficient use of parameters. We address this challenge by introducing an adaptive feature sharing framework that allows individual subnetworks to utilize shared features in a more targeted manner, thereby enhancing the network's representational ability and reducing redundancy. Our framework can be seamlessly integrated into various MIMO architectures and has been successfully applied to ImageNet, where it has yielded notable improvements, with MIMO models outperforming similar residual architectures by 1-3 percent and matching or even surpassing the performance of PruneRandBaseline. Our empirical findings emphasize the critical role of feature sharing in MIMO architectures and provide a unified understanding of the factors influencing this process. Furthermore, we introduce two novel metrics that enable systematic evaluation of MIMO models based on their ability to effectively share features. Additionally, we introduce a pruning-based method for accurately estimating image similarity and maintaining data privacy, which does not rely on pairwise calculations but rather leverages pre-trained model outputs. This approach has been demonstrated to produce accurate similarity rankings and has significant applications in privacy-preserving cases, distance metrics, and nearest neighbor search. Our framework, associated code, and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/tenneyil/JFT-Feature-Sharing. With this foundation, we aim to further develop and refine large-scale MIMO architectures that prioritize efficient feature sharing. The research was conducted at Alibaba Research, Hong Kong, under the supervision of Dr. Mostafa Henaway. The presentation has been reviewed by Dr. Yujie Wang and Dr. Zhenyu Xiong, experts in the field. The research complements Dr. Mostafa's research on data augmentation at https://github.com/Research-Alibaba/NASVisualizer and Dr. Yujie's research on CML. Additionally, Dr. Zhenyu recently published a notable paper on CML in the domain of language models. The research is scheduled to be presented at the summit in December 2023.

The study of how chronic diseases develop is crucial for creating effective prevention and treatment strategies. Until now, researchers have focused mainly on the physical aspects of these conditions, with little consideration given to the broader factors such as social connections, lifestyle, and environmental habits. Traditional statistical methods used for analyzing illness progression often fail when studying numerous factors simultaneously, leading researchers to resort to simplified approaches like one-dimensional correlations. Our team has developed a novel, comprehensive framework for analyzing complex, multi-faceted data related to health over time, which takes into account that people's health states exist on various levels and is based on the idea that a person's health is influenced by their previous health experiences across different areas. This new approach allows for the creation of personalized, detailed models of disease development that vary from person to person, taking into account the interplay between different factors such as genetics, lifestyle, and environmental habits. This paper introduces a novel twist on twistor actions, specifically for self-dual Yang-Mills theory and its higher-spin counterparts. These theories have been largely understudied in the twistor framework, with a focus instead on Yang-Mills theory and gravity. We overcome obstacles in the path integral by representing the non-linear self-dual connection in a fully self-contained manner. This approach also facilitates the representation of three-digit and four-digit self-dual Yang-Mills components. We further extend this method to its higher-spin counterparts, including those with spin one and spin two self-dual sectors. Notably, the resulting actions are not ultra-local, which may provide insight into resolving parity issues in these theories. We conclude by discussing potential applications and further research directions. While actions themselves are invariant under parity transformations, the corresponding partition functions are potentially sensitive to this issue, posing interesting questions for future investigation. We hope this work sparks renewed interest in these theories within the twistor community. (edited)

We introduce a new axiom system, called timed definitions, for specifying properties of reactive systems that exhibit timed behavior. 
Within the context of HOL, our approach involves a straightforward extension to the standard inductive definition framework, allowing definitions to be associated with a state that changes over time. 
Key features of our framework include the capacity for partial states, state updates that can be restricted, and definitions that may not have a terminal point. 
An important aspect of this method is the potential for indirect state changes, which is exemplified through the use of lifting, an operator that adds additional state variables to a given property. 
We apply timed definitions to describe various properties of real-time Maude, including the ideal versions of its citizen and cache mechanisms, as well as its implementation of the "c-box" transport mechanism. 
Additionally, we use timed definitions to create and refine properties related to real-time operating systems. 
Our method enables us to specify and prove properties that were previously impossible with traditional definition frameworks. 
Notably, our approach has allowed us to demonstrate the correctness of the "c-box" transport mechanism in real-time Maude, which involves proving the existence of a unique process with desired properties. 
To achieve this, we first define the necessary properties using timed definitions, then use HOL's proof assistant to verify that the defined properties match the real-time Maude implementation. 
Ultimately, our method allows us to generate a code snippet in real-time Maude that embodies the correctly-proved "c-box" transport mechanism. 
An additional benefit of our approach is the potential for indirect definition lifting, which allows us to create a comprehensive real-time Maude transport mechanism by combining the correctly-proved "c-box" definition with the standard, incorrect implementation of the single-state version. 
Indirect definition lifting is made possible because the standard implementation can be associated with a dummy state, which is then used to generate the complete real-time Maude transport mechanism. 
Our method's name, timed definitions, is derived from the ability to specify properties that exhibit both temporal behavior and state changes.

Our research focuses on the possibility that the supernova was a black hole explosion by examining various properties of the young supernova remnant Sgr A East, such as its energy, density, and temperature, as well as the distance of the star VFRH 2018S from the galaxy's center. We compared these values to similar properties of Type Ibn and Type Ia supernovae for an accurate identification. Our results indicate that the galactic supernova Sgr A East shares characteristics similar to those of a core collapse supernova with a progenitor star having approximately 3-5 solar masses and a radius of approximately 1.5-6 times 10 to the power of 11 kilometers. The estimated age of Sgr A East would be around 160-320 years, which is consistent with the relatively young age estimate. Our research supports the theory that the galactic supernova Sgr A East was a result of a black hole explosion, specifically a Type Ibn supernova, with an estimated explosion energy of around 10 to the power of 50 ergs. Our research predicts that a star with approximately 3-5 solar masses and a radius of approximately 1.5-6 times 10 to the power of 11 kilometers exploding as an Ibn supernova would appear similarly to the star VFRH 2018S when it was observed in 2018, which is estimated to be around 1.9 years prior to the explosion. Data oversampling has been extensively studied in the field of imbalanced classification.  Despite its importance, research on text classification, particularly in the oversampled domain, remains underrepresented. This study compares the effectiveness of four text classification algorithms - Random Forest, Multi-Support Vector Machine, Multi-K-Nearest-Neighbor, and Boosted Tree - in an oversampled environment. We investigated two oversampling techniques, Arizona State University Methods and Random Sampling Methods, and analyzed their impact on a dataset augmented using Character N-gram features. We evaluated the methods using 20 newsgroups, achieving a notable 13% increase in average precision with the random sampling approach, versus 8% with the Arizona State University Methods. Furthermore, we observed a significant 90 times improvement in recall when utilizing the random sampling technique, in contrast to the Arizona State University Methods' 60 times improvement. Overall, the random sampling approach demonstrated better performance, underscoring its value for text classification tasks with limited samples. This research contributes to the development of a novel method that enhances accuracy in oversampled environments. It also facilitates real-world applications, given that text data is often scarce and imbalanced in the domain of artificial intelligence. This study analyzes data from the U.S. to understand the relationship between local news coverage during the COVID-19 pandemic and key metrics such as cases and deaths, as well as the factors that influence news coverage in different communities. It utilizes a comprehensive dataset of 337 counties with high-speed internet access, comprehensive local news coverage, and CDC COVID-related deaths and cases data. Regression models reveal a significant, positive correlation between local news coverage and COVID-related deaths and cases. Notably, when controlling for population demographics and economic factors, news coverage is found to be unrelated to COVID cases, but positively correlated with deaths. Moreover, areas with higher-educated and whiter populations are found to have greater local news coverage. Interestingly, when controlling for population demographics, news coverage is found to be lower in counties with larger black populations and those that are economically disadvantaged. These findings imply that local news coverage is linked to the health consequences of COVID in the U.S., but not necessarily a determinant of cases. Rather, local news coverage appears to reflect existing health disparities. Ultimately, these results suggest that local news outlets play a significant role in shaping public understanding, but they reach audiences disproportionately. Potential explanations for these disparities include media bias, limitations in news production, and distribution, and how these affect what information reaches which communities. These are explored in a follow-up study. 

Key words: Local news, COVID-19, cases, deaths, population demographics, economic factors, media production and distribution, bias in news sources. 

This research appears in a published paper titled "Local News and COVID in the U.S.: How Coverage Relates to Cases, Deaths, and Audience Characteristics" and is presented at the 2022 International Conference on Social Information Sciences. 

Code and data can be accessed at https://github.com/leandrogiuliani/local-news-covid-us.

The preservation of total angular momentum in simulations using the Fast Multipole Method for Eulerian Eulerian interactions is addressed. We found that in rotations involving both translation and rotation, this method precisely maintains angular momentum. However, when either a point source or a solid body is involved in collisions, collisions do not always guarantee conservation of angular momentum. After developing a corrected version of the Fast Multipole Code that ensures angular momentum preservation, we conducted a series of tests to confirm this update. These tests not only verified that the updated code conserves angular momentum in selected benchmark tests but also identified specific collision scenarios where angular momentum was previously lost. We have further utilized the FMC's angular momentum preservation through a new method that maintains energy conservation in Eulerian-Eulerian interactions involving rotation. This novel approach is demonstrated in a disk collision experiment where energy is continually lost due to the inadequacy of traditional Fast Multipole methods in preserving both energy and angular momentum. In order to resolve this issue, we employed the new energy-preserving method, which as a byproduct ensures conservation of angular momentum in such scenarios. An additional test involving impacts on a spinning disk in a gas atmosphere, which naturally loses angular momentum, was conducted to confirm the effectiveness of the updated FMC. These integration efforts have broad implications for studies of angular momentum preservation in astrophysical and planetary science simulations, a critical area of study in the field. The updated FMC code is available for download at https://github.com/apgwoen/fastmultipole.icecube. com under the MIT license. Laser technology has significantly impacted science and society since its invention, and is expected to play an even more crucial role in future technological advancements. The development of compact, efficient, and cost-effective lasers that can operate at various levels of complexity is essential to fulfill this promise. Specifically, lasers functioning at the level of individual photons rather than average power have the greatest potential for breakthroughs in fields such as quantum information and communication. To achieve this goal, researchers are developing an innovative digital alkali spin laser. This study describes the recent advancements made in designing, constructing, and operating this type of laser, which uses the D2 transition of rubidium at a wavelength of 778 nm through a process involving direct semiconductor lasers, highly efficient optical resonators, and circulating highly active Rb vapor. To operate the laser at its highest potential, researchers implemented sophisticated control systems and algorithms that enable rapid and stable changes to the laser's operating conditions. The results include the production of 278 GW pulses with a 16-nJ yield, a spectral line width of 0.52 kHz, and an impressive relative stability of 2.6 fs. The team also demonstrated the ability of the laser to operate at its maximum capacity for prolonged periods, including up to 50 seconds, and stated its capability to achieve even greater stability with the right hardware modifications. These advancements represent a major step forward in the development of high-performance alkali lasers that operate using the D2 transition, and show great promise for future applications. The study also lays the groundwork for the creation of advanced optical systems that integrate photonic and femtosecond components, ultimately enabling a wide range of scientific and engineering breakthroughs. To take the technology to its full potential, researchers are now working on incorporating the latest ideas into the development of a functional, high-performance system. One such concept is the incorporation of a digital surface-iron mode optical resonator, and incorporating the latest advancements in photonic and nanophotonic technology. The incorporation of a stable optical clock based on an extended cavity laser, and incorporating the capabilities of a broad-band frequency comb technology, are also key areas of interest. The study provides the necessary foundational knowledge and inspires future advancements in the field, and the authors look forward to achieving a major breakthrough in the near future. The accompanying videos demonstrate the stability of the laser and provide an engaging look at its operation. The study's findings hold significant promise for future advancements in the field. The team is set to launch a two-year project aimed at developing a functional, high-performance system

A stochastic Newton method is proposed for solving a distributed convex optimization problem, where a global function is represented as the weighted sum of individual function components, each processed on a distinct machine. The framework allows for asynchronous communication among machines, and the linear subproblems solved on each machine are resolved exactly. For convex smooth objectives, the method's convergence is guaranteed, and the optimization process requires at most NIT_MAX iterations. When the objective is smooth and has L-smoothness, an additional step is needed to apply a projection onto a bounded domain, NIT_PROJ_NIT_MAX times. For objectives lacking smoothness but having strong convexity and a bounded lower bound, the method's convergence is further specified and specified as PROJ_LB_CONS_NIT_MAX. Numerical experiments validate the proposed method, and comparison tests demonstrate its superiority over a distributed subgradient method, a distributed quasi-Newton method, and a distributed method of multi-dimensional secant, in terms of convergence speed. This study investigates the detection of hate speech in two popular Indian languages, Hindi and Bengali, which have been neglected in the ongoing research on language-based detection methods. Despite the significant damage hate speech causes in societies, there have been limited efforts to develop effective detection techniques for these languages. We address this gap by employing a dataset rich in hate-speech examples from online social media platforms in both languages. The collected data undergoes an evaluation process, where low-quality labels were corrected, ensuring the accuracy of the dataset. The evaluation also included a comparison of different neural network architectures, such as CNN, RNN, LSTM, LSTMs with attention, and various combinations of these, as well as different activation functions and dropout rates. The investigation also involved examining the impact of training on a reduced corpus of Hindi text, including special matrices to represent the data, as well as the application of an early dropout system. The analysis was coupled with a transfer learning approach using both visual and text-based methods. The results of the study provide valuable insights that can aid researchers working to detect hate speech in other low-resource languages. The findings also emphasize the importance of thorough experimentation in the process of developing effective hate-speech detection methods. We have released the source code for the study on the GitHub platform, where it can be accessed freely. The study also addresses a critical issue in the field of hate-speech detection, which is the privacy risk associated with extracting data from social media platforms. The study has attempted to mitigate this risk by obtaining the necessary permissions and employing anonymization techniques to protect the data. The research team has also made a significant effort to make the study transparent, as reflected in the published code and the detailed description of the study's methods. The study has further emphasized the need to apply a reliable sampling strategy when processing the dataset. The study has also provided results indicating that text data, including counters and tokenized representations, can be as effective as visual data in hate-speech detection. In nuclear and particle physics, GTPCs are gaining popularity as versatile detectors. Due to their ability to provide spatial information, GTPCs are being considered for various applications such as nuclear decay measurements, beam tracking, and event reconstruction in collisions. The latter involves identifying particle-antiparticle pairs, which is crucial for a specific search for a new force called the X-force. However, a particular characteristic of X-force interactions makes them detectable only if the nucleus's momentum change can be detected, which is challenging with existing GTPC technologies. To detect these momentum changes, researchers are developing new methods for analyzing GTPC data. The approach involves introducing specific indicators of nucleus momentum shifts in electron-ion pairs. We will examine various information measures that can serve as indicators of these momentum changes. The quality of these indicators will be assessed using machine learning algorithms. We will demonstrate this concept on simulated data, representing two distinct GTPC scenarios. The primary goal of this study is to identify the most effective information measures and machine learning methods for detecting nuclear recoil by examining how different signals are classified. The results will be shared with the GTPC community to encourage the development of advanced, recoil-detecting capabilities. The corresponding software code will be made public on the GitHub platform. Special emphasis will be placed on involving early-stage researchers in this project and seeking their input throughout the investigation. The presentation of our findings will be accompanied by an introductory explanation of information measures and gradient boosting in the GTPC context. The project's focus on practical applications will facilitate the transfer of this research to other disciplines and detection systems. We conducted research involving commercial vehicle driving experts to explore how they interact with artificial intelligence and provide feedback on evaluations generated by these systems. The results reveal that, despite initial doubts, experts were satisfied with the expert system's ability to identify potential issues, and appreciated the opportunity to understand the basis for these warnings. We found that, when compared to standard procedures, the expert system's feedback enabled more drivers to pass the evaluation, and that the most valuable insights for experts came from the clear explanations provided by the expert system regarding the critical factors involved in evaluation outcomes. Our research indicates that, by integrating human judgment with artificial intelligence, the resulting combination is more accurate and less prone to errors than relying on the expert system alone or human judgment in isolation. We propose a potential business model and discuss policy implications for professional settings, highlighting the importance of careful consideration when relying on these expert systems. Our research indicates that, by integrating human judgment with artificial intelligence, the resulting combination is more accurate and less prone to errors than relying on the expert system alone or human judgment in isolation. The resulting findings have prompted us to establish partnerships with industry leaders to further explore and demonstrate the effective integration of human and artificial intelligence in professional settings, while also addressing crucial considerations for the successful implementation of these expert systems. The essential contribution of our research lies in the careful and systematic consideration of the intricate interplay between human and artificial intelligence in professional evaluation contexts, resulting in the development of an innovative model that combines these elements for the enhancement of assessment processes. The resulting interaction between these expert systems and human professionals has the potential to positively impact a wide variety of safety-critical industries. The goal of the Out-of-Category challenge was to develop models that could accurately predict unknown object categories based on minimal training data and when encountering unusual viewpoints of familiar objects. The challenge involved two tracks: Track 1 focused on predicting unknown categories, and Track 2 focused on recognizing novel viewpoints of familiar objects. The challenge utilized the MiniImageNet and VGGNet datasets for Track 1 and the CUB-200 and Stanford Online Dataset for Track 2. The results revealed that models employing ensemble techniques, soft targets, and data augmentation performed well on various tasks. Notably, a model utilizing feature augmentation achieved state-of-the-art results on Track 1, and a multi-stage baseline model outperformed others on Track 2 by incorporating intermediate feature extraction and using transfer learning to improve performance on rare categories. The challenge's findings will likely lead to significant future advancements in out-of-category challenges. The challenge's data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/mseitzidi/out-of-category-challenge. The results of the challenge were presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) Workshops in 2021. The paper titled "Out-of-Category Challenge" was first published in 2021.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies a significant ferroelectric phase transition accompanied by an unusually large entropy increase. This article investigates the high-temperature phase's structural organization and calculates the entropy within for different crystal lattice patterns using an ab-initio study. When the ferroelectric phase transition occurs, entropy of approximately 5.54 k_B per formula unit is released from the crystal lattice, closely aligning with the observed value of 5.97 k_B and indicating that the high-temperature phase's structural disorderiness is comprised of 7% ammonium ions and 34% chloride ions surrounding a dipoled-ion environment. This finding supports the hypothesis that ferroelectricity in ammonium sulfate arises from proton transfer between ions of opposite charge. This outcome also illustrates the significance of evaluating crystal structure disorderiness when investigating caloric materials. As robots increasingly co-work with humans in various environments, the issue of communication barriers among professionals arises. A lack of standardization in human-robot interactions can lead to confusion caused by inconsistent commands given to these robots. By implementing clear, standardized protocols for interactions, the barriers between humans can be overcome. In this research, a new approach called the Information Exchange Module is presented as a solution to facilitate interactions between robots and humans, specifically focusing on tasks requiring collaborative efforts. This module allows robots to understand and interpret the instructions given to them by checking their source against various potential standards. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the proposed module was tested in a simulated environment where a humanoid robot was instructed to perform a series of activities by a human based on different communication formats. The results obtained from asking humans to provide instructions using multiple command formats showed the robot's ability to accurately understand these instructions in a high percentage of cases. This approach was also validated by asking participants to analyze and predict the behavior of a robot before clicking the correct button to give their instruction. Our results indicated a significant correlation between participants' predictions and the robot's actual behavior, with those having more experience calling fewer robot functions, known as services, resulting in better predictions. These outcomes suggest that implementing standardization as a means of communication may be a feasible and efficient method for increasing the chances of successful human-robot collaborations. To accommodate various possible standards, the Information Exchange Module can automatically generate a set of possible instructions and then use machine learning to determine which one is most likely the correct one. Moreover, experiments were conducted with multiple command formats such as XML, plain text, and button selection, and the results showed that the robot could learn to interpret these commands effectively. In one of these experiments, a robot named Steve was taught to perform tasks based on human instructions given to him in text as commands to pick buttons. This learning process resulted in a high success rate of 94% in following the instructions once he had learned them. To make the system even more flexible, we established connections between button selections with other button selections. For example, we taught another robot named Tim the ability to understand that pressing a button called "grab" would cause him to reach out of his hands. These learning experiences with the Information Exchange Module showed that the proposed approach can be utilized across a broad spectrum of human-robot collaborative settings. For tasks that involve navigation in unfamiliar environments, effectively representing knowledge of an area is crucial, encompassing both a layout of the space and its geography. However, current methods used to represent space typically do not account for the importance of geographical landmarks, leading to potential drawbacks in tasks that require more detailed understanding. In an effort to improve this, a new method of representation has been created called the HiTMap, designed to provide a more comprehensive understanding of a geography that is both detailed and adaptable to changing circumstances. This new representation is part of a broader system that allows a robot to learn and understand a geography that is dynamic and includes both map-like characteristics and geographical features. By testing the method, results showed that using the HiTMap allowed a robot to reach its destination faster when the map was incomplete and included an understanding of the geography's layout, as opposed to a basic map. This research makes two key contributions, the first being the introduction of a new method of representation that takes into account the interplay between the geography's layout and its landmarks, and the second being a demonstration of how these representations can be used to improve a robot's navigation capabilities by providing more complete information about its environment. Conventional loop-closure detection methods often rely on consistent, tractable data patterns, but may introduce bias in certain situations, such as when the repetition is not identical or the context changes. A key issue with many existing techniques is that they can misinterpret variations in data as loops, resulting in prolonged and repeated detection processes that eventually lead to divergence. This work aims to address this problem by using a neural network to develop a more selective loop-closure detector that produces a filtered state estimate, thus enhancing navigation accuracy and efficiency. A deep learning-based filter is employed to accurately maintain a robot's location by minimizing potential biases that indicate loop-closures when none are present. The DNN filter's performance is evaluated in a realistic and challenging outdoor environment with complex features, such as uneven terrain, inclines, or the presence of plants, where the conventional 2-point summary statistic may incorrectly indicate loop-closures. The estimated standard deviations of the state filter are around 2.7 meters when the robot is walking at 0.5 meters per step, demonstrating reasonable uncertainty levels. The combined backend and DNN filter achieve a minimum sequence length of around 0.5 kilometers without any loop-closure detection without any residual drift, indicating successful navigation. We present an effective edge detection method for satellite images that relies on less computational power compared to deep learning-based solutions. By utilizing a combination of a fully connected autoregressive model and a Gaussian mixture model, our approach can identify sharper edges in the data without requiring the large amounts of a deep learning model needs. The efficacy of this method was tested on a satellite image dataset to compare its performance against two established deep learning-based models, with our approach yielding similar results and substantial reductions in training and inference times. The full source code for this method is publicly available to facilitate replication of the results. Additionally, a lightweight version of this method is currently being deployed on a low-cost Raspberry Pi computer to read analog edge data from satellite images. The resulting model can perform fast inferences on single images in under 0.2 seconds. We compared our approach against state-of-the-art models, including a ResNet18 and FastRCNN, and found that it produces comparable results with significantly faster training and inference times. The performance metrics for our approach include edge detection precision of 87% and recall of 93%, outperforming the ResNet18 model in recall and achieving similar precision. Additionally, our approach outperformed the FastRCNN model in both precision and recall. The study's key contributions include developing an innovative edge detection method, demonstrating its effectiveness on satellite image datasets, and providing efficient training and inference times. What happens when a language model like BERT processes negative feedback?  Despite current understanding of how it is handled by transformer architectures, our research reveals a significant problem with their handling of such feedback, which greatly limits their ability to improve over time.  Our study reveals that as the magnitude of target words increases, the expected distribution of probabilities in a BERT model becomes increasingly concentrated on a single word, typically an uncommon word in the dataset, such as the unknown token "[UNK]".  Our analysis using POMDP theory explains this phenomenon by suggesting that the model learns to "reject" undesirable input combinations that do not match expected output patterns by assigning them a uniform distribution over uncommon words.  If this rejection mechanism is not properly learned, the model may remain stuck in suboptimal performance and struggle to enhance its capabilities.  To that end, our research presents a novel training approach that incorporates a specialized rejection mechanism, designed to enhance BOM-RJ, a BERT-based model we adapted.  Our results demonstrate that this approach, along with data augmentation and a more efficient search algorithm, enable BOM-RJ to achieve state-of-the-art performance in various natural language inference tasks.  Furthermore, BOM-RJ is able to maintain its accuracy even when faced with adversarially crafted difficult examples, effectively making it more robust under harsh conditions.  For more details about the study, including associated code, it can be found at a publicly accessible repository.  Additionally, a related paper titled "Model-Free Learning of Rejection in Transformer Language Models" is available at a publicly accessible repository as well. To accurately translate dependent concepts, a better understanding of the context is required. In sequence-to-sequence models for machine translation, improving context awareness is particularly challenging due to the inherent sequential nature of the input data. Typically, models rely on looking back at previous information, whereas many real-world contexts benefit from anticipating the outcome. We introduce a novel lookup mechanism that combines context awareness with a forward-looking approach for context generation in neural machine translation. By storing key concept representations across various translation states and using a proximity measure, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this mechanism in multiple settings and achieve improved translation results. Experimental outcomes indicate that our proposed method excels over traditional context-generating techniques in several evaluation metrics. Moreover, utilizing precise definitions for words can enhance the accuracy of translations. However, existing knowledge sources often lack detailed word definitions obtained through labor-intensive processes. We present a new data-driven approach to efficiently extract definition summaries for words. These summaries can provide essential context for generating translations in various fields. Experimental results indicate the efficacy of our context-generating method and definition extraction algorithm in the domain of software translation and achieve up to +3.0 BLEU points in some settings. Most notably, our definition summaries are remarkably compact, requiring only 10% of the original definition text to produce similar translations. Our study is conducted using the Generalized Advanced Placement French and English Corpus, a 39M word dataset that combines software, language, and audio information to provide a comprehensive understanding of the context. However, looking ahead to the final target sequence is challenging as it necessitates knowledge of the context for every target state, which is typically not available in conventional models. As a result, we develop a novel lookup mechanism called the Contextual Context Transformer that efficiently captures context-dependent information by looking ahead to the final target sequence while also allowing the model to adapt to varying levels of context. Our approach can be easily integrated with existing sequence-to-sequence models, providing improved context awareness that surpasses traditional lookup mechanisms. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our method in various translation settings and achieve up to +4.0 BLEU points in some cases. Additionally, we extend our Contextual Context Transformer to handle challenging translation tasks involving multiple source sequences. We observe that robust context awareness is required to accurately translate dependent concepts in these complex tasks. Our approach can be easily applied to handle such cases, providing improved context awareness that surpasses traditional lookup mechanisms. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of our method in the domain of software translation and achieve up to +5.0 BLEU points in some cases.

Extra energy injected into the universe at the time of Big Bang could create massive particles larger than the universe itself, which may have remained undetected by current telescopes. We've analyzed a theoretical class of phenomena known as classical cosmological collider phenomena, where non-thermal universe conditions after inflation lead to the generation of trans-cosmological massive particles. Our focus is on theories with two distinct types of beyond-the-standard-model physics: a theory with massive neutral vector bosons and one incorporating inflation with specific properties. In the vector boson case, our findings align with previous research, while in the inflation model, we identified potential signatures of inflationary dynamics that could be detected in the near future. These signatures include production rates for massless particles that vary directly with the mass of the vector boson and the square of the time since the Big Bang, measured in the frequency range of millihertz. Specifically, we investigate the Brown-Thompson groups $F_n$, $T_n$, and $V_n$ and discover that they too have a constant divergence function. Furthermore, our research extends to the random walks on these groups and their corresponding Hausdorff dimensions. Additionally, we investigated the divergence characteristics of the braided Thompson groups $BF$, $\widehat{BF}$, and $\widehat{BV}$. The findings reveal that the divergent behavior evident in $F$, $T$, and $V$ is absorbed into a single function across these groups. Finally, our research extends to the Brown-Berrmann groups $B_F\widehat{F}_{n,1}$ and demonstrates that their divergence dimensions are directly linked to those of the braided Thompson groups. This makes it difficult to determine the expertise of MTurk workers, impacting the way their responses are viewed. Our research aims to address this by employing relevant corpus analysis and filtering tasks with a select pool of qualified workers. Our study involves an in-depth examination of the variability within MTurk crowdsourcing evaluations, focusing on sensitivity to the sample and annotator methodology. Additionally, we investigate the effectiveness of filtering strategies, employing both statistical and neural approaches, and evaluate the impact of providing crowdsworkers with guidelines, knowing which evaluations are qualified can be beneficial but also introduces new challenges. Our findings suggest that annotator variability is highly influential in the outcome of MTurk evaluations. Although filtering tasks can help identify qualified crowdsworkers and increase agreement among annotators, their own results can be inconsistent and prone to errors. This indicates that to achieve accurate MTurk evaluations, it is essential to have a defined understanding of what constitutes a qualified annotator. One possible approach to determine annotator qualifications is to focus on evaluating the expertise of a select pool of crowdsworkers rather than task-level, using advanced filtering strategies. Moreover, providing crowdsworkers with written guidelines can be beneficial but can also make it more difficult to identify qualified annotators, as their recommendations are subject to interpretation. This highlights the need for future MTurk evaluations to incorporate a more comprehensive approach to annotator qualification that goes beyond tasks. Our research provides an in-depth analysis of the factors influencing MTurk evaluations and proposes a method for identifying qualified crowdsworkers and producing reliable outcomes. Text-of-a-clip retrieval, where the task involves selecting the most relevant text based on a given video frame, has significant applications in various domains, such as semantic search and computer vision. Current methods use a two-stage approach, combining a pre-trained vision-language model for video frame-text matching, followed by a deep set similarity measurement to identify the most relevant text. Yet, existing techniques have limitations, such as inefficiently scanning text and clip features, and failing to accurately select the most relevant text. To address these limitations, we propose TS2-Net, a novel single-stage framework designed for robust text-of-clip retrieval. This framework leverages multi-token attention to efficiently select and align the most relevant tokens from both video frames and text, using a simple yet effective average similarity measurement. To prevent aligning incompatible tokens, we propose a multi-column transformer architecture, enabling closer interaction and alignment of relevant tokens. We conduct extensive experiments on two public datasets, demonstrating that TS2-Net achieves a notable single-stage breakthrough, surpassing two-stage approaches by a substantial margin with reduced computation and complexity. Furthermore, TS2-Net performs favorably against existing methods on various text-of-clip retrieval benchmarks. To facilitate replication, the TS2-Net code is available at https://github.com/zwang123/TS2-Net. https://github.com/zwang123/TS2-Net.

In response to the intricacies of real-world networks, researchers have developed various models that capture distinct network characteristics. The uniform attachment model and the preferential attachment model are two widely used approaches to study network development, yet most existing models solely employ one of these mechanisms or a combination with a third, less preferred approach. As a result, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding about the long-term behavior of networks that incorporate both uniform and preferential attachment processes. To address this gap, we explore the evolution of a hybrid model that incorporates both mechanisms. Our analysis reveals interesting insights into the node degree distribution, clustering coefficients, and the overall structure of the hybrid network. Notably, our findings indicate that a hybrid network exhibits a degree distribution resembling a power law, with a modified parameter value, and a clustering coefficient that stabilizes at a medium frequency. These characteristics may seem inconsistent with the initial design parameters. To verify our predictions, we conducted in-depth simulations across various parameter settings. Moreover, we compared our findings with those from a triple mechanism model that incorporates uniform, preferential attachment, and triadic closure processes. Our comparison reveals intriguing differences and similarities between the two models, with the hybrid model exhibiting closer resemblance to the triple mechanism model. Finally, our results demonstrate that a hybrid network exhibits robustness and vulnerability traits similar to those of a triple mechanism model. These findings imply that a hybrid model with a minor preferential attachment bias can produce a degree distribution similar to that of a triple mechanism model, with a scaling exponent of 2.18, and a clustering coefficient frequency of around 0.45, observed in triple mechanism models. Our analysis demonstrates that a minor adjustment in one of these widely used model parameters can produce a complex network frequency distribution with a scaling exponent greater than 1.5, which may account for the observed variability in the social network frequency distribution better than a single mechanism model. These findings are consistent with previous studies, with a scaling exponent ranging from 0.5 to 3.0. Our results may explain the variability in the social network frequency distribution reported in existing research, with a hybrid model outperforming a single mechanism model. The performance of the hybrid model is consistent with the observed characteristics of the nanoscale material nanowires.  Our analysis also reveals that a hybrid network exhibits a scaling exponent greater than 1.5, which may account for the observed variability in the social network frequency distribution reported in existing research. These findings are consistent with the observed characteristics of the nanoscale material nanowheels.

A key element in constructing a regression model using Gaussian Processes is selecting an appropriate kernel. Although there are numerous Gaussian Process kernels available, such as linear, rational quadratic, and periodic kernels, there are only a limited number of special cases that meet specific data requirements. To address this, we propose a method for creating Gaussian Process kernels by combining basic mathematical expressions, which can be evaluated at any point using an expression tree. This approach provides an infinite number of potential kernels and we outline a strategy for choosing the most suitable one given your data. The new kernels are shown to perform at least as well as existing ones in various machine learning tasks and our framework remains versatile, allowing for the development of additional kernels. One of our novel kernels developed using this method outperformed existing state-of-the-art kernels on synthetic data in a regression task and achieved a significant improvement of 9% in the marginal likelihood when regression kernels were used to analyze a CO2 time series in combination with the Recurrent Neural Torch library. The source code for our Gaussian Process model and expressions is available on our GitHub page. A new Python package called GaussianProcessKernels has been created to dynamically generate kernels and demonstrate their potential. The kernels can be employed directly in this package or any other Gaussian Process implementation, which in our case is the GaussianProcess model from the smpy package, due to its user-friendly interface and high efficiency. A quick start guide on integrating the GaussianProcess model and GaussianProcessKernels package is provided in the documentation. The model and packages serve as a model for other Gaussian Process implementations, which can simplify the adoption and testing of new kernels in real-world applications. The source code and packages can be accessed at the following GitHub pages: https://github.com/strawb/Georgia, https://github.com/strawb/GaussianProcessKernels.
