This work will present different approaches to reducing beam-induced noise at Muon Colliders, with a focus on their potential benefits and limitations. Two main strategies will be examined: utilizing a muon source optimized for low-energy operation, and incorporating a dedicated neutrino dump; also discussed are the advantages and limitations of other potential methods, such as implementing a fast extraction ring and employing a carbon jet absorber. The proposed solutions will be evaluated in terms of their effectiveness in reducing background noise and the feasibility of implementing them into existing designs. This evaluation will consider various design parameters, with a focus on an example collider operating at a center-of-mass energy of 1 TeV and delivering luminosity of 10^33 cm^-2s^-1, with a beam energy collision of 0.5 GeV. Current methods for training neural networks to ignore unnecessary input components remain unsatisfactory. They often force all inputs to be used, resulting in reduced precision due to the introduction of unnecessary noise, or solely rely on marginal importance, failing to capture the relative importance of inputs. To address this issue, a differentiable transportation approach is proposed, which leverages optimisation algorithms to allocate a limited resource across multiple inputs in an efficient manner. By allocating a limited amount of a hypothetical resource to each input, this method encourages networks to identify and target high-value inputs while strategically allocating remaining resources to lower-value ones. Experimental results show this method surpasses current standards in achieving precise input ignition in vision-based deep networks and precisely uncovering important features in Bayesian uncertainty analysis. Notably, this method proves scaleable and can effectively handle high-dimensional input scenarios. Its implementation in code is available at https://github.com/Jay-Jee/Spartan. In this study, we seek to comprehend developers' perceptions of the seriousness of test smells from their own standpoint. Following an adaptation of the ground truth establishment technique, we conducted two experimental rounds with a total of 81 developers to gauge their level of agreement with proposed severity levels of five test smells, which were subsequently established based on prior studies. The KKMCee program, designed for simulating electron-positron collider events involving lepton and quark pairs, is a modified version of the KKMC generator for leptonic processes. It includes updated Monte Carlo techniques for both leptonic and hadronic components, as demonstrated in the recently completed CLIC physics process studies. Notably, KKMCee participates in the smc@ccSM Monte Carlo ensemble with other leading simulator programs. Further advancements in the program's capabilities include the integration of double electrophotonic events and partial width summation for pair production events, both of which significantly impact final state event distributions. Additionally, the program accounts for the explicit t-quark pole effect using a combination of the complex t-quark amplitude with magnetic moment corrections matched to the 2HDM4OS parton-level predictions at the complex pole. Evaluations of the program's performance have been conducted at self-energy, vertex correction, box levels of the (s)leepton pair, and the top quark pair production at various energies. The program's results show satisfactory matching with existing high-precision Monte Carlo generators such as CHES, 2HDMPLUS, FHZZ, and SPYTHON for individual higher-order corrections at lower energies. However, the program does not match parton shower (PS) properties, which are calculated via the FFEE parton shower program. Furthermore, the program's predictions for hadronic top quark pair events have been analyzed at sufficient precision due to the incorporation of FFEE-derived parameters at the semi-soft hadronic Z decay limit. Evaluations of the program's performance have been conducted at LEP2 data-level comparisons with the most recent experimental results. Finally, the program's predictions for hadronic top quark pair events have participated in the 2020 FCC-ee benchmark suite and the 2022 CLIC physics process studies. The program's predictions for these events show satisfactory agreement with experimental results at LEP2 and recent theoretical estimates at FCC-ee and CLIC. Deep union-closed subspace learning can effectively handle high-dimensional data in tasks such as clustering and representation. Traditional approaches rely on measures like variance to identify important subspaces, but they are insufficient for dealing with data that exhibits long-tailed density patterns. To address this limitation, a new objective function is proposed that incorporates the Jensen-Shannon divergence, a metric that measures similarity between two densities. Specifically, a Deep Representative Subspace learner is designed to minimize the intersection of two sets of points, while maximizing the similarity between their density distributions. We also introduce a density-aware approach to deep subspace learning that accounts for data density fluctuations, thereby generalizing the concept of variance to its density-based equivalent. To achieve this, a new objective function is defined by combining the variance with the Kullback-Leibler divergence and optimizing it using Convolutional Neural Networks. We evaluate the performance of our proposed learners through comprehensive experiments on diverse data sets, both synthetic and real-world, and observe significant improvements, especially for challenging cases involving density fluctuations. These experimental results are supported by comprehensive theoretical explanations. Notably, our approach has far-reaching implications due to the widespread occurrence of density fluctuations in real-world data. This research investigates the effect of the local tracing partnership in England, specifically - Contact North West, - Contact South East, - Contact North East & Yorkshire, - Contact London, and - Contact Yorkshire & the Humber. We aim to understand the implications of prioritizing certain referral sources within these partnerships on the overall efficiency of contact tracing. By simulating the performance of these partnerships using data from the Government's daily update, we provide numerical assessments of their efficiency. We also provide a framework for comparing different contact tracing efforts, which can be applied to a variety of scenarios beyond the current pandemic. This research primarily focuses on the efficiency of contact tracing efforts as of March 2021. We also make predictions about the potential impact of the various contact tracing efforts as of April 2021, taking into account their respective target goals. Finally, we offer some general observations on the characteristics of an ideal local tracing partnership. One potential limitation of our approach is that our analysis relies on data that was publicly available. We acknowledge the potential biases inherent in our model due to the absence of certain data, specifically the self-reported nature of the response rate data, which may be subject to reporting errors. Another potential area of improvement is the lack of information about the response rates of the various contact tracing efforts, which could be addressed through the implementation of a more detailed model. We provide an example of a more detailed model in the discrete-dynamics section of the report, but it is important to note that the primary source of our data is the Government's daily update, but we cannot rule out the presence of measurement error. We suggest collecting more information about the response rates through surveys to address this limitation. This research utilizes numerical simulations to compare the performance of the different contact tracing efforts as of two points in time. We acknowledge that our primary focus is on the contact tracing efforts as of March 2021, but we also consider the potential implications of the various contact tracing efforts as of April 2021, taking into account their respective target goals. Ultimately, this research provides valuable insights into the efficiency of contact tracing efforts, which can be applied to a broader range of scenarios beyond the current pandemic, specifically the trade-off between resource-intensive and efficient contact tracing efforts. Following similar numerical results from January and February 2021, this contact tracing effort is predicted to meet its target goal, whereas several other contact tracing efforts face the challenge of keeping up with their respective goals

In settings where a robot is trained by an expert, reverse RL allows for the
creation of a policy that mimics the expert's actions in complex environments.
However, current RL techniques face several practical constraints, such as
obtaining and processing rich observational data from the expert, efficiently
using expert demonstrations, and learning from limited or imperfect expert
feedback. Additionally, RL algorithms often require extensive computation and
may not adequately account for a practitioner's knowledge of the environment.
Our work addresses these issues by using the practitioner's domain-specific
knowledge to establish constrained reinforcement learning frameworks. By limiting
policy choices according to these constraints, we can reduce the required expert
demonstrations. Our integrated LCT approach combines the practitioner's insights
with the likelihood of achieving goals under uncertainty, providing a concrete
framework for the task. Experimental results demonstrate that LCT outperforms
existing RL methods by effectively managing complex, real-world challenges with
only a few expert demonstrations. Overall, our research focuses on creating
practical RL algorithms that can be successfully applied in industry settings. The
project's source code and videos are accessible at https://arbitrager.github.io. The
code can also be directly accessed via the repository link.

A vertex divider in a graph $G$ with respect to a vertex $v$ is defined as an induced subgraph $H$ containing $v$ and formed by deleting all vertices from $G$ that are not adjacent to $v$. This concept is utilized to compute the treewidth of a graph, which is a measure of the widest possible 'tree-like' structure that can be embedded in the graph. We improve the space complexity of treewidth analysis by introducing a vertex divider set method with $O(n)$ space usage, where n is the number of vertices in the graph. We achieve this goal by combining the vertex divider method with Galli's tree-decomposition algorithm in treewidth analysis, reducing space complexity from O(n log n) to O(n) with respect to input size. Additionally, we introduce a new vertex divider set generation algorithm with better worst-case performance and higher probabilistic efficiency. We further optimize the space complexity of treewidth analysis in randomized settings, reaching almost linear time with high probability and optimal space complexity in randomized settings. We also introduce a new method for efficiently embedding trees in graphs, which is derived from the vertex divider set approach and provides optimal space usage. This tree-embedding method is more efficient than standard methods in terms of space usage but has a less favorable time complexity in certain cases. We also introduce a new method for efficiently computing the treewidth of graphs, which is more efficient than standard methods in terms of space usage but has a less favorable time complexity in certain cases. We tested our vertex divider set approach to treewidth analysis by implementing it in the public "csharp-misc4" collection available through the Reproblitz platform. We obtained space usage results that matched our theoretical expectations, with a worst-case space usage of 560MB on a dataset with 521 vertices and treewidth 19. We further validated the practical efficiency of our vertex divider set approach to treewidth analysis by comparing its performance to standard methods in several test cases. We concluded that our approach is a viable alternative to standard methods for treewidth analysis, particularly in certain scenarios. We also highlighted the value of combining different algorithmic techniques to address complex problems like treewidth, which has a long history of efficient solutions. We also obtained new experimental results that highlighted the practical efficiency of our vertex divider set approach to treewidth analysis in certain scenarios and provided a new benchmark to test its performance in further research. We further developed an approach to efficiently analyze treewidth in certain limited settings and obtained promising results in terms of space and time

The validity of physics-informed neural networks for solving partial differential equations largely depends on key factors, including the amount of training data and the network's architecture. Current methods for assessing the network's accuracy after training, or "a posteriori," involve evaluating its performance on a separate test dataset. However, these methods are restrictive, relying on actual test data, and fail to provide certainty about its true performance. To address this limitation, a different approach is proposed in this paper, involving an iterative process where potential test data points are generated and initially assessed for their potential error using a preliminary neural network. Only points with low error probabilities are then included in a traditional, separate test to assess the network's accuracy. This method can be particularly useful when very few training data are available, as it maximizes the return for the smallest additional investment of data, by selecting only those that are most informative. To demonstrate its potential, the algorithm is applied to a version of the hyperbolic partial differential equation. A key aspect of this proposal is its ability to be adapted to any physics-informed neural network, making it a promising tool for many other PDE-based applications in the future. To accommodate datasets that cannot be employed due to competition, or where results must be predictive and not explanatory, a modified approach is described, which still yields comparable uncertainty estimates at a significant reduction in required training data. Ultimately, both algorithms are referred to collectively as the certified machine learning approach, a term that is also used to describe the actual mistake probability calculation in the test phase, in addition to its associated generator of potential test data points, the pre-assessment neural network. Both components necessarily coexist in a sequential relationship, as the algorithm is applied in a iterative manner until the maximum allowable mistake probability is reached. A future perspective reveals how this certified approach can be employed in a Bayesian framework, similar to a forward model uncertainty assessment method, where one can define a manageable mistake probability and iteratively apply the algorithm until the desired level of uncertainty is achieved. Importantly, also from a theoretical point of view, it becomes evident how this certified approach can be employed as a regularization strategy, as it implicitly enforces a penalty that is proportional to the selected mistake probability. A particular notable case is when no data are available, as the algorithm is then reduced to a purely theoretical concept, where one can evaluate the network's accuracy without any actual data, as an extrapolation of what could have been the return for continued data collection, or what could have been the return for improving the network's architecture

Deep learning techniques are widely employed in graph-related applications such as graph classification and link prediction tasks. However, the field remains in its early stages with little research on the impact of data contamination, a common issue in real-world observations. In this paper, we introduce an autoencoder-based method that applies reinforcement learning to counteract data contamination in graph networks. Our contamination model is designed to specifically target graph data, causing existing deep learning models to significantly decline in performance. Our reinforcement learning-based method can effectively counteract this performance decline by learning the most important nodes for preserving vital network structure information, even in scenarios where only 10% of the data is marked as trustworthy. Furthermore, we reveal that using trustworthy node attributes rather than nodes leads to the introduction of latent contamination, causing existing models to struggle in distinguishing between vital and redundant information. Our method not only mitigates data contamination performance losses but also sheds light on the underlying mechanisms of deep learning models operating on graph data. Our research is supported by extensive experiments using various graph data types. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally defined concept relationships called ontologies. In subjects like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visualization of these complex structures is crucial for their maintenance. However, existing methods mainly focus on hierarchical structures, leading to poor representation of additional associations between distant concepts. To address this limitation, we introduce OntoPlot, a novel visual encoding that concisely communicates the connections between related concepts across multiple ontology graph facets. OntoPlot is capable of highlighting both hierarchical and long-range associations, enabling quick identification of key characteristics and related information. We evaluated its performance through a case study and found it to be applicable in real-world domain ontology management scenarios. Furthermore, a formal usability test demonstrated OntoPlot's efficacy in effectively communicating domain-specific knowledge to non-experts. Through a controlled user study Involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot to the widely used GraphView and TabView interfaces, finding that OntoPlot facilitates faster location of important associations and overall system performance. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to tackle the challenge of limited, domain-specific training data in end-to-end automatic speech recognition. By utilizing Inter-domain loss, we correct ASR's inherent speech-to-text bias, forcing alignments between speech and text representations across different domains. To address domain-related distortions in speech spectrogram and text representations, we propose a cycle-consistency training method, enhancing generalization with CycleGAN's unsupervised approach. Experimenting with the Librispeech corpus, we assess the effectiveness of our proposed method in both supervised and semi-supervised scenarios. Notably, our method achieves a mean word error rate of 8.53 and 11.25 for 100h and 960h datasets, respectively, demonstrating improved performance with reduced training data. Notably, with a diverse, open-source dataset, our method enhances speech recognition by correcting biases and adapting to different environments. Moreover, using a single, generic transcription, we achieve notable word error rate reductions in a semi-supervised scenario. This research opens up new possibilities for improving end-to-end ASR models, particularly those trained on non-standard text resources like social media data or transcripts with informal language. A novel method is introduced that leverages the dynamic interactions between robots and environment, by incorporating a novel active prediction technique based on GAN, to enhance navigation through uncharted territories using motion forecasting. Active navigation approaches often rely on a balance between exploring GAN-generated predictions and confining robot movements within a safely accessible area. Current active learning methods are inherently restrictive, focusing on mapping environment uncertainties to robot motions, thus limiting the robot's ability to adapt to unknown environmental risks. By distinguishing between the robot's physical space and the GAN-generated prediction space, our proposed framework optimally allocates sampling weight between exploring environment uncertainties and ensuring physical safety. We present a simple yet effective sampling strategy utilizing the GAN's prediction distribution, enhancing its ability to simulate risky behaviors. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets reveal our approach surpasses existing baselines both in GAN-based prediction accuracy and robust safety guarantees. Importantly, our proposed method achieves over 35% higher GAN-based prediction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models, even when the robot is confined to a limited physical space. Videos demonstrating our approach can be found at: https://sites.google.com/view/dapnav. Furthermore, all implementation details are available at: https://github.com/jhjCoder/dap-nova. Our theoretical study of binary mixtures composed of Gaussian chain molecules reveals that the Soret effect has varying sensitivity to the internal degrees of freedom of flexible molecules depending on the temperature and molecular structure. This flexibility influence on the Soret effect is significantly more pronounced in molecules with a more complex shape. Additionally, we found that the Soret coefficient is more susceptible to changes in temperature when accounting for the internal degrees of freedom of the molecules. This temperature dependence is similar to the scenario where the molecules have rigid, two-dimensional shapes. However, unique to flexible molecules is the presence of a minimum in the derivative of thermal diffusion velocity with respect to temperature that occurs at the same temperature at which the Soret coefficient reaches its minimum value. This distinct temperature behavior of the Soret effect for flexible molecules is attributed to the compromise between the influence of molecular structure and flexibility on thermal diffusion at different molecular dimensions. Ultimately, we found that the internal degrees of freedom of molecules can produce Soret effect behavior that mimics the thermal diffusion characteristics of anisotropic solid particles. This finding presents an innovative approach to creating "liquid solids" or "solid liquids" states that are characterized by a stable liquid structure despite being prone to thermal diffusion. This phenomenon has the potential to be experimentally realized in systems with rod-like molecules that have weak intermolecular interactions and are influenced by an external uniaxial force. Potential applications of this discovery include the development of heat-sensitive materials that can undergo phase transitions in response to temperature changes. The proliferation of data annotation methods utilizing human intelligence is hindered by efficiency concerns, as manually composing responses to prompts can be a significant time commitment. To address this issue, researchers are now employing machine-assisted methods that leverage pre-trained language models to generate high-quality annotations. As these systems become increasingly reliable, they are poised to significantly impact a range of applications, including the development of sophisticated computational assessment tools for language-based skills and the creation of informative and effectivesummarizations. In this study, we explore the potential of the CEMBTR-NN model, which combines a BERT-based language model with a neural network, to automate the assessment of written essays. By framing essay assessment as a machine comprehension task, we investigate whether a machine-assisted system can complement human instructors by accurately Comprehending Essential information from essays, identifying Targeted areas of improvement, and Refining responses to provide tailored feedback. In the context of the Italian exam, we observe that our CEMBTR-NN model surpasses a straightforward transformer-based approach, which relies solely on leveraging the pre-trained knowledge without incorporating any explicit regularization, leading to improved computational efficiency with minimal accuracy loss. Furthermore, our findings highlight that incorporating external knowledge can be beneficial but may ultimately result in system degradation if not properly managed. The next-generation CEMBTR-NN models, which accelerate training by approximately 50%, emerge as the most effective solutions for this application, along with other CEMBTR variants. To facilitate the development of more robust and efficient annotation systems, we release a dataset of natural-language prompts, as well as publicly licensing the source code to enhance standard transformer-based language models. Ultimately, our study demonstrates the potential of machines to augment human writing assessment tools, making the process more efficient and informative. In particular, our CEMBTR-NN approach increases the speed of Comprehension by approximately 3 times and enhances the overall evaluation metric by up to 7% in comparison to the conventional BERT-based solution. Furthermore, our study reveals that these gains can be achieved while reducing the total training time by up to two orders of magnitude by adapting the data augmentation strategy known as GraphAlign, which leverages the structural relationships between sentences in the essay. Consequently, our next research goal is to systematically integrate the GraphAlign method to its full extent within the training pipeline, thereby ensuring its seamless application for training efficient annotation systems. The source code for our study is publicly available at https://github.com/constantinilives/CEMBR-NN.

To improve the performance of pedestrian detectors in various domains, a relatively unexplored approach involves reducing the number of false positives after classification. A proposed method called Box Re-Ranking (BRR) uses unsupervised learning to eliminate false positives by leveraging positive-box similarities. BRR uses an adapted version of the instance similarity index (ISI) to create a distribution of instance similarities that is then used in a ranking process to eliminate false positives. Experiments conducted on three datasets - Citypersons, Citypersons with Domain Randomization, and CVPP - showed that BRR reduces false positives by 50.64%, 44.11%, and 42.11% respectively, outperforming other mitigation strategies. Additionally, a fully autonomous PANDA system that integrates domain adaptation and false positive mitigation has been developed, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Citypersons and Citypersons with Domain Randomization datasets. Furthermore, the system has also surpassed a strong baseline with a false positive rate reduction of 40.16% on the CVPP dataset. Importantly, the system does not require any labeled data and is thus well-suited for applications in autonomous vehicles. A public implementation of the BRR approach can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/asharakeh/Box-Re-Ranking, making it easily accessible for use. For the CVPP dataset, the code is available at https://github.com/autopp/cvpp. A related video demonstration can also be found at https://youtu.be/c4YtCt8o6GQ. A confidential project extension involving online adaptation is available at https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.07023.2023.

This research proposes an innovative method for generating music by transforming acoustic images into music through the combination of image translation and artifical vocoding, allowing for the exploration of new modes of creative potentiality. To facilitate this process, a large dataset called MagentaSDR was created, comprising 21,202 recordings of electronic music alongside corresponding spectral images, making it possible to develop counterfactual music models that can generate new music styles by transforming original spectral images. Furthermore, a series of five style-guided GANs were trained on this dataset to translate spectral images into various electronic music formats, demonstrating the ability to generate new music based on specific genres and sub-genres. Moreover, a vocoder module was implemented to generate high-quality audio from the music representations, revealing the existence of multiple creative pathways for artistic music generation. Finally, listening experiments were conducted to evaluate the generated music in terms of its quality, creativity, and authenticity. The results show that human evaluators preferred the outputs of multiple GANs and found that the combination of image translation and vocoding produced more innovative and engaging audio content. To facilitate replication, the MagentaSDR dataset and implementation details are publicly available on https://github.com/FrancescoGulino/MagentaSDR. This research aims to contribute to the understanding of multi-modal conditional GANs and their applications in identifying various forms of creative potentiality within complex datasets. Ultimately, it seeks to propel the development of more sophisticated artifical intelligence-powered art practices. To demonstrate its practical utility, this research presents multiple creative productions that are showcased on https://magnasdr.coderf.com. These examples highlight the potential of this artifical intelligence model to enhance human creativity, both as a tool for generating novel concepts during the creative process and as a way to produce intricate compositions independently. Ultimately, they illustrate how the boundaries between human and artificial creativity are increasingly becoming intertwined. To facilitate replication, the MagentaSDR dataset and implementation details are publicly available on https://github.com/FrancescoGulino/MagentaSDR. A presentation of this research, titled "Exploring Creative Potentiality with MagentaSDR: A Dataset and Implementation for Music Generation", was initially presented at the Audio Engineering Society Convention 2023 in San Antonio. Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. To achieve this, we create a novel technique to artificially manipulate digital ball paths according to a desired (fake) point of release, as opposed to adhering to physical laws. Through this approach, we can precisely control the uncertainty in viewers' judgments regarding the throwing point (the moment the ball leaves the thrower's hand) and their overall perception of a throwing motion. By applying the forced-choice technique and using both qualitative and quantitative analyses, we discover that viewers make varying assumptions about the throwing point, particularly when the virtual ball's Path Length (the distance between the thrower's hand and the ball's Position over Time) and Time of Release are simultaneously modified. Our findings indicate that changes in Path Length have more significant effects on viewers' judgments than changes in Time of Release. Moreover, we find that alterations in Path Length above a certain threshold affect viewers' overall perception of a throwing motion. Our study also highlights key characteristics of genuine throwing motions, which might be utilized in future AI-generated throwing animations that require increased realism. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of manipulating digital ball paths as a technique to gain insight into human perceptions of throwing motions. By understanding what makes a throwing motion believable, we can improve the authenticity of realistic animations. The primary goal of this article is to examine the properties of a specific type of multiplicative stochastic process, namely those that establish a minimum lower bound for each individual sample path, and to explore the implications of this lower bound on the behavior of the process. We demonstrate that this type of multiplicative stochastic process, which is influenced by a standard Brownian motion and confined to a positive domain, exhibits certain characteristic features such as moment growth, divergence in certain moments, and a sample-dependent lower bound that can be calculated analytically. Furthermore, in the context of stochastic differential equations, we demonstrate that the presence of a lower bound can facilitate the convergence of samples and also impact their growth rate. Our study also examines the practical applications of these findings, including the optimization of the maximum sample value and the calculation of the lower tail of the sample maximum. Additionally, as a specific example, we investigate how well a multiplicative stochastic process, such as the Yule-Hardy process in our study, can capture the characteristics of a specific type of distribution, namely the beta distribution. Ultimately, the work presented here provides valuable insights into the behavior of a specific type of multiplicative stochastic process, namely those that generate sample-dependent lower bounds, and also has the potential to expand our understanding of the sample-dependent dynamics in general. There is currently a gap in the understanding of how depth affects the feasibility of simulating general single-qubit evolution within the dynamic quantum simulation framework. This note aims to bridge this gap by proposing a new protocol for quantum simulation called QSA, which achieves correctness with any given confidence level. This is accomplished by employing random Clifford circuits of moderate depth applied both before and after a mysterious, unknown evolution process over a specific set of initial states. This result indicates that shallow circuits are capable of accurately simulating general single-qubit dynamics. This finding has significant implications for the concept of shallow depth as a viable approach to quantum computation. Furthermore, it challenges the previously held perspective that quantum phase-correctability is solely a consequence of being able to accurately simulate the evolution process over extensive periods of time. Instead, our work suggests that it may be primarily the ability to easily generate numerous states associated with the circuit's initial state that contributes to correctness. This insight could potentially inspire innovative forms of quantum computation. Lastly, our analysis also compares the QSA protocol to another notable protocol for quantum simulation, QA. While both protocols are comparable in terms of efficiency, they have distinct methodologies. One of the key benefits of QSA, in contrast to QA, is its capacity to produce a probability distribution over states rather than a single outcome, along with the ability to easily measure the associated expectation values. This capability is essential for numerous quantum simulation tasks. Moreover, our work highlights a potential issue with the QSA protocol's efficiency, which is predicated on the assumption that low-depth circuits have negligible interaction effects between different qubits. This assumption may not be necessarily accurate, and it could potentially compromise the QSA protocol's feasibility. Researchers are encouraged to explore this possibility. Overall, our analysis confirms that quantum computation can be performed using shallow circuits that fail the quantum Fisher information test. This finding is in contrast to another notable computation task that requires high quantum accuracy. This dichotomy could potentially inspire further comprehension of the complex relationship between quantum information theory and computation. The DSII equation is known for its role in modeling weakly nonlinear, strongly dispersive deep water wave scenarios. Despite this, the linearization of the equation yields unexpected behavior where the reflection coefficient exhibits a substantial response at low wave numbers, which contradicts typical expectations of oscillatory behavior. In this study, we provide a asymptotic solution for the dispersionless limit of the DSII equation. Unlike the Korteweg-de Vries equation, this solution reveals a unique feature where the reflection coefficient shows a significant response at low wave numbers with a magnitude proportional to the wave number. Our findings are further validated by a numerical analysis for small but non-zero dispersions. In addition, our results also provide new insights into the behavior of Euler-Poincaré-Archimedean system, which is known to be a geometrically motivated Hamiltonian PDE system. Our study provides the first step in understanding the behavior of DSII equation and Euler-Poincaré-Archimedean system by providing a systematic analysis of their integrability properties especially in the context of continuous integrability of these systems. Although the problem of continuous integrability for PDE systems is an open question in the field of partial differential equations, we are able to obtain a continuous version of the bi-Hamiltonian structure of DSII equation in this study. What is more, we are able to prove the complete integrability of Euler-Poincaré-Archimedean system via a direct extension of the integrality property from its continuous form to its discrete form using a novel method that combines Lie symmetries and square-integrability of the resonant tensor. Ultimately, our study provides key steps in understanding the complete integrality of DSII equation, which involves the proof of square-integrability of the resonant tensor via a novel method that combines homogenization and renormalization, a discovery which has the potential to be applied to a wide range of nonlinear wave equations. These methods not only provide a link between the integrability of DSII equation and Euler-Poincaré-Archimedean system but also provide a bridge between the continuous and discrete integrability of these systems. Language models used for text classification tasks are often vulnerable to subtle textual manipulations that can exploit their underlying structures, such as the shifting of context windows, that do not necessarily affect their overall performance. To address this limitation, we investigate the robustness of Sibyl variants, a type of language model, by subjecting them to various intentional mutations (such as token replacement, spelling errors, typographical errors, and context window adjustments) to observe their impact on classification performance in multiple categories. Our results experiment with different types of target words (based on part-of-speech and semantic meaning) to assess the model's susceptibility to specific word types. Our research reveals that Sibyl variants exhibit improved robustness with intentional mutations in multiple language scenarios. Our findings emphasize the need for evaluating the robustness of language models using a comprehensive and diverse set of mutation methods. The code for our research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AllureLatte/SibylRobustness. The information on the baseline models and our research data can be found at https://allurelatte.github.com/SibylRobustness/. For more information, please visit the research website at https://allurelatte.github.com/SibylRobustness/. 

More specifically, our research assesses the performance of Sibyl variants under 48 distinct mutation methods and multiple target word types (6 part-of-speech types and 160 specific words) across 9 text classification datasets. Our results experiment with both original (without context shifting) and extended context sets (with context shifting) to evaluate the model's performance for specific target words.

The research introduces new evaluation methods to thoroughly assess the robustness of Sibyl variants. Specifically, our research conducts an extensive analysis of the model's performance for various intentional mutations and an in-depth investigation of the impact of context shifting on the model's performance. 

Our research further reveals that Sibyl variants exhibit improved robustness for certain part-of-speech types (such as adjective and noun) but decreased robustness for other types (such as verbs). 

Based on our research findings, we present a number of recommendations and potential improvements for future research, such as developing mutation-based testing frameworks, improving the model's performance for low-frequency words, and exploring the use of external knowledge to enhance the model's robustness. 

Our research aims to contribute to the development of reliable and trustworthy NLP models by providing a set of intentional mutations to evaluate the model's performance and promote the development of more robust language models

In the field of reinforcement learning, utilizing multi-task learning has been proven beneficial. Both the underlying state representations and the learning algorithms used can be adapted across multiple tasks, though existing methods often require prior knowledge of the tasks involved. We propose a novel approach to state representation learning, allowing it to be based on general principles rather than prior knowledge. This method is empirical in nature and is directly applicable to a wide range of reinforcement learning scenarios. We show through experimentation that our method consistently produces effective state representations that can also be leveraged for meta-learning applications, while a thorough analysis explains its underlying effectiveness. We 'compress' a German-English model using two techniques: translation-based compression and knowledge compression, and compare their effectiveness in reducing model size while maintaining translation accuracy. The integration of AI in medical imaging has become typical due to the unique skills it offers for image analysis. In particular, the technique known as U-Net has yielded significant results in the automatic segmentation of medical images. In this research, we examine the application of U-Net for automatically segmenting pneumonia-affected areas on chest X-rays. Different from standard U-Net models, which rely on large labelled datasets through supervised learning, we investigate whether data augmentation can be employed to reduce the required number of labelled data. Various image augmentation methods were applied and their effects on model performance were tested using four distinct datasets with different sizes and quality. The experiments revealed that using specific combinations of augmentation techniques can achieve comparable results with existing state-of-the-art methods, even when training the model with a reduced labelled dataset of 10% compared to the full dataset. Additionally, this study identifies the key factors that influence model performance and provides suggestions for future research in this area. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that U--augmentations are an effective tool for adjusting the model's bias and achieving domain adaptation on limited datasets of high-quality images. However, more work is required to develop U-augmentations that can handle datasets of varying qualities. The proposed approach using U-augmentations has the potential to widen the application of automatic image analysis to diverse fields and domains, ultimately increasing patient safety and wellbeing. In another investigation, researchers explored, through a causal analysis, how news recommendations influence changes in a user's political opinion, only to find that the AI may cause harm if the user's opinion is changed and if this change led to decreased adherence to factual information. In one such example, an AI that assigns a user to a particular political group based on their browsing history may do so in a non-discriminatory manner, yet still cause fairness if the user is assigned to that group. Ultimately, by examining the relationship between definitions of harm and causal concepts, researchers were able to identify ways AI developers can incorporate definitions of harm, including incorporating the AI's capacity to cause harm, its distribution, and the unavoidable nature of harm into its training objectives. Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite previous successes with other types of lesions. Most existing techniques rely on strongly annotated data, which is scarce for COVID-19. Recently, weakly supervised learning approaches have gained attention, but they are not entirely effective due to annotation quality issues and the model's inherent biases. To overcome these problems, we introduce WinCELP, a framework that combines weakly supervised learning and post-hoc enhancement. By initially using weakly annotated data to identify general infection areas, it refines its predictions using intact images and annotated healthy lung areas. Our experiments using two datasets reveal that WinCELP yields significantly better lesion detection and segmentation outcomes compared to alternative techniques, alongside improved model generalizability and resilience to annotation errors. Additionally, qualitative assessments demonstrate that WinCELP produces more accurate and complete predictions for previously unannotated scans. To facilitate future research, we make our framework publicly available.

Our research explores the electron scattering phenomenon when it collides with a photon in a confined space.  We've discovered that this interaction has the potential to stabilize the electron orbit for an extended period by utilizing the quantum fluctuations of the vacuum.  This stabilization arises due to a balance between the electron's potential and the quantum field's contribution, essentially at the point where the rotation symmetry is restored.  We propose that this theoretical approach can be experimentally supported by analyzing the energy shifts in core excitons of transition metal dichalcogenides following a rapid change in the surrounding electromagnetic field.  Furthermore, our study provides a framework for understanding and utilizing light-matter interactions in novel applications.  To validate our theoretical predictions, we suggest studying the  K  edge in monolayer MoS$_2$ using scanning tunneling spectroscopy after exciting it with a short pulse of light.  We've found that there would be an observable time window in which the vacuum fluctuations induce a significant stabilization effect, lasting for a short period that varies depending on the energy, but it would likely be on the order of 1-200 femtoseconds.  This would provide an unprecedented level of electron stabilization that deviates significantly from the traditional predictions in the continuum model.  To confirm our theoretical predictions for this extremely short timescale, we plan to conduct ultrafast electron scattering experiments using advanced time-resolved spectroscopy techniques that allow us to monitor the transient changes in the electron distribution over very short periods.  We've initially demonstrated that this theoretical approach has a significant impact on the transient changes in the electron distribution in the initial 100 femtoseconds after the collision, with the stabilization effect being apparent for  a period of time that varies between 10-180 CO.  This result confirms our initial hypothesis and we are now planning to expand our research to examine the time-evolution of the vacuum field in the vicinity of atoms and the impact of initial conditions in the electron orbit.  To achieve this, we propose to conduct comprehensive numerical simulations in order to investigate the temporal evolution of the vacuum field and its impact on the transient changes in the electron distribution in different periods of time.  This research project has the potential to significantly deviate from the traditional predictions in the electron scattering phenomenon and we are now working on developing innovative experimental techniques that allow us to observe and study this interaction in the extremely short timescale. Determining depth in light field images is a complex problem, particularly in situations where there are abrupt cuts and areas of missing information. Existing approaches that rely on matching pixels in different views often struggle with estimation accuracy, especially in areas with occlusions or sudden changes. By contrast, pixel-to-pixel matching methods typically yield better results, but they are often computationally expensive and can be unsuitable for real-time applications. Our proposed solution involves developing an occlusion-aware cost builder to enhance the efficiency of pixel-to-pixel matching methods. Our method involves incorporating an occlusion-sensitive cost metric, learned using a fully convolutional neural network, to prioritize valid correspondences. By reducing the influence of irrelevant correspondences, even better estimation results can be achieved. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art techniques by achieving improved performance on well-established benchmarks for light field depth estimation. Additional details are also provided in the paper. Once the necessary data is collected, our method's performance will be further assessed using four additional datasets for the tasks of estimating depth in 360-degree images, estimating continuous depth in fourfold light field, joint estimation of depth and motion, and rendering depth in virtual scenes. Our code has been made available for public access on the GitHub platform. Despite our method's effectiveness, there are still areas for improvement, particularly in estimating extreme areas and validating local maxima. Our approach still overestimates depth values in areas of sudden changes. To address these limitations, an alternating regularization scheme is developed, combining the centrosymmetric radial distance with total variation regularization. Our approach demonstrates the ability to simultaneously estimate depth and motion in light field sequences. Our results reveal a balance between exaggerating depth values in areas of sudden changes and failing to detect true correspondences. Our approach provides a starting point for future research on solving the light field factorization problem in a holistic manner. Our results also highlight the importance of incorporating the geometric properties of light field images in estimating depth and motion. Our code has been released on the GitHub platform and will be updated with additional results. Once the necessary data is collected, our approach will be assessed using an explicit stereo matching method as the baseline. Our results will be compared with state-of-the-art techniques on various depth estimation tasks. Our code has been made available for public access.

Varying supergraviity actions, which have a conformal form and include a term proportional to the Ricci square, can be seen as equivalent to certain non-Minkowskian metric variations of the standard Einstein-Hilbert action. However, such actions give rise to equations that involve derivatives of the metric, making them non-universal and lead to issues such as non-conservation of energy-momentum and angular momentum. We propose a coTFT-based approach that avoids these problems, which involves modifying the Einstein-Hilbert term by adding probes and higher-derivative terms based on a specific covariant operator. When this modified term is coupled with other standard matter Lagrangians, we get a consistent, universal, and conserved energy-momentum tensor. Moreover, the term proportional to the Ricci square can be obtained by restricting ourselves to Riemannian variations of the metric. We derive the corresponding equations and apply our results to two solutions, which involve non-standard and 3D metrics respectively. We also solve the algebra for the superconformal case, which involves a specific set of probes and can be applied to yield the most general supergraviity actions, which have a conformal form in 3D and 4D spacetimes. We conclude by adapting our results to actions that involve volume moduli and yielding the graviphoton's Chern-Simons term. A related appendix is included to clarify the connection between the Einstein-Hilbert term and the action for massless states in four-dimensional SYM theories. Moreover, the energy-momentum tensor for the varrying supergraviity actions is obtained in geodesic method in any dimension, which reveals the possibility of making these actions universal and conserved by redefining the metric, which has a particular form in 4D and 3D spacetimes. We also identify an alternative solution to the non-Riemannian variety in 4D, which involves modifying the metric by a specific function, as well as an exact solution, which involves a non-trivial 3D torus fibre. In a widely used IEEE 802.11 home WiFi network, performance issues due to interference are a significant problem. The presence of these problems is especially prevalent when many devices are connected. A key issue is that within a home network, various WiFi access points may not be optimally configured, resulting in overlapping coverage areas and performance degradation when other networks are interfered with. Furthermore, the placement of secondary extender devices can also exacerbate the problem when they're used. However, a relatively new standard allows for the optimization of WiFi configuration. A proposed solution uses this standard to periodically scan and optimize WiFi configuration by temporarily deactivating primary access points and shifting coverage to secondary extenders when necessary. Moreover, the solution uses feedback mechanisms to address potential issues that may arise during the process. As a result, the solution enables seamless and high-performance WiFi connectivity across multiple access points and devices.
